Every file shown with a path above it is in examples/manual/, exactly as printed, and was built or applied on the versions in the front matter. Each chapter's folder has a VERIFY.md with the commands that were run and what came back, including the symptom of every trap. Shell examples were run in the shell lab, and every tagged behaviour also on macOS. Their scripts pass shellcheck. Docker examples use host port 8000 and up. The Kubernetes examples run on kind, a few of them on a three-node cluster (examples/manual/kind-multinode.yaml) so that spreading, draining and storage behave the way they do on a real cluster.

The map

The Shell manual (needs nothing)

  1. The Ground Floor: terminal, shell and kernel; files, paths and help
  2. Every Command Is a Process: arguments, environment, file descriptors and exit status
  3. How the Shell Reads a Line: the expansion order that explains every quoting bug
  4. Variables and Quoting: single, double and $'…' quotes; parameter expansion
  5. Exit Status and Tests: if runs a command; [, [[ and ((
  6. Redirection and Pipes: file descriptors, 2>&1, here-docs, process substitution
  7. Loops, Globs and Lines: for, while read, globs and reading files safely
  8. Functions and Arrays: scope, return values, "$@", indexed and associative arrays
  9. Processes and Signals: subshells, background jobs, trap, exec
  10. Finding Things: grep, find and xargs: searching text and files, safely with odd names
  11. sed: addresses, substitution, in-place editing
  12. awk: fields, patterns, one-liners and reports
  13. The Pipeline Toolkit: sort, uniq, cut, tr and friends, plus jq and curl
  14. Writing a Script: strict mode and its holes, options, cleanup, logging, shellcheck, tests
  15. Portability: every difference between bash, sh, GNU, BSD and BusyBox, in one place
  16. Reading Any Script: a method for decoding someone else's script, line by line

The Docker manual

  1. Every Instruction: what each Dockerfile line does, and the ones to avoid
  2. ENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1: how your process starts, and why it does not stop
  3. Context and Cache: fast builds, small contexts, BuildKit mounts
  4. Multi-Stage Builds: one file for dev, test and prod; choosing a base
  5. Users and Permissions: non-root, numeric UIDs, read-only filesystems, capabilities
  6. Supply Chain and Secrets: pinning, build secrets, multi-platform, SBOMs and scanning
  7. Networks: bridges, DNS, publishing ports safely, internal networks
  8. Volumes: named, bind and tmpfs mounts, ownership, backups
  9. Compose: The File: services, environment, health-gated startup
  10. Compose: The Project: overrides, profiles, includes, secrets, watch, limits

The Kubernetes manual

  1. Reading Any Manifest: anatomy, labels, explain, dry runs and server-side apply
  2. The Pod Spec: command and args, env sources, init containers, native sidecars
  3. Security Context: non-root, read-only, capabilities, seccomp, Pod Security Standards
  4. Lifecycle and Rollouts: probes done right, graceful shutdown, rollout strategy, disruption budgets
  5. Resources and Placement: requests, limits, QoS, affinity, taints, topology spread
  6. Config and Secrets: env versus files, reloads, projected volumes, what Secrets do not protect
  7. Storage: emptyDir, claims and classes, access modes, StatefulSets
  8. Networking: Service types, headless Services, Gateway API, NetworkPolicy
  9. Identity and Access: ServiceAccounts, tokens, least-privilege RBAC
  10. Packaging: Helm and Kustomize: charts worth reusing, overlays, when to pick which
  11. Debugging: the triage order, ephemeral containers, DNS and policy problems

The Bridge maps every Docker concept from the first manual to the Kubernetes field or object that replaces it, and says what changes in meaning on the way.

Shell manual · 1 · 13 min readThe Ground Floor#

You've met it: the very first command in this book, docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7, typed at a prompt and run by a shell · It Works On My Machine

You have typed commands into a terminal before: this book is full of them. This chapter is about the thing you typed them into. It starts from nothing: what a terminal is, what a shell is, how to move around files, how to read permissions, where help lives, and which keys save you hours. Everything later in this manual assumes it.

To follow along, open a terminal. On macOS that is Terminal (or iTerm, or the one in your editor). On Linux it is whatever your desktop calls Terminal. Then open the shell lab, so that what you see matches the book exactly:

cd examples/manual/shell-lab
./lab.sh

You get a prompt like learner@lab:/w$. That is bash 5, inside a container, with your current directory mounted at /w. exit (or Ctrl-D) takes you back.

The model

Four layers sit between your fingers and the work being done.

The terminal (also called a terminal emulator) is only a window. It draws characters, and it sends what you type somewhere. It does not understand commands.

The shell is a program that the terminal starts for you. It prints a prompt, reads one line, works out what you meant, and asks the kernel to run it. When that finishes, it prints the prompt again. Bash, zsh, dash and BusyBox sh are all shells. They agree on the basics and disagree on details. Those details are why this manual has portability tags.

The kernel is the operating system's core. It starts and stops programs (called processes while they run), and it owns the files.

Programs like ls, git and docker are files on disk. The shell finds them, and the kernel runs them. A few commands, such as cd, are not programs at all. They are built into the shell, and chapter 2 explains why.

Keep this picture. When something goes wrong, the first question is always which layer did it. A garbled screen is the terminal. A line that means something different from what you typed is the shell. "Permission denied" is the kernel.

The ladder

Rung 1 Which shell am I in?

The terminal starts whichever shell your account is set to use. On macOS since 10.15 (2019) that is zsh, not bash. On most Linux systems it is bash. Inside a container it is often BusyBox sh or dash. Ask before you trust an example:

$ echo "$0"
bash
$ echo "$BASH_VERSION"
5.2.37(1)-release
$ ps -p $$
    PID TTY          TIME CMD
      8 pts/0    00:00:00 bash

$0 is the name the shell was started as, $$ is its process ID, and $BASH_VERSION is set only in bash. On a Mac, a new Terminal window answers -zsh (the leading - means a login shell). Type bash to start bash inside it, and exit to return. That bash is /bin/bash, version 3.2.57 from 2007. Apple stopped updating it at the last release under the GPLv2 licence, so bash 4 and 5 features are missing from it. This manual tags those features bash 4+ and bash 5+. Everything else here works in it.

Rule Before you run an example, check which shell you are in (echo "$0"), and use bash, or the lab, for this manual.

Why The same line of text can mean different things in different shells. A shell does not tell you it is a different one. It just does something else.

Trap In zsh, an unquoted variable holding a b stays one word, while bash splits it into two (chapter 3). So x="a b"; for w in $x; do echo "[$w]"; done prints [a b] in zsh and [a] then [b] in bash. Arrays start at 1 in zsh and at 0 in bash. If an example here gives a different answer on your Mac, check echo "$0" first.

Rung 2 Paths: where you are, and how to say where something is

Files live in one tree. The top is / (called "root"). Every file has an absolute path from there, such as /Users/you/projects/pantry/app.py. The shell also has a current directory (also called working directory), and a relative path starts from it.

$ pwd                       # print working directory
/w
$ cd /etc                   # absolute: starts with /
$ cd ..                     # .. is the parent directory
$ pwd
/
$ cd ~                      # ~ is your home directory; plain `cd` goes there too
$ cd projects/pantry        # relative: from where you are now
$ cd -                      # back to the previous directory, and print it
/home/learner
$ ls ./app.py ../pantry     # . is the current directory itself

Press Tab while typing a path, and the shell completes it. Press it twice and the shell lists the candidates. This is the most useful key you will learn, because it also catches typos before you press Enter.

Rule Use Tab to type paths. In scripts, build paths from something you know (an absolute path, or the script's own directory), not from wherever the user happens to be standing.

Why A relative path means something different in every directory. The shell resolves it against the current directory at the moment the command runs.

Trap ~ is replaced only when it is unquoted, at the start of a word. cd "~/projects" fails with No such file or directory, because the shell passed the two characters ~/ through unchanged. Write cd ~/projects or cd "$HOME/projects".

Rung 3 Looking: ls, cat, less, head, tail, file

$ ls -la
total 20
drwxr-xr-x 3 learner learner 4096 Oct 24 08:56 .
drwx------ 1 learner learner 4096 Oct 24 08:56 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 learner learner   17 Oct 24 08:56 .env
-rwxr-xr-x 1 learner learner   35 Oct 24 08:56 deploy.sh
drwxr-xr-x 3 learner learner 4096 Oct 24 08:56 src

-l gives the long format and -a shows names starting with . (hidden files, also called dotfiles). The columns are:

Column Example Meaning
type + permissions -rwxr-xr-x - file, d directory, l symbolic link; then the permission bits (rung 5)
links 1 how many names point at this file; rarely matters
owner, group learner learner who owns it
size 35 bytes (ls -lh prints 4.0K, 1.2M)
date Oct 24 08:56 last modified; files older than six months show the year instead of the time
name deploy.sh

Then, to read files:

cat .env                 # print a whole (small) file
less app.log             # page through a big one: Space, b, /word to search, n for next, q to quit
head -n 20 app.log       # first 20 lines
tail -n 20 app.log       # last 20 lines
tail -f app.log          # keep printing new lines as they arrive; Ctrl-C to stop
file deploy.sh logo.png  # what kind of content is this? "Bourne-Again shell script", "PNG image data"
wc -l app.log            # count lines

Rule Use ls -la to see what is really in a directory, less for anything longer than a screen, and file before you cat something you do not recognise.

Why ls without -a hides configuration files (.env, .git, .bashrc). cat writes raw bytes to the terminal, and a binary file can contain bytes that the terminal treats as commands.

Trap The size column of a directory is the size of its list of names, not of what is inside. A directory holding a 100 KB file shows 4096 in ls -ld on Linux (96 on a Mac), and so does an empty one. Use du -sh dir for the space it really uses (104K). (If cat on a binary leaves your terminal printing garbage, type reset and press Enter, even if you cannot see what you type.)

Rung 4 Changing things: mkdir, touch, cp, mv, ln, rm

mkdir -p projects/pantry/logs   # make a directory, and any missing parents (-p: no error if it exists)
touch notes.txt                 # create an empty file, or update the date of an existing one
cp notes.txt notes.bak          # copy a file
cp -r src backup                # copy a directory and everything in it (-r: recursive)
mv notes.txt docs/              # move into a directory
mv draft.md final.md            # a rename is a move
ln -s /opt/tool/bin/tool ~/bin/tool   # symbolic link: a name that points at another path (target first, like cp)
rm notes.bak                    # delete a file
rm -r backup                    # delete a directory and everything in it
rm -- -weird-name               # -- means "no more options": for names that start with a dash

There is no undo and no trash can at the command line. rm asks the kernel to remove the name, and the space is reused.

Rule Before an rm -r, run ls on exactly the same path first, and look at what it lists.

Why Commands do exactly what the text says, immediately. Because Tab completion and the history (rung 6) make it easy to reuse a line, the ls costs you one keystroke and the mistake costs you the files.

Trap cp -r src dest does two different things depending on whether dest already exists. If it does not, you get a copy called dest. If it does, you get dest/src. Run the same line twice and the second run nests a copy inside the first. The same is true of mv with directories.

Rung 5 Permissions, and why you type ./

-rwxr-xr--  1 learner staff  35 Oct 24 08:56 deploy.sh
 └┬┘└┬┘└┬┘
  │  │  └── others: r--   read only
  │  └───── group:  r-x   read and run
  └──────── owner:  rwx   read, write and run

Each of three groups of people (the owner, the file's group, everyone else) gets three bits: read, write and execute (run). On a directory, r means list the names, w means create and delete names inside it, and x means enter it or pass through it.

chmod +x deploy.sh        # let everyone run it
chmod u+x,go-w deploy.sh  # owner may run; group and others may not write
chmod 755 deploy.sh       # the same bits as numbers: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 6 = rw-
chmod 600 secrets.env     # owner reads and writes, nobody else anything

To run a program, the shell looks for it in the directories listed in PATH (chapter 2). The current directory is not in that list, on purpose: otherwise a file named ls left in a shared directory would run instead of the real one. So to run a script that is right here, you name its path, ./deploy.sh.

Rule Make scripts executable with chmod +x, run them as ./name (or by their full path), and give secrets mode 600.

Why The kernel refuses to run a file without the x bit, and the shell looks for bare names only in PATH.

Trap The two failures look alike and are not. ./deploy.sh without the x bit gives Permission denied with exit status 126. deploy.sh without ./ gives command not found with status 127. Chapter 2 explains the numbers. Reaching for chmod 777 "to fix permissions" fixes neither, and it also lets everyone on the machine edit your script.

Rung 6 Help, and the keys that save hours

Every command documents itself, in one of three places:

man ls               # the manual page: Space and b to page, /word to search, n for the next hit, q to quit
man 1 printf         # section 1 = commands; man 3 printf is the C library function of the same name
ls --help            # GNU tools print a summary [GNU]; macOS ls rejects --help [BSD]
help cd              # bash's own builtins have no man page of their own: use help
type cd ls ll        # what is this name? a builtin, a program at a path, an alias, a function

And the keyboard. These work in bash and zsh:

Keys Does
Tab, Tab Tab complete a command or path, or list the choices
↑ / ↓ previous / next command from history
Ctrl-R search history backwards: type part of a command, Ctrl-R again for older matches, Enter to run, Ctrl-G to cancel
Ctrl-C interrupt the running program (send it SIGINT, chapter 9)
Ctrl-D end of input. At an empty prompt, it exits the shell
Ctrl-Z suspend the running program. fg brings it back, bg lets it continue in the background
Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E jump to the start / end of the line
Ctrl-W / Ctrl-U delete the previous word / everything before the cursor
Ctrl-L clear the screen (the command clear does the same)
Alt-. (Esc then .) insert the last argument of the previous command

Rule Reach for type, man and help before a search engine, and learn Tab, Ctrl-R and Ctrl-C before anything else on this list.

Why The local documentation describes the exact version installed, and on a Mac that is often not the version an online answer was written for.

Trap Ctrl-S looks like it does nothing, and then the terminal stops responding to everything. It is the old "pause output" signal (XOFF) from serial terminals. Ctrl-Q (XON) resumes. Run stty -ixon in your startup file if you never want it.

Rung 7 Dotfiles: what bash reads when it starts

Bash reads startup files from your home directory, which is how you keep settings between sessions. Which file it reads depends on how it was started:

How bash started Example Reads
login shell a new macOS Terminal window, ssh host, bash -l /etc/profile, then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile
interactive, not login a new tab in most Linux terminals, typing bash ~/.bashrc
not interactive running a script, bash -c '…' nothing (only the file named in $BASH_ENV, if set)

The usual arrangement is to put everything in ~/.bashrc, and make ~/.bash_profile a single line that reads it. Then every interactive bash gets the same settings:

# ~/.bash_profile: the whole file
[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc

source ~/.bashrc     # after editing: load the changes into the shell you are in (or open a new terminal)
echo "$-"            # the shell's option letters; an i in there means interactive
shopt login_shell    # on or off

Rule Keep settings in ~/.bashrc, have ~/.bash_profile source it, and write ~/.bashrc so that sourcing it twice changes nothing.

Why Files that read each other, plus source ~/.bashrc after each edit, mean your startup file runs many times in one session.

Trap export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" in ~/.bashrc adds another copy of ~/bin every time the file is read. After a few source ~/.bashrcs, echo "$PATH" is long and repetitive, and a lookup that fails searches every copy. The golden file adds the directory only if it is missing.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

Older tutorials, colleagues' dotfiles and inherited servers use some habits that predate the tools above. You should recognise them, and you should not copy them:

# from an inherited ~/.profile, around 2010
alias ls='ls -G'
which python || echo "no python"
\rm -f core
pushd /var/log; tail messages; popd
sudo !!
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
which cmd prints the path of the program cmd an external program from csh days that predates type. It looks only at PATH type cmd (interactive), command -v cmd (scripts) yes, but it ignores builtins, aliases and functions, and its output differs by system
\rm, command rm runs rm, ignoring any alias called rm a backslash, or command, stops alias expansion, which mattered when systems aliased rm to rm -i do not alias rm in the first place yes
alias ls='ls -G' colour on BSD and macOS ls -G is BSD's flag; on GNU ls, -G means "no group column" ls --color=auto, which GNU and current macOS both accept yes, with different meanings
pushd dir … popd a stack of directories: go there, then come back before cd -, and still useful several levels deep cd dir … cd -, or a subshell ( cd dir && … ) (chapter 9) yes bash
!!, !$, ^old^new, sudo !! history expansion: the last command, its last word, the last command with old replaced, the last command under sudo csh's history syntax, kept by bash for interactive use ↑, Alt-., Ctrl-R interactively only. Scripts have history expansion off
.profile holding bash settings the file every Bourne-family shell reads at login before bash, sh read only .profile .bash_profile sourcing .bashrc yes, but bash skips it when .bash_profile exists

Rule Recognise these when you read them. In your own files and scripts, use type/command -v, --color=auto and cd -.

Why They come from csh, the Bourne shell and BSD, and survive in copied dotfiles and answers written before the modern forms were everywhere.

Trap which gives confident wrong answers. On macOS, which cd prints /usr/bin/cd (a small wrapper script exists so other programs can run "cd"), but your shell's cd is the builtin, as type cd says. On Debian, which cd prints nothing at all and fails. Neither tells you about an alias or function that would really run. And inside a script, type ll says not found even when ll is an alias in your terminal, because scripts do not expand aliases. Use type when you are curious, and command -v in scripts.

The golden file

A minimal ~/.bashrc that is safe to source any number of times, works on Linux and macOS, and does nothing in non-interactive shells. Try it in the lab without touching your own:

cd examples/manual/b01
../shell-lab/lab.sh run bash --rcfile /w/bashrc -i   # an interactive bash using only this file; exit to leave

On your Mac, bash --rcfile bashrc -i does the same with /bin/bash. To adopt it, copy it to ~/.bashrc and create the one-line ~/.bash_profile from the comment at the top.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A colleague shares their ~/.bashrc. They say it "works fine", and they have used it for years.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. set -e makes the shell exit when any command fails. In a startup file, that is your terminal. The first mistyped command or failing grep closes the window. In the lab, false ended the shell with status 1 before the next command ran (rung 7: nothing in a startup file may make the shell exit).
  2. . at the front of PATH means that a program in the current directory beats the real one. In a directory containing a script called ls, typing ls printed not the real ls (rung 5).
  3. PATH is extended every time the file is sourced, with no check that the directories are already there. Each source ~/.bashrc adds more duplicates (rung 7). Use the case ":$PATH:" guard from the golden file.
  4. alias rm='rm -rf' deletes directories without a question and silences the error for a missing file, so a typo in a path is never reported. Everywhere else (a server, a colleague's machine, a script) rm behaves normally, so the habit the alias builds is wrong (rung 4, rung 8).
  5. Nothing stops the file at non-interactive shells. The echo and the cd run for scp, rsync and ssh host cmd as well. The extra output breaks file-transfer protocols, which expect a silent shell (rsync reports protocol version mismatch -- is your shell clean?). The cd silently moves every remote command, and fails wherever ~/projects does not exist. Return early unless $- contains i, as the golden file does.

Shell manual · 2 · 12 min readEvery Command Is a Process#

You've met it: CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "--workers", "2", "app:app"], a program and its argument list written out by hand, with no shell in between · ENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1

Almost everything that confuses people about the shell becomes simple once you know what a running program actually receives from it and gives back. That exchange is small and fixed, and it is the same for every program on Linux and macOS, from ls to docker to your own script. This chapter is about that exchange. The next chapter is about how the shell builds it from the line you typed.

The model

When the shell runs a command, the kernel starts a new process: a running copy of a program. That process gets exactly four things, and gives back exactly two.

  • argv (argument vector) is a list of strings. The first is the program's name, and the rest are its arguments. It is a list. The program never sees your line of text, your quotes or your spaces. It sees the list the shell built from them.
  • The environment is a set of NAME=value strings, copied from the parent.
  • The working directory is where relative paths start, also copied from the parent.
  • File descriptors (fds) 0, 1 and 2 are the program's input, normal output and error output. By default all three are your terminal.
  • The exit status is one number from 0 to 255. Zero means success, and anything else means some kind of failure.
  • And whatever the program wrote to fd 1 and fd 2.

Nothing else passes between them. A child process cannot reach back into its parent and change the parent's variables or directory. That one fact explains rungs 5 and 6.

The shell's whole job is to turn your line into an argv list, set up the environment, directory and fds, start the process, and collect its status. Everything in the rest of this manual is a detail of one of those steps.

The probe used throughout this manual makes the list visible:

$ ./args.sh one "two words" '' '$HOME'
argc: 4
argv[1]: <one>
argv[2]: <two words>
argv[3]: <>
argv[4]: <$HOME>
cwd: /w
fd 0: terminal
fd 1: terminal
fd 2: terminal

Four arguments. The quotes are gone, "two words" is one argument, the empty '' is an argument too, and the single quotes kept $HOME from being replaced. args.sh is this chapter's golden file.

The ladder

Rung 1 A command is a program plus a list of arguments

The shell splits your line into words at unquoted spaces and tabs. The first word names the program, and the others become its arguments. Quotes tell the shell where an argument starts and stops, and are then removed.

$ echo Hello,    world
Hello, world
$ echo "Hello,    world"
Hello,    world

In the first line, echo got two arguments, Hello, and world, and printed them with one space between, which is what echo does. The four spaces were never given to it. In the second line it got one argument containing the four spaces.

Rule Think of every command as a list of strings, and use quotes to say exactly where each string begins and ends.

Why Programs receive the list, not the line. The shell's quoting decides the list, and the program cannot recover anything the shell threw away.

Trap Spaces you meant to keep disappear without an error. echo Total: 5 prints Total: 5, and a file name with two spaces in it turns into two arguments that name files that do not exist. Run the line with ./args.sh in place of the command to see the list the program would get.

Rung 2 Where programs come from: PATH

When the first word has no / in it, the shell looks it up in this order:

  1. an alias (interactive shells only)
  2. a function you defined (chapter 8)
  3. a builtin, a command implemented inside the shell itself (cd, echo, export, type)
  4. a program file, searched for in each directory listed in PATH, left to right
$ echo "$PATH"
/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
$ type -a echo             # every match, in lookup order
echo is a shell builtin
echo is /usr/bin/echo
echo is /bin/echo
$ command -v jq            # the one that would run, or nothing and status 1 (use this in scripts)
/usr/bin/jq
$ /usr/bin/echo hi         # a word with a / skips the lookup entirely
hi

Rule Use type -a name to see what a name means and what it hides, and command -v name in scripts to check that a program exists before relying on it.

Why The same name can be an alias, a function, a builtin and two different programs all at once. The first match in lookup order is the one that runs, whatever the other matches do.

Trap Bash remembers where it found each program (it hashes the path), so it does not search again. If a new copy of a tool appears earlier in PATH, the shell keeps running the old one: type tool says tool is hashed (/tmp/b/tool). hash -r forgets the remembered paths. So does opening a new shell, or assigning PATH again.

Rung 3 Exit status: the only thing a program returns

$ ls /etc/hosts
/etc/hosts
$ echo $?                  # $? is the status of the last command
0
$ grep zzz /etc/hosts; echo $?
1
$ grep zzz /nope; echo $?
grep: /nope: No such file or directory
2
Status Means
0 success
1 general failure. For grep it means "no match", which is an answer, not an error
2 wrong usage, or a program-specific error (grep uses it for a real error)
126 found, but could not be run (no x bit, or not a program)
127 not found
128 + n killed by signal n: 130 is Ctrl-C (SIGINT, 2), 137 is SIGKILL (9), 143 is SIGTERM (15) (chapter 9)

A status is one byte. exit 256 becomes 0, and exit 300 becomes 44 (300 − 256).

Rule Read $? immediately, or better, test the command itself (if grep -q …, chapter 5). Read the program's manual for what its non-zero statuses mean.

Why Every command sets $?, including echo, [ and assignments with a command substitution. The value you wanted is replaced as soon as anything else runs.

Trap false; echo "message"; echo "status: $?" prints status: 0. That is the status of the echo, not of the command you cared about. Scripts that log a line between a command and its check report success for every failure.

Rung 4 Three streams: stdin, stdout, stderr

Every process starts with three open files: 0 stdin (input), 1 stdout (normal output) and 2 stderr (errors and diagnostics). At a prompt, all three are your terminal, so output and errors look like one stream. They are not.

$ ls /etc/hosts /nope > out.txt
ls: /nope: No such file or directory
$ cat out.txt
/etc/hosts

> out.txt redirected only fd 1 into the file. The error went to fd 2, which is still the terminal. A pipe | does the same: it connects only stdout to the next program's stdin. Chapter 6 is all about moving these around.

Rule Write normal output (data that another program might read) to stdout, and messages for a human (progress, warnings, errors) to stderr: echo "warning: …" >&2.

Why Someone redirecting or piping your output wants the data and nothing else, and they still need to see the errors.

Trap find / -name app.log > results.txt still floods the terminal with Permission denied lines, while the file holds only the matches. People "fix" this by redirecting both into one file and then parse error messages as results. Keep them apart (2>/dev/null to discard errors, chapter 6).

Rung 5 The environment, and why children never change parents

The shell has its own variables. Only exported variables are copied into the environment of the programs it starts.

$ DEBUG=1
$ bash -c 'echo "child sees DEBUG=[$DEBUG]"'
child sees DEBUG=[]
$ export DEBUG
$ bash -c 'echo "child sees DEBUG=[$DEBUG]"'
child sees DEBUG=[1]
$ X=7 bash -c 'echo "X=[$X]"'        # NAME=value before a command: exported to that command only
X=[7]
$ echo "after: X=[$X]"
after: X=[]

env lists the whole environment, and printenv NAME prints one variable.

Each child gets a copy. Whatever the child does with its copy (changes it, exports more, unsets things) disappears when it exits.

Rule export a variable when programs you start must see it. Use the NAME=value command prefix to set something for one command only.

Why A plain assignment creates a shell variable, which lives only in this shell. Export marks it to be copied into the environment of every child started afterwards.

Trap You set DEBUG=1, run your script, and it behaves as if you had not, because the variable was never exported. The reverse also bites: a script that runs export PATH=… does not change your terminal's PATH, because the script was a child.

Rung 6 The working directory, cd, and running vs sourcing a script

cd changes the current directory of the process that runs it. If cd were a program, it would change its own directory and exit, and your shell would not move. That is why cd is a builtin, and why a script cannot move you either:

$ cat m.sh
cd /
export GREETING=hi
$ cd /tmp
$ ./m.sh;  echo "ran: $PWD [$GREETING]"
ran: /tmp []
$ . ./m.sh; echo "sourced: $PWD [$GREETING]"
sourced: / [hi]

./m.sh started a new bash process to run the file. . ./m.sh (or source ./m.sh bash) read the file's lines into the current shell, as if you had typed them.

Rule Run scripts as programs (./name). Source a file (. file) only when its purpose is to change the current shell: startup files, a venv/bin/activate, a file of settings.

Why Running gives the script its own copy of everything, so it cannot damage your shell. Sourcing gives it your shell itself, including the power to change directory, set variables, or exit your terminal.

Trap A "setup" script that ends with cd ~/project and export ENV=dev reports success and changes nothing for you. The opposite trap is sourcing a script that calls exit: your terminal closes.

Rung 7 The first line, and the execute bit

#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "hello from $BASH_VERSION"

./hello.sh asks the kernel to run the file. The kernel sees that it starts with #! (called a shebang), runs the program named on that line, and passes it the script's path. So the line chooses the interpreter, whatever shell you typed the command in. #!/usr/bin/env bash runs the first bash in PATH. #!/bin/bash runs exactly /bin/bash (bash 3.2 on a Mac, even when you have installed a newer one).

How you run it Who interprets it Needs x bit Changes your shell
./x.sh the shebang's interpreter yes no
bash x.sh bash, whatever the shebang says no no
sh x.sh sh: dash on Debian/Ubuntu, BusyBox in Alpine, bash in POSIX mode on macOS no no
. x.sh, source x.sh the shell you are in no yes

Rule Start every bash script with #!/usr/bin/env bash, make it executable, run it as ./name, and never run a bash script with sh.

Why The shebang is the only thing that pins the interpreter. sh x.sh silently swaps bash for whatever sh is on that machine. On Debian, [[ then fails with [[: not found, and the if around it simply takes the else branch, with status 0.

Trap A script saved with Windows line endings (CRLF) fails with env: 'bash\r': No such file or directory and status 127, even though the file is right there and executable. The kernel read bash followed by a carriage return as the interpreter's name. Convert with sed -i 's/\r$//' x.sh GNU (on macOS: sed -i '' 's/\r$//' x.sh BSD), and set your editor to LF.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# deploy.sh, 2009: "works on our servers"
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin; export PATH
. ./config.sh
hash -r
if [[ -n "$TAG" ]]; then
  ./release "$TAG"
fi
exit $((errors + 0))
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
#!/bin/sh on a script that uses bash features asks for "sh" on many Linux systems /bin/sh was bash, until Ubuntu 6.10 (2006) and Debian 6.0 (2011) switched it to dash for speed #!/usr/bin/env bash macOS yes (its sh is bash), Debian/Ubuntu/Alpine no: [[: not found
VAR=x; export VAR assign, then export the original Bourne shell could not export and assign in one command export VAR=x yes
. ./file source a file . is the POSIX spelling; source came from csh . in portable code, either in bash yes; source is bash
hash -r forget remembered program paths needed after installing tools mid-script rarely needed: assigning PATH already clears the table yes
#!/usr/bin/env bash -e tries to pass -e to bash works on macOS, which splits shebang arguments set -e on the next line, or #!/usr/bin/env -S bash -e (-S added in GNU coreutils 8.30, 2018) macOS yes BSD; Linux no: env: 'bash -e': No such file or directory
exit $errors with a count uses the status as a counter quick way to report "how many failed" exit 1 if any failed, and print the count yes, but 256 errors exit 0

Rule In old scripts, read #!/bin/sh as a question to check ("does this use bash features?"), not as a fact.

Why For years /bin/sh was bash on most Linux machines, so #!/bin/sh scripts full of bash features worked everywhere their authors tried them.

Trap The same script works on your Mac and fails in the Alpine or Debian container, or on the CI runner. The failure is often silent: if [[ … ]] prints [[: not found and takes the else branch, and the script carries on. Shellcheck flags bash features under #!/bin/sh (SC3010 and friends). Run it on anything you inherit.

Decide

You want Run it as
a tool that does a job and exits ./tool.sh (shebang, chmod +x)
to run a script that is not executable, or to force bash bash tool.sh
to change your current shell: settings, cd, activate an environment . ./settings.sh
to check that a script is POSIX sh dash tool.sh or lab.sh sh tool.sh, not sh on a Mac

The golden file

The probe used throughout this manual. Put it on your PATH (or call it by path), and run it in place of any command whose arguments puzzle you.

cd examples/manual/b02
./args.sh one "two words" '' '$HOME' *.sh      # what would the program get?
./args.sh x > out.txt                           # fd 1 is now a file; the fd report stays on screen
ARGS_EXIT=3 ./args.sh; echo $?                  # 3

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A colleague wrote this to "get a terminal ready for Pantry". They run it as ./setup-dev.sh, it prints ready, and then nothing works.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. It is run as a program, so its cd and its variables die with it. After ready: now in /home/learner/projects/pantry, the terminal was still in /tmp with PANTRY_ENV empty (rung 6). Something meant to change your shell has to be sourced (. ./setup-dev.sh), or it should just print what to type.
  2. PANTRY_ENV=dev is not exported, so even when sourced, the programs started afterwards (the Pantry server, tests) do not see it (rung 5). Use export PANTRY_ENV=dev.
  3. #!/bin/sh with [[ … ]]. On Debian, sh is dash, which printed [[: not found. The if took its else branch, and using .env never appeared. On a Mac it works, so the author never saw this (rungs 7 and 8).
  4. The if [ $? -ne 0 ] tests the status of echo "creating virtualenv", not of python3. With python3 failing on purpose, the script still printed ready and exited 0 (rung 3). Test the command itself: if ! python3 -m venv .venv; then ….
  5. cd ~/projects/pantry is not checked. When the directory is missing, the script continues wherever it was started and creates .venv there (it printed ready: now in /tmp). Use cd ~/projects/pantry || exit 1 (chapter 5).

Shell manual · 3 · 11 min readHow the Shell Reads a Line#

You've met it: for pod in $(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods -o name); do in the triage script, which works only because the shell splits that command's output into words · Debugging

Chapter 2 showed what a program receives: a list of strings. This chapter shows how bash turns the line you typed into that list. It always takes the same steps in the same order. Once you know them, you can predict what any line does before you run it, and almost every "the shell did something weird" moment turns out to be one of these steps doing exactly what it always does.

The model

Three things about this pipeline explain most surprises:

  • The order is fixed. Brace expansion happens before variables are expanded, so {1..$n} cannot work. Tilde expansion happens before variables too, so a ~ that comes out of a variable stays a ~.
  • Steps 5 and 6 are the dangerous ones (red). They act only on text that came out of an expansion in step 4 (or, for globs, any unquoted pattern), and only where that text was not inside double quotes. That is why "quote your variables" is the most repeated advice in shell scripting: double quotes switch off steps 5 and 6.
  • Results are never re-read as shell syntax. When $x expands to "a b" or {1,2} or ~ or $HOME, those characters are just characters. The quotes in the value do not group, the braces do not expand, the $ does not expand. Only splitting and globbing touch the result.

Here is the line in the diagram, with src='my docs', traced by putting args.sh (chapter 2) in front of it. Here and from now on, its cwd and fd lines are left out:

$ src='my docs'
$ args.sh cp $src/*.txt "$dest"
argc: 4
argv[1]: <cp>
argv[2]: <my>
argv[3]: <docs/*.txt>
argv[4]: </tmp>

Step 4 produced my docs/*.txt. Step 5 split it at the space into my and docs/*.txt, because $src was unquoted. Step 6 tried docs/*.txt as a pattern. There is no docs directory here, so it matched nothing and was left as it was. cp would be asked to copy a file called my and a file called docs/*.txt. "$src"/*.txt gives one word, and the glob then runs on my docs/*.txt.

The ladder

Rung 1 Words, operators, comments and line breaks

The shell first cuts the line into words at unquoted spaces, tabs and newlines, and picks out operators, the characters with their own meaning: | & ; ( ) < >, and their combinations (&&, ||, >>, 2>&1). A # at the start of a word begins a comment that runs to the end of the line.

echo a#b                    # prints a#b: the # is inside a word
echo a #b                   # prints a: the # starts a word, so it is a comment
cd /tmp; ls                 # ; ends a command, like a newline does
docker run --rm \
  -e MODE=dev \
  pantry:dev                # a backslash right before the newline joins the lines

Rule End a continued line with a backslash as its very last character, and break long commands one option per line.

Why \ escapes the next character. Before a newline, the escaped newline disappears and the lines join. Before anything else, it escapes that character instead.

Trap A space after the backslash (invisible in most editors) escapes the space, not the newline. The command ends there, and the next line runs as a separate command: -e: command not found, or in a script, a step that silently loses half its options. cat -A file GNU (cat -e on macOS BSD) shows \ $ where the line should end in \$.

Rung 2 Quotes decide what is one word

Quoting Inside it Example Becomes
none everything is special echo $HOME/*.txt expanded, split, globbed
'single' nothing is special, not even \ '$HOME and *' exactly that text
"double" only $, ` and \ are special "$HOME and *" /home/you and *, one word
\x the next character only \$HOME, my\ file $HOME, my file 
echo 'Total: $5 * 2'                # Total: $5 * 2
echo "Saved to $HOME/out"           # Saved to /home/learner/out
echo "Price: \$5, \"quoted\""      # Price: $5, "quoted"
touch my\ file.txt                  # one file, named "my file.txt"

Pieces next to each other with no space form one word, whatever their quoting: "$dir"'/it'"'"'s here' is the single word /tmp/it's here.

Rule Use single quotes for fixed text, double quotes around anything containing $, and nothing unquoted unless you want splitting and globbing.

Why Quotes are instructions to the shell about word boundaries and expansion. Step 7 removes them, so the program never sees them.

Trap A single quote cannot appear inside single quotes, not even escaped. echo 'it's here' leaves a quote open, so the shell keeps reading. At a prompt you get a > and it waits for more. In a script you get unexpected EOF while looking for matching ''', reported at the end of the file, far from the real mistake. Write "it's here", or 'it'\''s here'.

Rung 3 Expansion results are data, not syntax

Steps 2 to 4 run in a fixed order, and what they produce is never parsed again for quotes, braces, tildes or $:

$ x='*.sh'; args.sh $x "$x"
argv[1]: <sizes.sh>
argv[2]: <*.sh>
$ b='{1,2}'; args.sh $b
argv[1]: <{1,2}>
$ t='~'; args.sh $t ~
argv[1]: <~>
argv[2]: </home/learner>

The unquoted $x was globbed (step 6 runs on results). The braces and the tilde in variables were left alone (steps 2 and 3 had already happened).

Rule Never store shell syntax (quotes, braces, ~, $) in a variable and expect it to act when the variable is expanded. To keep a list of arguments, use an array (chapter 8).

Why Expansion results only go through splitting and globbing. Re-reading them as code would mean any data containing a quote or $ could change what your script does.

Trap opts='--name "my app"'; docker run $opts pantry passes three arguments, --name, "my and app", with the quote characters inside them. Docker rejects the name, or worse, accepts a container literally called "my. Use opts=(--name "my app") and "${opts[@]}" (chapter 8).

Rung 4 Word splitting: why every expansion gets double quotes

After step 4, every unquoted expansion result is split into words wherever it contains a character from IFS (the Internal Field Separator, by default space, tab and newline). Runs of whitespace count as one separator, leading and trailing whitespace disappears, and a result that is empty disappears completely.

$ y='  a   b  '
$ args.sh $y
argc: 2
argv[1]: <a>
argv[2]: <b>
$ args.sh "$y"
argc: 1
argv[1]: <  a   b  >

Rule Put double quotes around every expansion ("$var", "$(cmd)", "${arr[@]}"). Leave one unquoted only when you want it split, and then say so in a comment.

Why Splitting and globbing apply only to unquoted results, so quoting is how you tell the shell that this value is one piece of data. A file name, a message or a path can contain spaces, tabs, * or nothing at all.

Trap An empty variable does not become an empty argument. It becomes no argument. With x='', [ $x = yes ] is run as [ = yes ] and fails with [: =: unary operator expected (status 2). rm -rf $dir/* with dir empty becomes rm -rf /*. "$x" keeps an empty value as one empty argument.

Rung 5 Globbing: patterns the shell matches against file names

Pattern Matches
* any run of characters, including none, but not a leading . and never /
? exactly one character
[abc], [a-z], [!0-9] one character from the set, a range, or not in the set ([^…] also works in bash)

The shell expands the pattern into the sorted list of matching names before the command runs. ls *.txt does not ask ls to search; ls just receives the names. Names starting with . match only a pattern that starts with ..

for f in *.log; do                  # each matching name, as one word, spaces and all
  gzip -- "$f"
done
ls -d .[!.]*                        # dotfiles: the pattern has to start with a dot
cp -- "$dir"/*.txt /tmp             # quote the variable part, leave the * outside the quotes

Globs are not regular expressions. In a glob, . is a dot, * stands alone, and [1-10] is a set of the characters 1 and 0, not the numbers one to ten.

Rule Loop and act on globs directly (for f in *.log), never on the output of ls. In bash scripts, turn on shopt -s nullglob bash so that a pattern with no match produces nothing.

Why The glob gives you every name as exactly one word, whatever it contains. ls output is text meant for people, and the shell splits it again at every space.

Trap By default, a pattern that matches nothing is passed on unchanged. rm *.tmp in a directory with no .tmp files runs rm on a file literally named *.tmp (cannot remove '*.tmp'). for f in *.log runs once, with f set to *.log. nullglob makes it run zero times. failglob bash makes it an error that aborts the command. zsh reports no matches found and refuses to run the command at all. That is one more reason to test bash scripts in bash.

Rung 6 Brace expansion is not globbing

$ echo {a,b,c}.txt          # always generates the words, whether or not files exist
a.txt b.txt c.txt
$ echo {1..5}
1 2 3 4 5
$ mkdir -p app/{src,test,docs}
$ cp config.yaml{,.bak}     # config.yaml config.yaml.bak: a quick backup

Brace expansion bash is step 2, a text generator. It does not look at the disk. POSIX sh (dash, BusyBox) does not have it at all and prints {a,b,c}.txt unchanged. Zero-padded ranges like {01..10} need bash 4 bash 4+. bash 3.2 prints 1 2 3 … without the padding.

Rule Use braces to type less (mkdir -p a/{b,c}, cp f{,.bak}), and use seq or a C-style loop (chapter 7) when the range comes from a variable.

Why Braces expand at step 2, before variables exist in the line (step 4).

Trap n=3; for i in {1..$n} loops once, with i set to the literal {1..3}. There is no error. Use for ((i = 1; i <= n; i++)) bash or for i in $(seq 1 "$n").

Rung 7 Seeing what the shell did

$ set -x                         # trace: print each command after expansion, before running it
$ cp "$src"/*.txt /tmp
+ cp 'my docs/a.txt' 'my docs/b.txt' /tmp
$ set +x                         # trace off
$ printf '%q\n' "$f"             # show a value in a form you could paste back into the shell [bash]
my\ file.txt
$ declare -p f                   # show a variable's exact value and type [bash]
declare -- f="my file.txt"
$ PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}: '   # make the trace show file and line

bash -x script.sh traces a whole script without editing it. In the trace, bash adds quotes so that you can see where each word starts and ends. Those quotes are for display only.

Rule When a line does not do what you expect, trace it (set -x or bash -x) or put args.sh in front of it, before changing anything.

Why The trace shows the argv after every step of the pipeline, which is exactly what the program received.

Trap The trace prints everything, expanded, to stderr, and that includes secrets. set -x followed by curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" writes + curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer s3cr3t' into your CI log for anyone to read. Turn tracing off (set +x) around lines that handle secrets, or do not trace in CI.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# 1990s-style argument handling
OLDIFS=$IFS
IFS=,
set -- $LIST
IFS=$OLDIFS
set -f; pattern=$1; set +f
name=$(echo $2)                       # "trim" the whitespace
eval "value=\$$3"                     # the variable whose name is in $3
exec "$TOOL" ${1+"$@"}
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
OLDIFS=$IFS; IFS=,; …; IFS=$OLDIFS split on commas, then restore no arrays and no read -a in the Bourne shell IFS=, read -r a b c <<< "$line" bash, or set IFS only in a function with local IFS yes, but if IFS was unset, "restoring" it sets it to empty, which turns word splitting off for the rest of the script
set -f … set +f turn globbing off and on to split a value without * in it expanding quote the expansion yes
x=$(echo $y) squeeze runs of whitespace, trim the ends splitting plus echo as a cheap trim parameter expansion (chapter 4) yes, but it also globs (* becomes file names) and mangles -n or -e
eval "v=\$$name" read the variable whose name is in $name no indirect expansion in the Bourne shell ${!name} bash yes, and it runs any code inside $name (see Trap)
${1+"$@"} "all arguments" the V7 Bourne shell turned an empty "$@" into one empty argument "$@" yes, harmless. macOS ships it in /usr/bin/cd today

Rule When you meet eval, an IFS save and restore, or ${1+"$@"}, read it as a workaround for something old, and replace it with the modern form when you own the script.

Why Each existed because the Bourne shell lacked arrays, indirect expansion, read -a or a correct "$@". Autoconf's manual still documents ${1+"$@"} for shells from the 1980s.

Trap eval runs its argument as shell code, data included. With name='HOME; touch /tmp/pwned', eval "val=\$$name" reads $HOME and creates /tmp/pwned. Replace the touch with anything at all, and a variable name from a file, a URL or an argument becomes a way to run commands on your machine. Never eval data you did not write.

The golden file

Sizes of every file matching some patterns, correct for spaces in names, leading dashes, directories and patterns that match nothing. It expands the globs itself, with splitting turned off:

cd examples/manual/b03
./sizes.sh '*.sh' '../b02/*.sh' '*.nope'; echo "status $?"   # the last pattern is reported, status 1

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It is run as ./archive-logs.sh "my logs" 2 by a nightly job. The job is always green.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. $dir is unquoted everywhere. With my logs, mkdir -p $dir/old created ./my and ./logs/old, the ls and mv worked on the wrong paths, and the real logs were never touched. The job still printed archived to my logs/old (rung 4).
  2. {1..$keep} does not expand, because braces come before variables. The script printed keeping *.log.{1..2} (rung 6). Use for ((n = 1; n <= keep; n++)).
  3. for f in $(ls …) splits the listing at spaces. web server.log.4 became …/web and server.log.4, and mv failed on both (rung 5). Loop over the glob itself: for f in "$dir"/*.log.*.
  4. With nothing to archive, the glob was passed through unchanged, and ls printed cannot access '/tmp/empty/*.log.*'. Turn on nullglob, or skip names that do not exist (rung 5).
  5. [1-$keep] is a glob character set, not a number range. With keep=10 it became [1-10], the characters 1 and 0, so app.log.5 was archived even though the newest ten should stay (rung 5). Compare numbers with arithmetic (chapter 5) after extracting the suffix with ${f##*.} (chapter 4).

Shell manual · 4 · 10 min readVariables and Quoting#

You've met it: : "${REDIS_HOST:?REDIS_HOST must be set}" at the top of Pantry's entrypoint, one line that checks a setting and stops with a clear message · ENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1

Shell variables hold strings, and almost everything you do with them happens at step 4 of chapter 3's pipeline: parameter expansion. Bash has a small language inside ${…} for defaults, required values, trimming paths, replacing text and changing case, all without starting another program. This chapter covers that language, command substitution and arithmetic, and the quoting that keeps the results intact.

The ladder

Rung 1 Assigning and reading

name=pantry                 # no spaces around =
greeting="hello, $name"     # quotes needed only because of the comma and space
count=3
echo "$name"                # read: $name
echo "${name}_backup"       # braces mark where the name ends
unset count                 # remove the variable
readonly VERSION=1.4.2      # cannot be changed or unset afterwards

Names are letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit. They are case-sensitive. By convention, environment variables and constants are UPPER_CASE and a script's own variables are lower_case, so they cannot accidentally clash with PATH, HOME or USER.

Rule Write name=value with no spaces, and use ${name} whenever the next character could be part of a name.

Why x = 1 is not an assignment. It runs a command called x with the arguments = and 1 (x: command not found, status 127). And the shell reads a name greedily: everything that can be part of a name, is.

Trap echo "$file_backup" reads a variable called file_backup, which does not exist, so it prints an empty line without an error. You meant "${file}_backup". (Chapter 14's set -u turns this into an error.) Also, assigning to a readonly variable in a script does not just fail: it ends the whole script.

Rung 2 Which quotes, and why printf beats echo

Write When
'single' fixed text, especially containing $, *, \ or !
"double" text with variables or command substitutions inside
$'ansi-c' bash text containing escape sequences: $'line1\nline2', $'a\tb', $'it\'s'

To print, use printf. Its first argument is a format, in which %s is replaced by the next argument as a string, %d by an integer, and \n is a newline:

printf '%s\n' "$message"                 # exactly the message, then a newline
printf '%-10s %5d\n' "$name" "$count"    # left-aligned in 10 columns, right-aligned in 5
printf 'Saved %d files to %s\n' 3 "$dir"

Rule Use echo only for fixed text. Use printf '%s\n' "$var" for anything that contains a variable.

Why printf behaves the same in every shell. Never put a variable in the format itself (printf "$msg"): a % in the data would be read as a format code.

Trap echo is not the same command everywhere. echo 'a\tb' prints a\tb in bash and a tab in dash. echo -e 'y\tz' prints -e y z in dash, -e included. And a variable that happens to be -n or -e is taken as an option and disappears. Output that looks right on your Mac comes out different in a Debian container.

Rung 3 Defaults, and values that must be set

Expansion If x is unset or empty If x has a value
${x:-default} gives default gives $x
${x:=default} assigns default to x, then gives it gives $x
${x:?message} prints message and exits (in a script) gives $x
${x:+other} gives nothing gives other

Without the colon (${x-default} and so on), only unset counts. A variable that is set to the empty string keeps its empty value. A common idiom applies defaults without running anything, using the do-nothing command ::

: "${PORT:=8080}"                         # set PORT to 8080 unless it already has a value
: "${API_TOKEN:?API_TOKEN must be set}"   # stop here with a clear message
curl ${VERBOSE:+-v} "$URL"                # add -v only when VERBOSE is non-empty (unquoted on purpose)

Rule Use the colon forms (:-, :=, :?) unless you really mean "set to empty is different from not set".

Why Empty values come from everywhere: a .env line PORT=, a CI variable that exists but has no value, export X= in a profile. Almost always, empty should mean "use the default".

Trap PORT= in a .env file, then ${PORT-8080}, gives an empty port, and the server fails to start, or listens on a random one. ${PORT:-8080} gives 8080. The exit status of a failed :? also differs between shells (1 in bash 5, 2 in dash and BusyBox, 127 from bash 3.2 in a subshell), so test for non-zero, not for a number.

Rung 4 Cutting strings: prefixes, suffixes and length

# removes from the front and % from the end. One character removes the shortest match, and two remove the longest. The pattern is a glob (chapter 3), not a regular expression.

f=/srv/v1.2/archive.tar.gz
${f##*/}      # archive.tar.gz            everything up to the last /   (like basename)
${f%/*}       # /srv/v1.2                 from the last / to the end    (like dirname)
${f%.*}       # /srv/v1.2/archive.tar     the last extension
${f#*/}       # srv/v1.2/archive.tar.gz   up to the first /
${#f}         # 24                        the length

To remember which is which: on a US keyboard, # is left of $ and % is right of it.

Rule Take a path apart with ##*/ (the name) and %/* (the directory), and remove one extension with %.*, after first cutting off the directory.

Why These run inside the shell, with no extra process, and they work on any string, including names with spaces. They exist in every POSIX shell.

Trap %%.* removes from the first dot, wherever it is. ${f%%.*} on /srv/v1.2/archive.tar.gz gives /srv/v1, because the directory name has a dot in it. On a name with no directory, report.final.csv loses final.csv, not just .csv. And ${b%.*} on .bashrc is empty. Cut the directory off first (base=${f##*/}), then work on base.

Rung 5 Replacing, slicing and changing case

x=hello-world
${x/o/0}        # hell0-world      first match replaced          [bash]
${x//o/0}       # hell0-w0rld      every match                   [bash]
${x/#hello/bye} # bye-world        only at the start (% for the end)  [bash]
${x:0:5}        # hello            5 characters from offset 0    [bash]
${x: -5}        # world            the last 5 (note the space)   [bash]
${x^^}          # HELLO-WORLD      upper case                    [bash 4+]
${x,,}          # hello-world      lower case                    [bash 4+]

Dash rejects all of these with Bad substitution. BusyBox accepts most of them, but its /# did not anchor in testing. ${x^^} and ${x,,} are bash 4. On macOS's /bin/bash they fail with bad substitution. The portable way to change case is tr: printf '%s' "$x" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'.

Rule Use these freely in bash scripts. For case changes in a script that must run on a stock Mac, use tr.

Why Each saves a sed or cut process and a pipe, and handles any characters. The bash 4 case operators are the ones most often missing in practice, because macOS still ships bash 3.2.

Trap ${x:-5} and ${x: -5} differ only by a space. The first is "default to 5" (rung 3), so on a non-empty x it returns all of x. The second is "the last five characters". Without the space you get no error, just the whole string.

Rung 6 Command substitution: a command's output as a value

today=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
here=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)       # nested: each $( ) is its own quoting context
if version=$(git describe --tags 2>/dev/null); then   # the status of the command survives
  echo "building $version"
fi

$(command) runs the command (in a subshell, chapter 9) and is replaced by what it printed to stdout. Quote it like any other expansion: "$(cmd)". The quotes inside the parentheses do not clash with the quotes around them.

Rule Use $( ), quote it, and check the command's status when the value matters (if x=$(cmd); then).

Why $( ) nests without escaping and reads clearly. Unquoted, its output goes through word splitting and globbing like any other expansion.

Trap Command substitution removes all trailing newlines. x=$(printf 'a\n\n\n') gives a, and a file read with content=$(cat file) loses its blank last lines. Usually that is what you want. When it is not, add a sentinel and remove it: x=$(cmd; printf .); x=${x%.}.

Rung 7 Arithmetic: integers only

echo $((7 / 2)) $((7 % 2)) $((2 ** 10))   # 3 1 1024: integer division, remainder, power [bash]
i=$((i + 1))                              # POSIX
((i++))                                   # [bash], and see chapter 5 for its exit status
echo $((16#ff)) $((2#1010))               # 255 10: other bases [bash]
awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 1.5 * 2 / 7 }'   # 0.43: decimals need awk (or bc)

Inside $(( )), variables do not need a $, and spaces are free. $((7 / 2)) is 3: the shell has no decimals, and $((1.5 * 2)) is a syntax error.

Rule Do integer arithmetic with $(( )), and hand anything with decimals to awk.

Why It is built in, fast and POSIX (** and base# are bash extensions).

Trap A number with a leading zero is read as octal (base 8). $((010)) is 8, and $((08 + 1)) fails with value too great for base. That ends the script. Days, months, times and version numbers like 08 and 09 arrive this way from date and from file names. Remove the zeros first (m=${m#0}), or force base 10 with $((10#$m)) bash.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# counter.sh, circa 2003
TOP=`dirname $0`
N=`expr $N + 1`
LEN=`expr length "$NAME"`
NAME_UC=`echo $NAME | tr a-z A-Z`
let TOTAL=TOTAL+N
typeset -i COUNT=0
echo -n "Average: "; echo "scale=2; $TOTAL / $N" | bc
eval "VALUE=\$$KEY"
SUM=$[A + B]
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
`cmd` (backticks) command substitution the Bourne shell's only form. $( ) was standardised by POSIX.2 (1992) $(cmd) yes, but backslashes inside are processed again: `echo \$HOME` prints your home, $(echo \$HOME) prints $HOME. Nesting needs \`
expr $n + 1 arithmetic, string length, substrings, regex matches the Bourne shell had no arithmetic $((n + 1)), ${#s}, ${s:0:3}, [[ =~ ]] yes, but expr length is GNU (macOS: syntax error), * must be escaped, and see Trap
$[ a + b ] arithmetic an early bash syntax. bash 2.0's release notes dropped it in favour of $(( )) $((a + b)) bash still accepts it, undocumented. Dash and BusyBox print it literally
let x=x+1, typeset -i arithmetic assignment, an integer-typed variable ksh features copied into bash x=$((x + 1)) yes bash
`dirname $0`, `basename $f .txt` path parts no parameter expansion for paths in the Bourne shell ${0%/*}, ${f##*/} then ${base%.txt} yes, one process each, and unquoted they break on spaces
echo $x \| tr a-z A-Z upper-case no case operators before bash 4 (2009) ${x^^} bash 4+, or tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' yes. Ranges like a-z misbehave in some locales; the classes are safer
echo -n print without a newline BSD echo had -n, System V used \c printf '%s' "$x" yes in bash and BusyBox; dash supports -n but not -e
echo "…" \| bc decimal arithmetic the shell has only integers awk 'BEGIN { … }' yes, but bc is often missing from containers
eval "V=\$$KEY" read the variable named in $KEY no indirection in the Bourne shell ${!KEY} bash yes, and it runs any code in $KEY (chapter 3)

Rule Translate expr, backticks, $[ ], let and basename/dirname calls into $(( )), $( ) and parameter expansion when you work on a script.

Why Each modern form runs inside the shell, handles any characters, and has one set of rules everywhere bash runs.

Trap expr exits with status 1 when its result is 0 or empty. That is a feature for if expr …, but under set -e, n=$(expr $n - 1) ends the script the moment the counter reaches zero, with no message (in every shell tested). $((n - 1)) has no exit status of its own to trip over.

Decide

You need Use
fixed text 'single quotes'
text with variables "double quotes"
a tab, newline or other escape inside a value $'…' bash, or printf
output of any of the above printf '%s\n' "$x", not echo
a value that must be safe to paste back into a shell printf '%q' "$x" bash

The golden file

Pantry's settings in one sourced file. Its first line tells shellcheck which shell to assume, since a sourced file has no shebang. It has required values, defaults that an empty value cannot dodge, normalisation that works on bash 3.2, validation with globs, and derived values built in one place. Chapter 14's pantry-ctl sources it.

cd examples/manual/b04
PANTRY_ENV=PROD PANTRY_PORT=9000 bash -c '. ./pantry-env.sh && echo "$PANTRY_ENV $PANTRY_URL $PANTRY_IMAGE"'
PANTRY_ENV=dev PANTRY_PORT=08080 bash -c '. ./pantry-env.sh'; echo "status $?"   # rejected: leading zero
bash pantry-env.sh; echo "status $?"                                              # 2: must be sourced

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A helper that names backup files. It "works on the test file".

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. `dirname $file` is unquoted (and uses backticks). With my data/report.csv, dirname got two arguments and printed two lines, . and data, so the backup name came out split across two lines (rung 6, rung 8). Use dir=$(dirname -- "$file"), or ${file%/*} once you know the path contains a /.
  2. ${base%%.*} cuts at the first dot. v1.2-plan.md became v1 plus the "extension" 2-plan.md, giving notes/v1.2026-10-24.2-plan.md (rung 4). Use ${base%.*} and ${base##*.} for the last extension.
  3. A name with no dot is not handled. For Makefile, both ${base%%.*} and ${base#*.} return the whole name, giving ./Makefile.2026-10-24.Makefile (rung 4). Check for a dot first: case $base in *.*) … ;; *) ext= ;; esac.
  4. ${KEEP-7} has no colon, so KEEP= (empty) is kept. $((keep - 1)) then printed keeping -1 older backups (rung 3). Use ${KEEP:-7}.
  5. KEEP=08 is read as octal, and the arithmetic failed with 08: value too great for base. The script exits 1 after printing half its output (rung 7). Validate it (case $keep in *[!0-9]*)), then use $((10#$keep - 1)).

Shell manual · 5 · 10 min readExit Status and Tests#

You've met it: kubectl -n "$NS" logs "$name" --tail=2 2>/dev/null || true in the triage script, where || true means "this may fail, and that is fine" · Debugging

The shell has no true or false values. Every decision it makes, in if, while, && and ||, is about one thing only: the exit status of a command (chapter 2). Zero means success and counts as true. Anything else counts as false. Even [, the thing that looks like a condition, is a command that exits 0 or 1. Once you see that, the strange-looking parts of shell conditions stop being strange.

The ladder

Rung 1 if runs a command

if grep -q "ERROR" app.log; then        # the condition is the command: grep exits 0 on a match
  echo "errors found"
elif [ -s app.log ]; then               # [ is a command too; -s: file exists and is not empty
  echo "clean log"
else
  echo "no log yet"
fi

if ! command -v jq >/dev/null; then     # ! inverts a command's status
  echo "please install jq" >&2
fi

if runs the command after it. Exit status 0 takes the then branch, anything else the elif or else branch. Many commands have a "quiet" option made for exactly this: grep -q, cmp -s, diff -q.

Rule Put the command itself after if. Use [ … ] only when you really are comparing strings, numbers or file attributes.

Why The command's status is the answer. Capturing output and testing it (if [ "$(grep -c x f)" -gt 0 ]) runs more processes, and loses the difference between "no match" and "error".

Trap if [ false ] takes the then branch. [ with one argument tests whether that string is non-empty, and false is a five-letter string. The same goes for [ 0 ] and [ "$flag" ]. To run the false command, write if false. To test a flag, compare it: [ "$flag" = yes ].

Rung 2 &&, ||, and your own exit codes

mkdir -p "$out" && cp report.csv "$out"/      # run the second only if the first succeeded
cd "$dir" || exit 1                           # stop if the cd failed
grep -q x f || true                           # failure is expected and fine: make the status 0

a && b runs b only if a succeeded. a || b runs b only if a failed. The status of the whole line is that of the last command that ran. Your own script reports its result the same way, with exit N (and a function with return N, chapter 8):

Exit with Meaning, by convention
0 it worked
1 it failed (the general case)
2 it was called wrongly: bad options or arguments (print usage)
your own small numbers documented failure kinds, like wait-for.sh's 1 for "timed out"
avoid 126, 127, 128+ the shell uses these for "cannot run", "not found" and "killed by a signal"

exit without a number exits with the status of the last command, which is often not what you meant.

Rule Use && and || for one-step "and then" and "or else" chains, and if for anything with two outcomes. End every script with an explicit exit that matches its result.

Why a && b || c reads like an if/else, but it is not one. c runs when a fails, and also when b fails.

Trap [ -d "$dir" ] && cd "$dir" || mkdir "$dir". If the directory exists but cd fails (no permission), mkdir runs, fails as well, and the script continues in the wrong directory. In the lab, true && false || echo "c ran" printed c ran. Write the if.

Rung 3 [ is a command: strings, numbers and files

[ is a command (also called test) whose last argument must be ]. Because it is a command, it needs spaces around every part, and because its arguments are expanded first, every variable in it needs quotes.

[ -z "$x" ]            # empty string          [ -n "$x" ]  # not empty
[ "$a" = "$b" ]        # strings equal         [ "$a" != "$b" ]
[ "$n" -eq 3 ]         # integers: -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge
[ -e "$p" ]            # exists                [ -f "$p" ]  # regular file   [ -d "$p" ]  # directory
[ -r "$p" ]            # readable              [ -w "$p" ]  # writable       [ -x "$p" ]  # executable
[ -s "$p" ]            # exists, not empty     [ -L "$p" ]  # symbolic link
[ "$a" -nt "$b" ]      # a is newer than b

= compares text and -eq compares numbers: [ 10 = 010 ] is false and [ 10 -eq 010 ] is true.

Rule Put spaces around [, ] and every operator, double-quote every variable, and use = for strings and -eq/-lt/… for numbers.

Why Unquoted, an empty variable disappears and the test changes meaning. [ -n $x ] with x empty becomes [ -n ], which asks "is -n a non-empty string?". The answer is yes, so the test is true for an empty x, in every shell.

Trap [ "$a" > "$b" ] does not compare anything. > is a redirection (chapter 6). The shell creates (or empties) a file named after $b, runs [ "$a" ], and the test is true whenever $a is not empty. In the lab it printed true? and left a file called zzz behind. Compare numbers with -gt, or strings with [[ $a > $b ]] (rung 4).

Rung 4 [[ … ]]: bash's safer test

if [[ $file == *.txt ]]; then …                  # glob pattern match (right side unquoted)
if [[ $version =~ ^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+) ]]; then   # regular expression
  major=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}                       # the captured groups
fi
if [[ -f $cfg && $mode != test ]]; then …         # && and || inside the brackets
if [[ $a < $b ]]; then …                         # string order, not a redirection

[[ … ]] bash is part of bash's syntax, not a command. That is why it can skip word splitting and globbing on the variables inside it ([[ -n $x ]] is safe unquoted), and why &&, < and > mean what they look like. Dash has no [[ at all. BusyBox accepts [[ and =~, but sets no BASH_REMATCH, and treats < inside it as a redirection.

Rule In bash scripts, prefer [[ … ]] for string and file tests. Keep [ … ] for scripts that must run in sh.

Why It removes the two classic [ failures, missing quotes and > as a redirection, and adds pattern and regex matching without starting grep.

Trap On the right side of == and =~, quoting turns the pattern into plain text. [[ $f == "*.txt" ]] is true only for a file literally named *.txt, and [[ $f =~ "^r" ]] looks for the characters ^r. Leave patterns unquoted, or put a regex in a variable and use it unquoted: re='^v[0-9]+'; [[ $v =~ $re ]].

Rung 5 Arithmetic tests: (( … ))

if (( count > 3 )); then …          # C-like comparison, no $ needed  [bash]
(( retries++ ))                      # increment
(( n % 2 == 0 )) && echo even

(( expr )) bash evaluates an arithmetic expression and exits 0 if the result is non-zero, and 1 if it is zero. That makes comparisons read naturally, because a true comparison has the value 1.

Rule Use (( … )) for numeric conditions in bash, and [ "$n" -gt 3 ] in sh scripts.

Why <, >= and == mean what they look like inside (( )), variables need no $, and there is no quoting to get wrong.

Trap The status follows the value, not whether it worked. (( count++ )) with count=0 has the value 0 (post-increment returns the old value), so its status is 1. Under set -e (chapter 14), bash 5 ends the script right there, on the first increment, with no message. macOS's bash 3.2 does not. Use count=$((count + 1)), which is an assignment and always succeeds.

Rung 6 case: matching one value against patterns

case $1 in
  start | up)      start_service ;;           # | separates alternatives
  stop)            stop_service ;;
  -h | --help)     usage; exit 0 ;;
  *.tar.gz | *.tgz) tar -xzf "$1" ;;           # glob patterns, as in chapter 3
  '')              echo "missing argument" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  *)               echo "unknown: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;   # everything else: put it last
esac

The value is compared with each pattern in turn. The first match runs its commands up to ;;, and case ends. Patterns are globs, the value needs no quotes (it is not split), and case works in every POSIX shell.

Rule Use case whenever one value decides between several branches: arguments, file types, environments, yes/no answers.

Why It is clearer than a chain of elif [ … ], it matches patterns in every shell, and the *) branch makes "everything else" explicit.

Trap ;& (fall through into the next branch's commands) and ;;& (keep testing the next patterns) bash 4+ are syntax errors in macOS's bash 3.2: syntax error near unexpected token '&'. A syntax error stops the whole script before it runs a single line, so one bash-4 branch makes a script dead on arrival on a Mac. List the patterns together with | instead.

Rung 7 Loops on commands: while, until, and retrying

while read -r line; do …; done < file     # repeat while the command succeeds (chapter 7)
until curl -fsS "$url" >/dev/null; do     # repeat while it fails
  sleep 1
done

attempt=1 delay=1                          # retry with a limit and a growing delay
until docker pull "$image"; do
  if [ "$attempt" -ge 5 ]; then
    echo "giving up after $attempt attempts" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  sleep "$delay"
  attempt=$((attempt + 1)) delay=$((delay * 2))
done

while and until, like if, run a command and look at its status. break leaves the loop and continue starts the next pass.

Rule Every retry loop needs a limit (attempts or a deadline), a delay, and a message when it gives up.

Why Retrying covers a temporary failure: a service still starting, a network blip. A permanent failure, such as a wrong host name or a 404, never goes away, and only the limit ends the loop.

Trap until curl -fsS "$url"; do sleep 1; done with a typo in $url loops forever and prints the same error every second. In CI it runs until the job's own timeout kills it an hour later, with nothing to say why. The golden file has the deadline built in.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# 1998-vintage conditions
if test "x$1" = "x-v"; then VERBOSE=1; fi
if [ ! -z "$FILE" -a -r "$FILE" -o "$FORCE" = yes ]; then
  process
fi
grep -q done status
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "done"; fi
while :; do check && break; sleep 5; done
if expr "$NAME" : 'pantry-.*' >/dev/null; then echo match; fi
[ "$a" == "$b" ] && echo same
select opt in start stop quit; do …; done
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
test … the same command as [ … ] the original name; [ came later as an alias [ … ], or [[ … ]] in bash yes
[ "x$a" = "xfoo" ] compare with an x glued to both sides old test misread values like -n, ! or ( as operators. Autoconf's manual still recommends a leading X [ "$a" = foo ] yes, but not needed in any POSIX shell
-a, -o inside [ ] and, or one test call instead of two [ … ] && [ … ], [ … ] \|\| [ … ], or [[ … && … ]] marked obsolescent in POSIX.1-2008 and removed in POSIX.1-2024. See Trap
[ ! -z "$x" ] not empty [ -n "$x" ] yes
if [ $? -eq 0 ] test the previous command's status a habit carried over from other languages if command; then yes, but anything run in between replaces $? (chapter 2)
while : loop forever : is the do-nothing command that always succeeds while true reads better, and is the same yes
expr "$x" : 're' regex match the Bourne shell's only regex [[ $x =~ re ]], or case with a glob yes, and it prints the match length
[ "$a" == "$b" ] string equality bash accepts == inside [ = in [ ], == in [[ ]] bash, BusyBox and macOS yes. Dash: [: unexpected operator bash
select x in … a numbered menu ksh's interactive menus case on an argument, or read yes bash

Rule Translate test "x$a", -a/-o and if [ $? … ] into plain modern tests when you edit a script, and use = (not ==) in [ ].

Why These idioms protected against bugs in shells that no longer exist, or saved a process when processes were expensive. The modern forms are shorter and harder to get wrong.

Trap -a and -o still fail today on ordinary data. With x='!', [ "$x" = "!" -a "$y" = 1 ] fails in every shell tested: bash and bash 3.2 say too many arguments, dash says unexpected operator, BusyBox says unknown operand. The if then takes its else branch as though the values were different. Two separate tests joined by && worked in all of them.

Decide

Test Use for Works in
[ … ] strings, numbers, files in a script that must run in sh every shell
[[ … ]] strings, files, glob patterns and regexes in bash bash, zsh, ksh (BusyBox partly)
(( … )) numeric comparisons and counters in bash bash, zsh, ksh
the command itself "did it work?" every shell
case one value against several patterns every shell

The golden file

Waits for a port or a URL with a deadline, then gets out of the way. Its exit status is the whole interface: ./wait-for.sh -t 60 redis:6379 && ./start.sh. Chapter 14's pantry-ctl uses it before starting Pantry.

cd examples/manual/b05
./wait-for.sh -t 3 127.0.0.1:9; echo "status $?"                # 1 after about 3 seconds: nothing listens
(sleep 2; nc -l 19123) & ./wait-for.sh -t 10 127.0.0.1:19123     # ready after about 2 seconds (macOS nc;
                                                                 # in the lab: /opt/busybox/bin/nc -l -p 19123)

Review checklist

Spot the bug

The deploy job rolls back when this exits non-zero. It has never rolled anything back.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. [ -n $SKIP_HEALTH ] is unquoted. With SKIP_HEALTH unset it becomes [ -n ], which is true. Every run printed health check skipped and exited 0, so the check never checked anything (rung 3). Use [ -n "${SKIP_HEALTH:-}" ].
  2. == inside [ ] under #!/bin/sh. In the Debian container, dash said [: 200: unexpected operator, so healthy was never printed, even for a 200 (rung 8).
  3. [ "$code" > 499 ] is a redirection, not a comparison. It created a file named 499 in the current directory and tested [ "$code" ], which is true, so a healthy service was reported as server error (200) (rung 3). Use [ "$code" -ge 500 ].
  4. The script never exits non-zero. Its status is that of the last echo, so a 404 or a 500 still gave 0, and the deploy job never rolled back (rung 2). Add exit 0 after healthy and exit 1 in the other branches, or end with [ "$code" = 200 ].
  5. The URL argument is not checked. Without one, curl complained, $code was empty, and the script still exited 0 (rung 2). Start with [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "usage: check-health.sh URL" >&2; exit 2; }.

Shell manual · 6 · 10 min readRedirection and Pipes#

You've met it: SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"], the line that stops a failing curl … | tar in a Dockerfile from passing as success · Every Instruction

Chapter 2 introduced the three streams every process starts with: stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2). This chapter is about pointing them somewhere else: into files, out of files, into other programs, or nowhere.
