All of it happens in step 8 of chapter 3's pipeline, after expansion and before the program starts. The program itself never knows. It writes to fd 1 as usual, and fd 1 now happens to be a file.

The ladder

Rung 1 Pointing streams at files, and why the order matters

Write Means
cmd > file fd 1 to file (created, or emptied first)
cmd >> file fd 1 to file, appended
cmd < file fd 0 reads from file
cmd 2> errors.log fd 2 to a file
cmd > out.log 2>&1 fd 1 to the file, then fd 2 to wherever fd 1 now points: both in the file
cmd &> out.log the same, shorter bash
cmd > /dev/null 2>&1 discard everything. /dev/null swallows whatever is written to it
cmd 2> /dev/null discard only the errors

2>&1 means "make fd 2 a copy of fd 1 as it is right now". Redirections are applied left to right, so the order changes the result:

Rule To capture both streams, write > file 2>&1, in that order.

Why Each redirection acts on the fd table as it stands after the ones before it. 2>&1 copies, it does not link, so a later change to fd 1 does not move fd 2.

Trap cmd 2>&1 > file leaves the errors on the terminal and only stdout in the file. Your log is clean, and the errors went to a terminal nobody was watching. And in dash and BusyBox sh, cmd &> file is not a redirection at all: it parses as cmd & (run in the background) followed by > file (empty the file). The command's output lands on the terminal later, and file stays empty.

Rung 2 Pipes connect stdout to stdin

grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5   # the five most common errors
cmd 2>&1 | tee build.log                                   # stderr into the pipe too
cmd |& tee build.log                                       # the same, shorter [bash 4+]

a | b starts both programs at the same time and connects a's stdout to b's stdin. Each part of a pipeline is a separate process (in bash, even a builtin or a while loop at the end, chapter 7). Only stdout goes through. stderr still goes to the terminal, unless you redirect it first.

Rule Build pipelines from small commands that each read stdin and write stdout, and redirect stderr into the pipe only when the next command should read it.

Why Pipes are how separate tools combine into one job. Because all the parts run at once, a pipeline over a huge file uses almost no memory, and head can stop it early.

Trap Reading and writing the same file in one command line destroys it. sort f > f empties f. The shell sets up > f (truncating it) before sort starts, so sort reads an empty file. cat f | sort > f is a race, which sometimes survives and sometimes does not. Write to a new file and rename it (rung 6), or use sort -o f f, which reads everything before writing.

Rung 3 A pipeline's status, and pipefail

$ ls /nope | wc -l; echo "status $?"
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
0
status 0
$ set -o pipefail
$ ls /nope | wc -l; echo "status $?"
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
0
status 2
$ false | true | (exit 3); echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"     # every part's status [bash]
1 0 3

By default, a pipeline's status is the status of its last command. With set -o pipefail, it is the status of the last command that failed, so any failure in the pipeline counts. It worked in every shell tested here, including dash and BusyBox. PIPESTATUS bash keeps each part's status, until the next command replaces it.

Rule Turn on set -o pipefail at the top of every bash script (chapter 14 makes it part of strict mode).

Why Otherwise curl "$url" | tar -xz "succeeds" when the download fails, and grep pattern missing.log | wc -l reports 0 matches with status 0 instead of an error.

Trap pipefail also reports failures you may not care about. grep -q x f | … or a head -1 at the end can make an early command die from SIGPIPE (it was still writing when the reader stopped), and the pipeline then fails with status 141. For pipelines that end early on purpose, check PIPESTATUS, or add || true to that one line.

Rung 4 Here-documents and here-strings

cat <<EOF > settings.ini          # unquoted delimiter: $variables and $(commands) expand
[server]
name = $SERVER_NAME
started = $(date +%F)
EOF

cat <<'EOF' > deploy.sh           # quoted delimiter: everything is literal
echo "Deploying $TAG to $HOST"    # these stay as written, for deploy.sh to expand later
EOF

if true; then
	cat <<-EOF                    # <<- removes leading TABS (not spaces) from each line
	indented with tabs to match the code
	EOF
fi

read -r first rest <<< "one two three"   # here-string: one line of input [bash]

A here-document feeds the lines up to the delimiter (here EOF, but any word works) to the command's stdin. Quoting the delimiter decides whether anything inside is expanded.

Rule Quote the delimiter (<<'EOF') whenever the text is a template, a script or a config with its own $ signs, and leave it unquoted only when you want this shell's variables in it.

Why In an unquoted here-document, every $word, $(…) and backtick expands, exactly as inside double quotes.

Trap cat <<EOF around an nginx config, a Makefile or a generated script quietly replaces $host, $1 or $PATH with this shell's values, usually empty ones. The generated file looks right until a line like proxy_set_header Host $host; arrives as proxy_set_header Host ;. Escape the ones you need to keep (\$host), or quote the delimiter.

Rung 5 Process substitution: a command where a file name goes

diff <(sort old.txt) <(sort new.txt)          # compare two sorted outputs, with no temporary files
comm -13 <(sort a) <(sort b)                  # lines only in b
while read -r pod; do …; done < <(kubectl get pods -o name)   # chapter 7: the loop is not in a subshell
cmd > >(tee out.log) 2> >(tee err.log >&2)    # send each stream to a file and the screen

<(cmd) bash runs cmd and is replaced by a file name (like /dev/fd/63) that reads its output. >(cmd) gives a name that writes into cmd. BusyBox also accepts both. Dash rejects them with a syntax error.

Rule Use <( ) when a program wants file names and what you have is command output, and you would otherwise write temporary files.

Why It avoids creating, naming and cleaning up temporary files, and both commands run at the same time.

Trap The exit status of the command inside <( ) is lost. diff <(false) <(true) exits 0: two empty inputs are equal, and nothing reports that one side failed. Not even pipefail sees it. When the producer can fail (a curl, a kubectl), run it first into a variable or a temporary file and check it.

Rung 6 Writing files safely

cmd | tee out.log                    # write to a file and keep showing it
cmd | tee -a out.log >/dev/null      # append, quietly
set -o noclobber                     # > refuses to overwrite an existing file
cmd >| out.log                       # overwrite anyway, on purpose

tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.config.XXXXXX")  # atomic replace: write a new file next to the old one,
generate > "$tmp" && mv -f "$tmp" "$dir/config.yaml"   # then rename it over the old one
echo "127.0.0.1 pantry.test" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts  # write a root-owned file

A redirection is performed by your shell, as you, before the command starts. That explains two things. sudo echo x > /etc/hosts fails with Permission denied, because sudo raises the privileges of echo, not of your shell's >. Use | sudo tee. And > file empties the file first, before the command has produced anything.

Rule Generate a file into a temporary name in the same directory, check the result, then mv it into place.

Why mv within one filesystem is a rename, which happens in a single step. Anyone reading the file sees either the old complete version or the new one, and a failed generator leaves the old file untouched.

Trap generate > config.yaml, where generate fails halfway or right away, leaves config.yaml truncated or empty. The previous good config is gone, and the service that reads it on its next restart has nothing. In the lab, a failing generator turned an 11-byte config into 0 bytes.

Rung 7 exec redirections and extra file descriptors

exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1   # from here on, everything this script prints also goes to run.log [bash]
exec 3> debug.log                # open fd 3 for writing, for the rest of the script
echo "detail" >&3                # write to it
exec 3>&-                        # close it
exec 4< hosts.txt                # open fd 4 for reading
read -r first <&4                # each read takes the next line
read -r second <&4
exec 4<&-

exec with only redirections (no command) applies them to the current shell itself, permanently. File descriptors 3 to 9 are free for your own use.

Rule Use exec >… once at the top of a script that must log everything, and extra fds when a loop needs a second input or output besides stdin and stdout.

Why One line redirects every later command, including ones in functions you did not write. An extra fd lets a loop read a file on fd 3 while its body still reads the terminal or the network on fd 0 (chapter 7).

Trap After exec > run.log 2>&1, your script's errors go into the log file too, so a failure in a cron job or a terminal shows nothing at all. Use exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1 to keep a copy on the screen, or print the log's path to the terminal before the exec.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# nightly.sh, 2006
cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l
: > /var/tmp/nightly.out
nohup ./long-job.sh > job.out 2>&1 &
mkfifo /tmp/pipe.$$; sort < /tmp/pipe.$$ > sorted.txt & producer > /tmp/pipe.$$
echo "nameserver 1.1.1.1" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf > /dev/null
yes | ./installer.sh
make >& build.log
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
cat file \| cmd feed a file to a command readability, or habit. Called a "useless use of cat" cmd < file, or cmd file yes. One extra process, and cmd cannot seek in a pipe
: > file truncate (or create) a file : is the no-op command, so only the redirection happens > file in bash, or keep : >, which is the portable form yes
nohup cmd & keep running after the terminal closes terminals sending SIGHUP on logout nohup is still right for that; for services, use a supervisor (systemd, a container) yes
mkfifo named pipes connect two commands through a file name no process substitution in the Bourne shell <( ), >( ) bash yes, and still useful between unrelated processes
\| sudo tee file > /dev/null write a root-owned file redirections are done by your shell, not by sudo the same: it is still the right way yes
yes \| cmd answer "y" to every question installers without a non-interactive option the program's own -y/--yes/--non-interactive flag yes, but it answers questions you never read
cmd >& file stdout and stderr to a file csh syntax, accepted by bash > file 2>&1 bash yes bash. In sh, >& needs an fd number

Rule Replace cat file | with a redirection, and >&/&> with > file 2>&1 in anything that might run under sh.

Why These came from csh habits, from shells without process substitution, and from the days before programs had non-interactive flags. The modern forms do the same with fewer processes and fewer surprises.

Trap yes | ./installer.sh agrees to everything, including questions added in a later version: overwrite the existing configuration, remove the old data directory. The script keeps "working". Find the installer's documented non-interactive flags, and set only the answers you mean.

Decide

You want Write
text with this script's variables filled in cat <<EOF
text exactly as written (a script, a template, a config with $) cat <<'EOF'
either, indented with the code <<-EOF or <<-'EOF', indented with tabs
one short line of input <<< "$value" bash, or printf '%s\n' "$value" \|
many lines from a command a pipe, or < <(cmd) bash when the loop must not run in a subshell

The golden file

Renders a config from a here-document. The shell's values are filled in, nginx's own variables are kept, messages go to stderr, a dry run goes to stdout, and the real write is atomic. A failure at any point leaves the old file as it was.

cd examples/manual/b06
SERVER_NAME=pantry.test ./render-config.sh --dry-run out.conf      # print, write nothing
SERVER_NAME=pantry.test ./render-config.sh /tmp/pantry.conf        # render-config: wrote /tmp/pantry.conf
./render-config.sh /tmp/pantry.conf; echo "status $?"              # 2: SERVER_NAME missing, file untouched

Review checklist

Spot the bug

Cron runs this every night in the pantry user's home directory, and emails whatever it prints. Two weeks in, report.txt is empty.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. 2>&1 at the end applies only to uniq, the last command of the pipeline. With the log missing, grep's error went to stderr (into cron's email), not into summary.txt. Redirect where you mean it, for example { grep … | uniq -c; } > summary.txt 2>&1, or let errors reach stderr on purpose (rungs 1 and 2).
  2. There is no pipefail, so the pipeline's status was uniq's: 0. A missing log produced an empty summary and a "successful" run (rung 3). Add set -o pipefail, and check that $log exists first.
  3. The here-document is unquoted, so $5 expanded to the script's (empty) fifth argument: the report line read at per incident (rung 4). Escape it (\$5) or quote the delimiter.
  4. sort report.txt | uniq > report.txt empties the file before sort reads it. After the first run, report.txt was 0 bytes, history and all (rung 2). Use sort -u -o report.txt report.txt, or write to a temporary file and mv it (rung 6).
  5. summary.txt and report.txt are relative paths, so they land wherever cron starts the job (the home directory), not next to the log or the script (chapter 1, rung 2). Use absolute paths, or cd to a known directory and check that the cd worked.

Shell manual · 7 · 10 min readLoops, Globs and Lines#

You've met it: for i in $(seq 1 100); do curl -s localhost:30080/; done | grep -o '(v[12])' | sort | uniq -c, a loop whose output feeds a pipeline, used to count which version answered · A Concierge at Every Door

Most scripts are loops: over arguments, over files, over the lines of a file or of a command's output. Each of those has one correct form, and each wrong form fails only on unusual input, such as a name with a space, a missing last newline, or a command inside the loop that reads stdin. This chapter gives the correct form for each, and shows exactly what the wrong one does.

The ladder

Rung 1 for over words, arguments and numbers

for env in dev staging prod; do echo "deploying to $env"; done   # a fixed list
for arg in "$@"; do echo "[$arg]"; done                          # every argument, each whole
for arg; do echo "[$arg]"; done                                  # the same: "in "$@"" is the default
for ((i = 0; i < 3; i++)); do echo "$i"; done                    # C-style counter [bash]
for i in $(seq 1 "$n"); do echo "$i"; done                       # counter in any shell

for name in words runs the body once per word, after the words have gone through every expansion of chapter 3. That is the whole rule, and every surprise follows from it.

Rule Loop over "$@" for arguments, an array (chapter 8) or a glob for lists, and ((…)) bash or seq for numbers.

Why Each of those produces exactly one word per item. A list held in one string has no way to say where items end except by splitting on spaces.

Trap for x in "$list" with list="a b c" runs once, with x set to all of a b c: the quotes made it one word. Without the quotes it runs three times, but then an item that contains a space becomes two items. Neither is right when the items can contain spaces. Keep lists in arrays.

Rung 2 Looping over files: globs, not ls

shopt -s nullglob                  # [bash] no match: the loop runs zero times
for f in ./*.log; do
  gzip -- "$f"
done

for f in ./*.log; do               # portable version, for sh
  [ -e "$f" ] || continue          # no match: the literal pattern does not exist, so skip it
  gzip -- "$f"
done

A glob produces each matching name as exactly one word (chapter 3), sorted, whatever characters it contains. Writing ./*.log rather than *.log means every name starts with ./, so a file called -rf.log cannot be mistaken for an option.

Rule Loop over a glob, and handle the no-match case with nullglob or a [ -e "$f" ] check.

Why The glob is evaluated by the shell, which knows exactly where each name begins and ends. ls output is text for people, and the loop would split it again on spaces and newlines.

Trap for f in $(ls *.txt) splits my report.txt into my and report.txt, and the loop then works on two files that do not exist (or, worse, on two other files that happen to have those names). It also mangles names containing * or ?, which are globbed a second time.

Rung 3 Recursion: ** and its limits

shopt -s globstar                      # [bash 4+] make ** match any depth of directories
for f in ./**/*.log; do …; done        # every .log file below here, at any depth

In bash 4 and later, ** with globstar matches files in all subdirectories. For anything beyond that, such as filtering by age or size, skipping directories, or very large trees, use find (chapter 10), which also works in every shell.

Rule Use ** only in scripts that check they run on bash 4 or later. Otherwise use find … -print0 with a NUL-delimited loop (rung 7).

Why globstar does not exist in bash 3.2, and without it ** silently means *.

Trap On macOS's /bin/bash, shopt -s globstar fails with invalid shell option name, the script carries on, and **/*.log matches only files exactly one directory down. In the lab it found top.log, a/mid.log and a/b/deep.log, and on the Mac only a/mid.log, with no further error. A backup or cleanup script then quietly skips most of the tree.

Rung 4 Reading lines and fields: while IFS= read -r

while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do     # every line, exactly as written
  printf '%s\n' "$line"
done < file.txt

while IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ _ home shell; do  # split each line into fields on :
  echo "$user has uid $uid and home $home"
done < /etc/passwd

read -r -a words <<< "p q r"                       # split one line into an array [bash]

Each part of the first line is there for a reason:

Part Without it
IFS= leading and trailing spaces and tabs are trimmed from each line
-r backslashes are treated as escapes and disappear: lead\ing becomes leading
\|\| [ -n "$line" ] a last line with no newline at the end is read, but read reports failure, and the loop stops before using it
< file after done (see rung 5 for what goes wrong with cat file \|)

With field names, read splits on IFS and the last variable gets the rest of the line: read -r a b on 1 2 3 4 gives b='2 3 4'. _ is a conventional name for a field you do not need.

Rule Read lines with while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do … done < file, and fields with IFS=<sep> read -r f1 f2 rest.

Why Plain read line was designed to read words typed by a person, not data. It trims, unescapes, and drops an unterminated last line.

Trap Whitespace separators merge. With IFS set to a tab, the line a<TAB><TAB>c gives y=c and z empty: the empty middle field disappeared, and every later column is shifted one place left. Non-whitespace separators keep empty fields (a,,c gives y empty and z=c). For tab-separated data with empty fields, use awk -F'\t' (chapter 12).

Rung 5 Piping into while: the subshell trap

count=0
grep ERROR app.log | while IFS= read -r line; do count=$((count + 1)); done
echo "$count"          # 0: the loop ran in a subshell, and its count died with it

count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do count=$((count + 1)); done < <(grep ERROR app.log)   # [bash]
echo "$count"          # the real number

mapfile -t lines < <(grep ERROR app.log)    # [bash 4+] every line into an array at once

In bash, dash and BusyBox, every part of a pipeline runs in its own child process, the while loop at the end included. Variables set inside it vanish when the pipeline ends (chapter 2: children never change parents). zsh runs the last part in the current shell, so the same line works in zsh, which is one more reason to test in bash.

Rule Feed a loop that must set variables with done < file or done < <(command), not with command | while.

Why With a redirection, the loop runs in the current shell, so its variables survive. <( ) (chapter 6) turns a command into something you can redirect from.

Trap The loop clearly runs, it prints lines, it increments, and afterwards the count is 0, with no error. shopt -s lastpipe bash 4+ makes bash run the last part in the current shell, but only when job control is off (in scripts), and macOS's bash 3.2 rejects the option. The redirect form works everywhere bash does.

Rung 6 Commands inside the loop that read stdin

while IFS= read -r host; do
  ssh -n "$host" uptime                 # -n: ssh reads nothing from stdin
done < hosts.txt

while IFS= read -r host; do
  some-tool "$host" < /dev/null         # the general fix: give the command empty input
done < hosts.txt

while IFS= read -r host <&3; do         # or: read the list on fd 3, leaving stdin alone
  ssh "$host" uptime
done 3< hosts.txt

Inside while … done < file, stdin of every command in the body is that file. A command that reads stdin, such as ssh, ffmpeg, docker exec -i, kubectl exec -i or cat, swallows the rest of the list.

Rule When a loop reads its list from stdin, run every command in the body that might read stdin with < /dev/null (or its own flag, like ssh -n), or read the list from fd 3.

Why The loop and the commands inside it share one stdin. Whatever the inner command reads, read never sees.

Trap The loop processes the first line and then stops, with status 0 and no error. In the lab, with cat standing in for ssh, a three-host list printed checking web1 and nothing else.

Rung 7 Names with newlines: NUL-delimited loops

find . -name '*.log' -print0 |
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do       # -d '': read up to a NUL byte instead of a newline [bash]
    gzip -- "$f"
  done

find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 gzip --    # the same, without a loop (chapter 10)

A file name can contain any byte except / and NUL (the zero byte), including a newline. So the only separator that is safe for lists of names is NUL. find -print0 produces NUL-separated lists, and xargs -0 and read -d '' consume them.

Rule For lists of file names from a command, use NUL separators from end to end: -print0 into read -d '' or xargs -0.

Why A newline-separated list of names is ambiguous as soon as one name contains a newline, whether by accident, through a bug in another program, or on purpose by someone who wants your script to act on the wrong file.

Trap find . -name '*.txt' | while read -r f turned the single file new⏎line.txt into two names, ./new and line.txt. Neither exists, so any rm or mv on them fails or hits something else. read -d is bash: dash rejects it (Illegal option -d), and BusyBox accepts it.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# cleanup.sh, mid-2000s
for i in `seq 1 10`; do echo "pass $i"; done
for f in `ls /var/tmp/app`; do rm /var/tmp/app/$f; done
IFS='
'
for line in $(cat targets.txt); do deploy "$line"; done
ls *.bak | while read f; do mv $f old/; done
find /var/log -name '*.gz' -exec rm {} \;
find . -name '*.tmp' | xargs rm
set -- *.conf; [ "$1" = '*.conf' ] && echo "no configs"
jot 10
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
for i in `seq 1 10` count no arithmetic loop in the Bourne shell for ((i = 1; i <= 10; i++)) bash, or seq with $( ) yes
for f in `ls dir` loop over files habit for f in dir/* yes, but breaks on spaces (rung 2)
IFS=$'\n' then for line in $(cat f) loop over lines no reliable read -r loop in early shells while IFS= read -r line (rung 4) yes. See Trap
ls \| while read f loop over files a glob yes, and loses variables (rung 5)
find … -exec cmd {} \; run cmd once per file the original -exec -exec cmd {} + (many files per run) yes, but one process per file: slow on big trees
find … \| xargs cmd run cmd on many files -exec … + came later find … -print0 \| xargs -0 cmd yes, but splits names on spaces and newlines
set -- *; [ "$1" = '*' ] detect "no match" no nullglob in sh nullglob bash, or [ -e "$1" ] yes
jot 10 print 1 to 10 BSD's counting tool BSD seq 10 (macOS has it too), or a loop macOS yes; Linux: jot: command not found

Rule In loops you inherit, replace ls, backticks, IFS juggling and plain xargs with globs, while IFS= read -r and NUL-separated find.

Why Every one of these works on the test data and fails on a name with a space, an empty line or a *, which real data contains sooner or later.

Trap IFS=$'\n'; for line in $(cat targets.txt) looks like a line loop, but it is still word splitting plus globbing. Empty lines disappear, and a line that is a pattern expands into file names. With the target *.key in the file, the loop deployed to secret.key, a file in the current directory, instead of the line that was written.

Decide

You have Loop with
the script's arguments for arg in "$@"
a fixed list, or an array for x in a b c, for x in "${arr[@]}"
files in one directory for f in ./*.ext with nullglob
files in a tree, with conditions find … -print0 \| while IFS= read -r -d '' f bash, or -exec … +
lines of a file while IFS= read -r line \|\| [ -n "$line" ]; do … done < file
lines of a command, setting variables … done < <(cmd) bash, or mapfile -t bash 4+
a count for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)) bash, or seq

The golden file

Renames files by extension. It loops over a glob with nullglob, protects names that start with a dash, never overwrites, and changes nothing until you add --apply. Its option loop is chapter 5's case, and its counts are chapter 4's arithmetic.

cd /some/photos
rename-ext.sh jpeg jpg            # the plan, and a count; nothing changes
rename-ext.sh --apply jpeg jpg    # do it; status 1 if any file had to be skipped

Review checklist

Spot the bug

The on-call runbook says: "run ./check-hosts.sh hosts.txt; if it says 0, all is well." It has said 0 for a month.

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. cat "$1" | while … runs the loop in a subshell, so down is incremented there and is still 0 outside. With down1 failing, it printed DOWN: down1 and then 0 hosts down (rung 5). Use while … done < "$1".
  2. ssh reads stdin, which is the host list, so it swallowed the remaining lines after the first host. With web1 first, no other host was ever checked (rung 6). Use ssh -n, or < /dev/null, or read the list on fd 3.
  3. The last line of hosts.txt has no newline, and read host without || [ -n "$host" ] drops it. With stdin fixed, down3 was still never checked (rung 4). Also use IFS= read -r.
  4. The script always exits 0, even when it prints DOWN lines, so nothing but a human reading the output can notice a failure (chapter 5, rung 2). End with [ "$down" -eq 0 ], so that the status says whether all hosts are up.

Shell manual · 8 · 10 min readFunctions and Arrays#

You've met it: docker_clean() { docker compose -f pantry/compose.yaml down -v --remove-orphans 2>/dev/null || true; … } in examples/reset.sh, the script that puts your machine back at any chapter's starting line · From Docker to Kubernetes

Functions let a script name a step and reuse it. Arrays let it hold a list whose items can contain anything, which is the one thing a plain string cannot do safely. Both behave differently from what you might expect from other languages. Functions return only a status, variables are global unless you say otherwise, and arrays are bash-only, with associative arrays missing entirely from macOS's bash. This chapter covers what you need to write both correctly and to read them in other people's scripts.

The ladder

Rung 1 Defining and calling, and the function's arguments

greet() {                         # define: name, (), then a { } body
  echo "hello, $1"                # $1, $2, … are the function's own arguments
  echo "called with $# arguments: $*"
}
greet world                       # call it like any command

wrapper() {
  docker "$@"                     # pass every argument on, each one whole
}
shift                             # drop $1; the others move down one place
set -- new "list here"            # replace all the positional parameters

Inside a function, $1, $2, $#, $@ and $* are the function's arguments, not the script's. $0 stays the script's name. The three ways to say "all the arguments" differ only in quoting, and only one is right for passing them on:

Form wrap "a b" c passes on
"$@" a b, c: two arguments, each whole
"$*" a b c: one argument, joined with the first character of IFS
$@ or $* unquoted a, b, c: split again (chapter 3)

Rule Pass arguments on with "$@", always quoted. Use "$*" only to build one string for a message.

Why "$@" is the one expansion that produces exactly the words that were given, however many there are and whatever they contain.

Trap A script runs top to bottom, and a function exists only after its definition has run. Calling greet on line 1 of a script that defines it on line 5 fails with greet: command not found, and the script carries on. Put all functions first and the main code last (often in a function called main, called on the final line: main "$@").

Rung 2 Returning: a status, or printed output

is_port_open() {                  # answer a yes/no question with the status
  (exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$1/$2") 2>/dev/null
}
if is_port_open localhost 6379; then …; fi

image_tag() {                     # produce a value: print it, and let the caller capture it
  printf '%s:%s\n' "$1" "${2:-latest}"
}
tag=$(image_tag pantry v3)

set_default() {                   # assign into a variable the caller names [bash]
  printf -v "$1" '%s' "$2"
}
set_default region eu-west-1

return N ends the function with status N, which works exactly like a command's exit status (chapter 5). Without return, the status is that of the last command the function ran. A function produces values the way programs do: by printing them.

Rule Use the status for success or failure and yes or no, print the value and capture it with $( ), and keep printf -v for the rare case where a subshell would cost too much or lose state.

Why A function is a small command. The caller tests it with if and captures its output with $( ), the same as any program.

Trap return takes only a number from 0 to 255. return 300 gives 44 in bash and BusyBox (dash even reports 300), and return ok is an error: numeric argument required, status 2 in bash 5 and 255 in bash 3.2. A function that tries to "return" a count or a string returns nonsense. Print it instead.

Rung 3 Scope: global unless you say local

name=report
process() { name=tmp; }           # assigns the caller's (global) name
process
echo "$name"                      # tmp

process() {
  local name=tmp i                # these exist only during this call
  for i in 1 2 3; do …; done
}

Every variable a function assigns is global unless it is declared local. local is not in POSIX, but dash and BusyBox both have it. Bash scoping is dynamic: a function can see the local variables of whoever called it, as if they were global.

Rule Declare every variable a function uses with local at the top of the function, loop variables included.

Why Without it, a helper silently overwrites the caller's variables. Common names like i, f, line, name and status collide all the time.

Trap local x=$(cmd) hides cmd's failure: the status of that line is the status of local, which is 0. Under set -e the script carries on with an empty x. In the lab, local out=$(false) was followed by the next line running, and local o2; o2=$(false) stopped the script. Declare first, then assign.

Rung 4 Indexed arrays, and commands built as arrays

files=(a.txt "my notes.txt")       # an array of two items                     [bash]
files+=(c.txt)                     # append
echo "${#files[@]}"                # 3: how many
echo "${files[1]}"                 # my notes.txt: indexes start at 0
for f in "${files[@]}"; do …; done # each item, whole
echo "${files[@]:1:2}"             # a slice: 2 items from index 1
unset 'files[0]'                   # remove one (indexes do not move: 1 2 remain)

cmd=(docker run --rm -v "$dir:/data")    # a command, item by item
[ -n "$debug" ] && cmd+=(-e DEBUG=1)     # add options conditionally
cmd+=(pantry:latest)
"${cmd[@]}"                              # run it

Arrays bash are lists of strings in which each item keeps its spaces, quotes and glob characters, because "${arr[@]}" expands to one word per item, like "$@". Dash and BusyBox have no arrays. Their only list is set -- and "$@".

Rule Whenever you build a list (of files, of options, of a command line), use an array, and expand it as "${arr[@]}".

Why A string can only be split on whitespace, so any item containing a space breaks. An array keeps the boundaries you put in it.

Trap cmd="docker run -v $dir:/data img"; $cmd works until dir contains a space. Then -v /data/my and files:/data arrive as two arguments, and docker mounts the wrong path or rejects the command. The array version passed /data/my files:/data as one argument. On macOS's bash 3.2 there is one more catch. With set -u, expanding an empty array ("${a[@]}") fails with a[@]: unbound variable. Write ${a[@]+"${a[@]}"} in scripts that must run there.

Rung 5 Associative arrays, and checking the bash version

declare -A port=([web]=8080 [redis]=6379)    # keys are strings      [bash 4+]
port[db]=5432
echo "${port[redis]}"                        # 6379
for svc in "${!port[@]}"; do                 # the keys, in no particular order
  echo "$svc listens on ${port[$svc]}"
done
[ -n "${port[cache]+set}" ] || echo "no cache configured"   # test for a key

if [ "${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}" -lt 4 ]; then     # guard: stop with a clear message
  echo "$0: needs bash 4 or later (this is $BASH_VERSION)" >&2
  exit 2
fi

declare -A makes a map from string keys to values. It is the most useful bash 4 feature, and the most common reason a script fails on a Mac.

Rule Use associative arrays when you need lookups by name, and put a version guard at the top of every script that does (the golden file's require_bash 4).

Why Without the guard, the script does not fail where the problem is. It fails much later, or not at all, with wrong data.

Trap On bash 3.2, declare -A prints invalid option, and if the script continues, the assignment that follows creates an ordinary indexed array. Every key is evaluated as arithmetic, where an unknown word is 0, so keys collapse into a few numbered slots. In the test, all three lookups (redis, web, db) returned 5432, and the map claimed to have one key. Nothing else reported an error.

Rung 6 Libraries: source, its path, and include guards

here=$(cd "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)   # the directory this file is in
. "$here/lib.sh"                                        # load helpers into this shell

# in lib.sh:
[ -n "${LIB_SH_LOADED:-}" ] && return 0                 # sourced already: do nothing
LIB_SH_LOADED=1

. file (or source file) runs the file in the current shell (chapter 2), which is how a script loads shared functions and settings. BASH_SOURCE[0] bash is the path of the file being read, even when that file was itself sourced, where $0 would be the outer script or the shell.

Rule Source libraries by a path built from BASH_SOURCE[0], give them an include guard, and prefix or carefully name their functions so they cannot clash with commands.

Why A library is used from many scripts, started from many directories. Its location has to be computed, never assumed.

Trap . lib.sh with no slash does not mean "the lib.sh next to this script". Bash looks for it in PATH first, and then in the current directory. Run from the script's own directory it works. From anywhere else it fails (lib.sh: No such file or directory), and with some other lib.sh on your PATH, it silently loads that one. In the lab, a stray lib.sh on PATH printed a different lib.sh, found on PATH.

Rung 7 Errors inside functions

die() { echo "error: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

load_config() {
  [ -r "$1" ] || { echo "cannot read $1" >&2; return 1; }   # report, then return early
  …
}
load_config "$cfg" || die "no usable configuration"

A function reports failure with a non-zero status and a message on stderr. The caller decides whether that ends the script. die is the common helper for "stop now".

Rule Inside functions, check each command that can fail and return 1 with a message. Do not rely on set -e inside them.

Why set -e (chapter 14) is switched off for everything that runs inside a condition: the command after if, while, !, and the left side of && and ||. If the function is called in one of those places, its body runs with set -e off, however deep the calls go.

Trap With set -e on, f() { false; echo "kept going"; } stops the script when f is called on its own line. Called as if f; then, it prints kept going and reports success, because the echo was the last command. The same function is safe or broken depending on how it is called.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/bash
# from a 2008 deploy library
function log {
  echo "[deploy] $*"
}
get_version() ( cd "$1" && cat VERSION )      # body in ( ): a subshell, so no local needed
find_host() { RET=$(grep -m1 "$1" hosts); }   # "returns" a string in a global
setvar() { eval "$1=\$2"; }                   # assign to a variable whose name is in $1
set -A servers web1 web2                      # ksh array syntax
. `dirname $0`/common.sh
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
function name { … } define a function ksh syntax, accepted by bash name() { … } bash yes bash. Dash: syntax error
f() ( … ) a function whose body is a subshell gives it private variables and cd, before local existed local, or a ( ) inside the body only where needed yes, but it can never set anything for its caller
RET=… globals "return" a string functions can only return a number print it and capture with $( ), or printf -v yes, and any other function can overwrite it
eval "$1=\$2" assign to a variable named in $1 no indirect assignment in the Bourne shell printf -v "$1" '%s' "$2", or declare -n ref=$1 (namerefs, bash 4.3) bash 4+ yes, and it runs any code in $1 (chapter 3)
set -A arr … create an array ksh syntax arr=(…) ksh only. Bash: set: -A: invalid option
. `dirname $0`/lib.sh load a file from the script's directory $0 was the only way to know where the script was . "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/lib.sh" yes, but see Trap

Rule Read function f {, subshell bodies and RET globals as pre-local habits, and replace eval assignments with printf -v when you touch them.

Why Each of these works around something bash now does directly: local variables, indirect assignment, arrays.

Trap $(dirname "$0") (and BASH_SOURCE too) gives the directory of the link when the script is run through a symbolic link, a common way to "install" a tool into ~/bin. The library is then looked for in ~/bin and not found. Resolve the link first with readlink -f (on macOS since 12.3, 2022), or install the library where the link is.

Decide

The function needs to give back Use
success or failure, yes or no its exit status: return 0 / return 1
one value (a string, a number) printf it, and the caller writes x=$(f …)
a value, without a subshell, into a variable the caller names printf -v "$name" … bash
several values print them one per line and read them with read or mapfile, or set documented globals
a list print it NUL- or newline-separated, or fill an array the caller names

The golden file

The helper library the remaining scripts share: logging to stderr, die, checks for required programs and the bash version, joining, and run, which shows a command, exactly quoted, before running it (or instead of running it, with DRY_RUN=1). It works on bash 3.2.

cd examples/manual/b08
bash -c 'LIB_PROG=demo; . ./lib.sh; run printf "<%s>\n" "a b" "*"'      # logs "+ printf \<%s\>\\n a\ b \*", then runs it
bash -c '. ./lib.sh; require_bash 4; echo "bash 4 or later"'             # on macOS /bin/bash: error, status 1

Review checklist

Spot the bug

Run as backup-sets.sh photos "music library". It reported a failure for photos, which had just been copied. A colleague on a Mac says it does not run at all.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. declare -A with no version check. On macOS's bash 3.2 it is an invalid option, and with set -e the script stopped at line 6 with status 2. Without set -e it continued with an indexed array whose keys had collapsed, and ${dirs[photos]} pointed at the Documents directory (rung 5). Add a BASH_VERSINFO guard.
  2. for name in $@ and copy_set $name are unquoted, so "music library" was split into music and library, two sets that do not exist (rung 1). Use "$@" and "$name".
  3. cmd="cp -R ${dirs[$1]} $root/"; $cmd is a command in a string. For $HOME/My Music it ran cp -R /home/learner/My Music /tmp/bk/ and failed on My and Music (rung 4). Use cp -R -- "${dirs[$1]}" "$root/", or an array.
  4. copy_set uses name and known without local. Its loop overwrote the caller's name, so the main loop reported FAILED photos for sets that had nothing to do with photos (rung 3).
  5. copy_set is called in an if, so set -e is off inside it. A failed cp was followed by touch, the function returned 0, and the script printed copied … for a set that was never copied (rung 7). Check the copy: cp … || return 1.

Shell manual · 9 · 11 min readProcesses and Signals#

You've met it: exec "$@" at the end of every entrypoint script, which replaces the shell with your program so the program becomes PID 1 and receives the signals · ENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1

Chapter 2 said every command is a process. This chapter is about several processes at once: subshells, background jobs, the signals that stop them, and cleaning up when they do. It is the shell side of what the Docker manual taught about PID 1 and graceful shutdown, and it is what lets a script run work in parallel and still tidy up after itself when someone presses Ctrl-C.

The model

Two operations build everything here. fork makes a child process that is a copy of the shell. exec replaces a process's program with another, keeping the same process (and PID). A normal command is fork, then exec in the child. A subshell is fork without exec: the child keeps running shell code. exec cmd on its own is exec without fork: the shell becomes cmd, which is why exec "$@" makes your program PID 1 in a container. Because a child is a copy, nothing it does to its variables or its current directory reaches the parent (chapter 2).

The ladder

Rung 1 Subshells and grouping

( cd build && make )          # a subshell: the cd is undone when the ( ) ends
echo "still in $PWD"

{ echo "=== report ==="; date; df -h; } > report.txt   # grouping: one redirect for several commands

total=$(du -sb . | cut -f1)   # command substitution runs in a subshell, and its output is captured

( … ) runs its commands in a child shell. { …; } groups commands in the current shell, only so a redirection or a pipe can apply to all of them (note the spaces and the final ; or newline).

Rule Use ( … ) to contain a cd or a changed variable, and { …; } only to share a redirection.

Why The subshell gets its own copy of the directory and the variables, so whatever it changes is thrown away when it ends. That is exactly what you want around a cd.

Trap Anything set inside ( … ) is lost when it ends, and so is anything set in a while loop on the right of a pipe (chapter 7, same cause). ( cd src; VERSION=$(cat VERSION) ) leaves VERSION unset afterwards, with no error. If you need the value, use { …; }, or capture the subshell's output.

Rung 2 Background jobs: &, $! and wait

long-task &                   # run in the background; the shell does not wait
pid=$!                        # the PID of that job (only right after &)
echo "started $pid"
wait "$pid"                   # wait for it; $? is its exit status
echo "it finished with $?"

download a & download b & download c &   # three at once
wait                                      # wait for all background jobs

& starts a command without waiting. $! is the PID of the most recent one. wait PID waits for a specific job and reports its status; plain wait waits for all of them but gives status 0.

Rule Save each background PID in an array as you start the jobs, then wait on each one and check its status.

Why Plain wait tells you only that everything finished, not whether anything failed. To know which job failed, you have to wait for each PID.

Trap download a & download b & wait returns 0 even if both downloads failed, so the script carries on as though the files are there. wait "$pid" after a specific job gives that job's real status (143 if it was terminated, and so on). wait -n bash 4+ returns as soon as any one job finishes, which is how the golden file keeps a fixed number running; macOS's bash 3.2 does not have it.

Rung 3 Signals and exit codes

A signal is a message to a process. The ones that matter in scripts:

Signal Number Sent by Default
SIGINT 2 Ctrl-C stop; exit 130 (128 + 2)
SIGTERM 15 kill PID, docker stop, Kubernetes stop; exit 143 (128 + 15)
SIGHUP 1 terminal closed stop
SIGKILL 9 kill -9 stop at once, cannot be caught
SIGQUIT 3 Ctrl-\ stop and dump core 
kill "$pid"            # send SIGTERM (polite: the program may clean up)
kill -INT "$pid"       # send SIGINT, as Ctrl-C does
kill -9 "$pid"         # send SIGKILL (last resort: no cleanup possible)
kill -0 "$pid"         # send nothing; just check whether the process exists (status 0 if it does)

A process killed by signal n reports exit status 128 + n (chapter 2). That is how wait and $? tell you a job was terminated rather than exiting on its own.

Rule Stop a process with plain kill (SIGTERM) and give it a moment. Use kill -9 only when it ignores that.

Why SIGTERM and SIGINT can be caught, so a program can flush its data and remove its temporary files first. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the program stops mid-write, with no chance to clean up.

Trap kill -9 as a first resort leaves exactly the mess the program's own cleanup would have prevented: a half-written file, a stale lock, a container that never drained. Reach for SIGTERM first; kill -9 is what you send when SIGTERM did not work.

Rung 4 trap: cleaning up on the way out

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$tmp"' EXIT          # runs however the script ends: normally, by error, or by signal

trap 'echo "interrupted" >&2; exit 130' INT    # Ctrl-C: message, then exit (which runs the EXIT trap)
trap 'exit 143' TERM

work_in "$tmp"

trap 'commands' SIGNAL… runs commands when a signal arrives, instead of the default. The pseudo-signal EXIT runs when the shell exits for any reason, which makes it the right place for cleanup.

Rule Create temporary files with mktemp, and remove them in an EXIT trap set right after. Add INT and TERM traps that stop any background children and then exit with the right code.

Why An EXIT trap runs on a normal end, on an error under set -e, and on a signal you turned into an exit. One trap covers every path out of the script, so nothing is left behind.

Trap Bash does run an EXIT trap when a SIGTERM or SIGINT ends the script: in the test, a cleanup-only script sent SIGTERM still removed its files and exited 143. But the trap runs as the shell dies, and a background child the shell started is not its concern, so that child keeps running. Trap INT and TERM explicitly to kill the children first (and to choose the exit status), as the golden file does. SIGKILL (9) runs no trap at all, ever: it cannot be caught.

Rung 5 exec: replace the shell

exec "$@"                              # become the given command (entrypoint scripts end like this)
exec mytool --config /etc/my.conf      # the shell is gone; nothing after this line runs
exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1          # exec with only redirections changes fds, without replacing (chapter 6)

exec cmd replaces the shell process with cmd. The PID stays the same, and there is no extra shell left sitting between the caller and the program.

Rule End a wrapper script that sets things up and then hands off to one long-running program with exec that-program "$@".

Why Without exec, the shell stays as the parent, forwarding signals (or not) and taking up a process slot. With it, the program is the process, so docker stop and kill reach the program directly (the Docker manual's PID 1 problem).

Trap Nothing after exec cmd runs, by design. An exec in the middle of a script, or an EXIT trap you expected to clean up afterwards, silently never happens: exec replaces the shell, traps and all. Put exec last.

Rung 6 Timeouts and whole-group signals

timeout 30 slow-command            # [GNU] kill it after 30s; status 124 if it timed out
timeout -s KILL 30 slow-command    # SIGKILL instead of SIGTERM, for something that ignores TERM

( sleep 5 & wait ) &               # a job and its children; killing the group needs the leader

timeout GNU runs a command with a time limit. On timeout it sends SIGTERM and reports status 124.

Rule Bound any command that can hang (a network fetch, a lock wait) with timeout, and on macOS install GNU coreutils or use a watchdog in the script.

Why A command with no timeout that hangs makes the whole script hang, until a human notices or an outer CI timeout kills it with no useful message.

Trap timeout is GNU and is not on macOS by default: timeout: command not found, status 127. A script that relies on it fails on every Mac, and the failure is a missing command, not a timeout. brew install coreutils provides gtimeout; otherwise write the watchdog yourself (cmd & p=$!; (sleep 30; kill "$p" 2>/dev/null) & …).

Rung 7 Keeping a fixed number running

max=4
for item in "${items[@]}"; do
  while [ "$(jobs -pr | wc -l)" -ge "$max" ]; do   # wait for a free slot
    wait -n 2>/dev/null || sleep 0.1               # [bash 4+], else poll
  done
  process "$item" &
done
wait                                               # let the last ones finish

To run many tasks a few at a time, start a job, and before starting the next one, wait until fewer than max are running. jobs -pr lists the PIDs of still-running background jobs.

Rule Cap parallelism with a slot check (wait -n on bash 4.3+, a poll on 3.2), or hand the whole job to xargs -P (chapter 10).

Why Starting one background job per item, with no cap, can launch thousands at once. They exhaust memory, file descriptors or the remote service's connection limit, and finish slower than a handful at a time would.

Trap for … do fetch "$url" & done; wait with a long list opens every connection at once. The server starts refusing them, and your "parallel" fetch is slower and half-failed. Cap it. wait -n is bash 4+: on bash 3.2 it is invalid option, so the golden file polls with sleep there instead.

Rung 8 Old forms you will meet

#!/bin/sh
# watchdog.sh, mid-2000s
TMP=/tmp/build.$$
trap "rm -f $TMP" 0 1 2 15
( long-build ) & BUILD=$!
( sleep 300; kill $BUILD ) & TIMER=$!
wait $BUILD
PID=`ps ax | grep '[m]yserver' | awk '{print $1}'`
kill -HUP $PID
( cmd & )
nohup ./worker.sh &
Old form What it does Why it existed Write instead Still runs?
trap … 0 1 2 15 trap by number: EXIT, HUP, INT, TERM signal names came later trap … EXIT HUP INT TERM yes, but the numbers are easy to misread
/tmp/build.$$ a temp file named after the PID before mktemp mktemp or mktemp -d yes, but the name is predictable, so in a shared /tmp it is unsafe (see Trap)
( sleep 300; kill $PID ) & a homemade timeout no timeout command timeout 300 cmd GNU yes, and still needed on macOS, which has no timeout
ps ax \| grep '[m]yserver' find a process by name no pgrep. The [m] stops grep matching its own line pgrep -f myserver yes, but fragile: it matches arguments and paths too
grep -v grep drop grep's own line from ps output same, the clumsier way pgrep, or the [m] trick yes
kill -HUP $PID to reload ask a daemon to re-read its config HUP meant "reload" by convention the service's own reload (systemctl reload, an API) yes, where the program still honours it
( cmd & ) start cmd fully detached double fork, so it is not a job of this shell and wait ignores it setsid cmd GNU, or a supervisor yes
nohup cmd & survive the terminal closing terminals send HUP on logout nohup for a one-off; a service manager for anything lasting yes

Rule Replace $$ temp files with mktemp, ps | grep with pgrep, and homemade timeouts with timeout where it exists.

Why Each old form has a sharp edge: a race, a wrong match, a signal the program no longer honours. The modern tools close those edges.

Trap A fixed name like /tmp/build.$$ is predictable ($$ is just the PID), so in a directory everyone can write, such as /tmp, another user can create or point that name at a file they should not be able to touch before your script writes to it. mktemp instead creates a brand-new file with an unguessable name and mode 600 (owner-only), and tells you the name it chose. Use it for every temporary file.

Decide

You want Use
to contain a cd or a variable change ( … ) subshell
one redirection over several commands { …; } group
to run one thing in the background cmd & pid=$!, then wait "$pid"
a fixed number of parallel tasks the slot loop (rung 7), or xargs -P (chapter 10)
to clean up on every exit trap '…' EXIT, plus INT/TERM traps that exit
to hand off to one long program exec cmd "$@" as the last line
a time limit timeout N cmd GNU, or a watchdog on macOS

The golden file

Runs a command over many items, a few at a time, collects each run's output and status, and cleans up on any exit. It uses wait -n on bash 4.3+ and polls on 3.2, and turns Ctrl-C into a tidy stop. It reuses wait-for.sh from chapter 5. Chapter 14's pantry-ctl uses it to check many services at once.

cd examples/manual/b09
./pmap.sh -j 2 sh -c 'echo "$1"; sleep 1' _ -- one two three four   # two at a time, ~2s total
./pmap.sh -j 3 ../b05/wait-for.sh -t 20 -- redis:6379 db:5432       # wait for several ports at once

Review checklist

Spot the bug

Cron runs this nightly to warm a report cache. The log always says it is fine, and the cache is always a day behind.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. ( cd cache ) changes directory in a subshell that ends immediately, so every file is written in the current directory, not in cache/ (rung 1). Use cd cache || exit 1 in the main shell, or write full paths like cache/$name.txt.
  2. The three curls run in the background with &, but nothing waits for them. cat ./*.txt ran before any download finished, so index.txt was built from whatever was already there (rung 2). Add wait before the cat, and check each job's status.
  3. cat ./*.txt reads every .txt in the directory, including yesterday's files and anything unrelated, and (because of bug 1) the reports were written here too. The index was built from stale files, which is why it was a day behind (chapter 7, rung 2, plus bug 1). Read the exact files: cat cache/daily.txt cache/weekly.txt cache/monthly.txt.
  4. There is no set -o pipefail, and curl runs in the background, so a 404 (the monthly.txt that does not exist) never affected the script's status. It printed index built and exited 0 every night (chapter 6, rung 3). Collect each download's status with wait "$pid".
  5. timeout is GNU and missing on macOS, where every curl line failed with timeout: command not found before curl even ran, and the script still exited 0 (rung 6). Guard it (command -v timeout), or drop it in favour of curl --max-time.

Docker manual · 1 · 12 min readEvery Instruction#

In the story: the recipe card, one step per line · Write the Recipe Down

A Dockerfile has about eighteen instructions, and you will write six of them every day. This chapter covers all the ones you will meet. For each one it gives the rule a reviewer applies and the reason behind it, so that when someone hands you a Dockerfile you can say what every line does and which ones are wrong. Two instructions are big enough to get their own chapters: ENTRYPOINT and CMD are in D2, and USER is in D5. Here they appear only where they have to.

Every Dockerfile in this chapter starts from the same idea. Each instruction either changes the filesystem, which makes a new layer, or changes the image's configuration (environment, user, default command, metadata), which costs nothing at runtime. Knowing which kind a line is answers most questions about it.

Changes the filesystem (new layer) Changes the configuration only
RUN, COPY, ADD FROM (picks the starting point), WORKDIR*, ENV, ARG, LABEL, EXPOSE, USER, HEALTHCHECK, STOPSIGNAL, SHELL, ENTRYPOINT, CMD, VOLUME, ONBUILD

* WORKDIR creates the directory if it is missing, which adds a tiny layer the first time.

The ladder

Rung 1 The five lines

Almost every Dockerfile you write starts as these five instructions in this order: a base, a working directory, the files, the build step, the default command.

FROM names the image you build on. Every stage starts with one. WORKDIR sets the directory that every later RUN, COPY, CMD and ENTRYPOINT uses, creating it if needed. Use it instead of RUN cd /app, because a cd lasts only until the end of its own RUN line. COPY <src> <dest> copies from the build context, which is the directory you pass to docker build, not the directory the Dockerfile sits in. RUN executes a command at build time and saves the resulting filesystem as a layer. CMD is what runs when someone starts a container without naming a command.

docker build -t pantry-manual:d01-r1 -f rung1.Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker run --rm -d -p 8001:8080 pantry-manual:d01-r1 && curl -s localhost:8001/livez

Rule Start every Dockerfile from the five lines (FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, CMD), using absolute paths for WORKDIR and exec form (["…"]) for CMD.

Why Each line has one job. WORKDIR persists across instructions while cd does not, and COPY sources are resolved against the build context, so the image is reproducible from that directory alone.

Trap COPY ../shared/lib.py . fails with "not found", however the path looks from where you are standing. A build can only see inside its context. Move the file into the context or make the context bigger (docker build -f app/Dockerfile . from the parent).

Rung 2 ARG and ENV, and where each one is visible

ARG is a build-time variable that you set with --build-arg. ENV is an environment variable baked into the image that every container gets. They look alike, and they have different lifetimes.

Built with --build-arg APP_VERSION=v7:

#5 0.211 PY at build time: ''  APP_VERSION at build time: 'v7'
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d01-r2
PY= APP_VERSION= PANTRY_VERSION=v7

Three things happened. PY was used by FROM (the base really was python:3.12-slim) and is empty inside the stage. An ARG declared before the first FROM is visible only to FROM lines. To use it inside a stage, declare it again with a bare ARG PY after the FROM. APP_VERSION existed during the build and is gone in the container. PANTRY_VERSION survived because an ENV line copied it.

The scope rules in one list:

  • ARG before FROM: visible in FROM lines only. Redeclare it (ARG PY) inside each stage that needs it.
  • ARG inside a stage: visible from that line to the end of that stage. Every stage has its own.
  • ENV: visible from that line on, in this stage and in any stage built FROM this one, and in every container.
  • Both are visible in docker history (D6). Neither is the place for a password.

Rule Use ARG for build inputs and ENV for runtime settings. When a build input must reach runtime, copy it explicitly with ENV X=${X}.

Why ARG values live only for the build of their stage, and an ARG before FROM lives only for the FROM lines. ENV values are written into the image configuration and inherited.

Trap ARG VERSION=1.2 at the top of the file, then RUN echo $VERSION prints an empty line and nothing errors. You notice when a version string or download URL inside the image is blank. Redeclare ARG VERSION after FROM.

Rung 3 COPY, and the two cases where ADD is right

ADD does everything COPY does, plus two surprises. It unpacks local tar archives, and it downloads URLs.

/added:
notes.txt
/copied:
notes.tar.gz
/licenses:
flask.txt

The same notes.tar.gz arrived packed through COPY and unpacked through ADD. If the file had been a .tar.gz you meant to ship as is (a dataset, a backup), ADD would quietly have changed your image. The remote ADD with --checksum is the one form worth keeping. BuildKit downloads the file, checks its SHA-256, and fails the build if it does not match:

ERROR: failed to solve: digest mismatch sha256:489a8e11…07ea: sha256:0000…0000

COPY has useful flags of its own. --chown and --chmod set ownership and mode while copying (D5), --from copies out of another stage or image (D4), and --link puts the copied files in an independent layer that survives a base-image change without a rebuild (D3).

Rule Use COPY for everything local. Use ADD only to unpack a local archive on purpose, or to fetch a remote file with --checksum.

Why COPY does exactly one thing. ADD's extra behaviours depend on what the file is, so the same line does different things to different inputs.

Trap ADD https://…/tool.tar.gz /opt/ without --checksum downloads whatever the server sends today, and a remote archive is not unpacked (only local ones are). You notice when /opt/tool.tar.gz is sitting there unextracted, or when last month's build and today's differ. Add --checksum, or RUN curl … | sha256sum -c in a pipefail shell (rung 5).

Rung 4 EXPOSE and LABEL: configuration, not behaviour

EXPOSE 8080 records that the process listens on 8080. It does not open anything. Without -p, nothing reaches the container from the host. With -P, Docker publishes every exposed port on a random host port:

$ docker run -d --name d01e pantry-manual:d01-r4 ; docker port d01e
$ docker run -d --name d01p -P pantry-manual:d01-r4 ; docker port d01p
8080/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:55000

LABEL adds key/value metadata to the image configuration. Use the OCI keys (org.opencontainers.image.source, .revision, .version, .title, .description, .licenses). Registries show them, scanners and Renovate read source to link an image to its repository, and docker inspect prints them. Group them in one LABEL instruction to keep the configuration tidy.

Rule Write EXPOSE for every port the process listens on, and set the OCI LABELs, knowing neither changes what the container does.

Why Both write to the image configuration only. EXPOSE is read by -P, by humans and by tools. Publishing is always the runner's decision (-p, Compose ports, a Kubernetes Service).

Trap You see EXPOSE 8080 and expect curl localhost:8080 to work, and you get "connection refused" with the container running. docker port <name> shows what is really published, and an empty answer means nothing is.

Rung 5 SHELL and the pipe that hides failures

RUN in shell form (RUN some command) runs through /bin/sh -c. A shell reports the exit status of the last command in a pipe, so a failing command on the left of | is invisible.

#5 3.661 ERROR: No matching distribution found for no-such-package-xyz
#6 0.201 the build carried on

pip failed, tail succeeded, and the build moved on. Switching the shell to bash with pipefail makes the whole pipe fail when any part of it does:

#5 ERROR: process "/bin/bash -o pipefail -c pip download no-such-package-xyz 2>&1 | tail -n 1" did not complete successfully: exit code: 1

SHELL changes the shell for every later shell-form RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT in the stage. Alpine has no bash. There, use SHELL ["/bin/ash", "-eo", "pipefail", "-c"], since busybox ash supports pipefail.

Long RUN lines read better as a heredoc, which BuildKit supports:

RUN <<EOF
set -eux
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
EOF

set -e stops at the first failure, -u fails on unset variables, and -x prints each command in the build log.

Rule Put SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"] (or the ash equivalent) before any RUN that contains a pipe, and use set -eux in multi-line RUN heredocs.

Why A shell's exit status is that of the last command in a pipe, and BuildKit fails a step only on a non-zero exit status.

Trap RUN curl -fsSL $URL | tar -xz with a dead URL "succeeds" and leaves an empty directory. You find out at runtime, when the binary is missing. The build log shows curl's error a few lines above a step marked DONE.

Rung 6 HEALTHCHECK with what the image already has

HEALTHCHECK tells Docker how to test whether the process is working, not just running. docker ps then shows (healthy), (unhealthy) or (health: starting), and Compose can wait for healthy (D9).

The options:

  • --interval: time between checks.
  • --timeout: how long one check may take.
  • --start-period: a grace period during which failures do not count.
  • --retries: consecutive failures before the container is unhealthy.

The command must exit 0 for healthy and 1 for unhealthy.

The common mistake is the one in this file:

d01hg  Up 16 seconds (healthy)
d01hb  Up 17 seconds (unhealthy)
$ docker inspect -f '{{json (index .State.Health.Log 0).Output}}' d01hb
"/bin/sh: 1: curl: not found\n"

The app was fine. The check could not run, because -slim images do not ship curl. Use the language runtime the image already has, or a tiny static probe binary in distroless images.

Two limits are worth knowing. Docker only reports health. It does not restart an unhealthy container on its own (Compose's restart and Swarm do different things, D9). And Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK completely, because it uses probes (K4).

Rule Write HEALTHCHECK in exec form, using only binaries the final image contains, with a --start-period that covers startup.

Why The check runs inside the container, so a missing tool fails every check. --start-period keeps a slow start from counting as failure.

Trap The container is unhealthy and the app answers fine. docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' <name> shows the check's own output, which is usually "not found" or a connection error to the wrong port.

Rung 7 VOLUME belongs to the runner, not the image

VOLUME /data in a Dockerfile tells Docker to mount a volume at /data in every container, and to create an anonymous one if the runner did not provide one.

$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d01-r7
late.txt
seed.txt
volumes before=119 after two plain runs=121

Every docker run without --rm and without its own mount left behind a new anonymous volume, named by a 64-character hash, which nothing will ever reuse. On a CI machine that builds and runs tests a hundred times a day, that is a hundred volumes a day.

Notice late.txt. With BuildKit (the default builder since Docker Engine 23.0, 2023), a RUN after VOLUME keeps its changes. The legacy builder threw them away, which is why older advice says "never modify a path after declaring it a volume". The leak exists with either builder.

Rule Do not put VOLUME in application images. Let the runner mount storage (-v, Compose volumes, a Kubernetes volume, D8).

Why VOLUME cannot be undone by a child image or by the runner. Every container gets a volume at that path whether it wants one or not, and anonymous volumes outlive their containers unless removed with -v.

Trap docker volume ls shows hundreds of hash-named volumes and the disk fills up. docker volume ls -f dangling=true lists the orphans, and docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Volumes}}' <image> shows which image declares them.

Rung 8 ONBUILD and other lines to recognise

ONBUILD <instruction> stores an instruction in the image and runs it when another Dockerfile uses this image as its FROM. It was popular for "builder" base images. You will meet it in old repositories, and you should not write it.

A child Dockerfile that says only FROM pantry-manual:d01-onbuild-base and CMD [...] fails with an error about a line it does not contain:

#6 [2/4] ONBUILD COPY requirements.txt .
ERROR: failed to solve: … "/requirements.txt": not found

Other lines to recognise and replace:

  • MAINTAINER name: deprecated. Use LABEL org.opencontainers.image.authors=….
  • STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT: which signal docker stop sends. D2 covers it.
  • # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1: the first line of a file, not an instruction. It pins the Dockerfile frontend to the latest stable 1.x, so features such as heredocs, --checksum and RUN --mount work on any BuildKit, whatever the daemon's own version.
  • # check=error=true: makes BuildKit's build checks fail the build instead of warning (see Decide).

Rule Do not write ONBUILD. Give child images explicit COPY and RUN lines, and start every Dockerfile with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.

Why ONBUILD triggers are invisible in the file you are reading (only docker inspect shows them). The syntax line makes features independent of the Docker version on the machine that builds.

Trap A build fails on COPY requirements.txt and your Dockerfile has no such line. docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.OnBuild}}' <base image> reveals the hidden steps.

Decide

You want to… Use Not
Copy local files COPY ADD
Unpack a local .tar.* into the image ADD file.tar.gz /dest/ COPY + RUN tar (an extra layer holding the archive)
Download a file at build time ADD --checksum=sha256:… <url> ADD <url> with no checksum
Pass a value into the build ARG + --build-arg ENV (it leaks into every container)
Configure the running app ENV (defaults), runtime -e / Compose / ConfigMap (real values) ARG (gone at runtime)
Pass a secret into the build RUN --mount=type=secret (D6) ARG or ENV (both readable in docker history)
Persistent data a mount chosen by the runner (D8) VOLUME in the image
Strict builds # check=error=true ignoring the warnings

BuildKit runs a set of build checks on every build and prints warnings such as JSONArgsRecommended (shell-form CMD), UndefinedVar and FromAsCasing. docker build --check . runs only the checks, and the # check=error=true directive under the syntax line turns warnings into failures. In CI, use the directive.

The golden file

Every instruction from the ladder, used the way a reviewer expects in a single-stage image. D4 splits it into stages, and D5 hardens it into the final golden Dockerfile.

docker build -t pantry-manual:d01 --build-arg PANTRY_VERSION=v3 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker network create d01net
docker run -d --rm --name d01-redis --network d01net --network-alias redis redis:7-alpine
docker run -d --rm --name d01-web --network d01net -p 8001:8080 pantry-manual:d01
curl -s localhost:8001/           # Hello from Pantry (v3). You are visitor #1. …
docker ps --format '{{.Status}}'  # Up 14 seconds (healthy)

requirements-serve.txt is Pantry's own requirements.txt plus gunicorn, a production WSGI server. Flask's built-in server is for development, and it has no SIGTERM handler, which D2 shows matters.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A Dockerfile from a pull request. It builds, and the container serves requests.

This file has 6 problems.

Show answers
  1. FROM python:latest is unpinned, and it is the full image. On the day of testing it resolved to Python 3.15.1 and produced a 1.66 GB image, against 205 MB for the golden file. Pin python:3.12-slim (and by digest, D6).
  2. ADD . . uses ADD where COPY is meant. Because it copies the whole context before installing dependencies, every code change reinstalls everything (D3), and Dockerfiles, gitops/ and old-maps/ ended up in the image. Copy requirements*.txt first and app.py after the install.
  3. pip install … | tee without pipefail hides a failed install. With flask==99.0.0 in requirements, pip printed "No matching distribution" and the build still produced an image. Add the SHELL line from rung 5, or drop the tee. pip also runs without --no-cache-dir, which leaves 1.9 MB of cache in the layer.
  4. VOLUME /app gives every container an anonymous volume over the code directory, and they pile up. Remove it.
  5. There is no USER, so the process runs as uid=0(root). Add a numeric non-root user (D5).
  6. CMD python app.py is shell form. /bin/sh is PID 1, the build prints JSONArgsRecommended, and docker stop waited the full 10 seconds before killing it. Use exec form with a server that handles SIGTERM (D2).

Docker manual · 2 · 10 min readENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1#

In the story: the dish the kitchen always makes, and the default order if nobody asks for anything else · Write the Recipe Down, The Night It Fell Over

Two lines decide how your container starts. Two facts about Linux decide whether it stops. Most "my container takes ten seconds to stop", "my arguments are ignored" and "Ctrl-C does nothing" problems come from one of these four things, and none of them shows up until you look.

The two lines are ENTRYPOINT and CMD. Docker glues them into one command line. The two facts are both about the first process in a container. It has process ID 1, and in Linux PID 1 is special in two ways. Signals it has no handler for are ignored instead of killing it, and it inherits every orphaned process in the container and is expected to reap them.

The ladder

Rung 1 Exec form and shell form

Both CMD and ENTRYPOINT (and RUN) come in two forms. Exec form is a JSON array, CMD ["python", "app.py"]. Docker runs that program directly, with those arguments. Shell form is plain text, CMD python app.py. Docker wraps it as /bin/sh -c "python app.py".

$ docker exec d02-shell cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '
/bin/sh -c python app.py
$ time docker stop d02-shell
11s

The shell is PID 1. docker stop sends SIGTERM to the shell, the shell does not pass it to Python, and after ten seconds Docker gives up and sends SIGKILL. BuildKit warns about exactly this. The build prints JSONArgsRecommended: JSON arguments recommended for CMD to prevent unintended behavior related to OS signals.

Exec form has one limit: no shell means no variable expansion. CMD ["echo", "$HOME"] prints $HOME literally. When you need expansion, use an entrypoint script (rung 6), or CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec mytool --port \"$PORT\""] with an explicit exec.

Rule Write CMD and ENTRYPOINT in exec form, every time.

Why Exec form makes your program PID 1, so it receives signals directly. Shell form puts /bin/sh in front, and the shell does not forward them.

Trap docker stop always takes exactly ten seconds, and the exit code is 137 (128 + 9, killed). docker exec <name> cat /proc/1/cmdline shows /bin/sh -c … as PID 1.

Rung 2 ENTRYPOINT and CMD together

When both are set, Docker runs ENTRYPOINT followed by CMD. CMD becomes the default arguments, and docker run IMAGE args… replaces them. Measured on Alpine with echo:

ENTRYPOINT CMD docker run IMG docker run IMG x y
(none) ["echo","cmd"] cmd runs x y (here: "x: executable file not found")
["echo","ep"] (none) ep ep x y
["echo","ep"] ["cmd"] ep cmd ep x y
echo ep (shell) ["cmd"] ep ep
["echo","ep"] echo cmd (shell) ep /bin/sh -c echo cmd ep x y

Read the last two rows twice. A shell-form ENTRYPOINT swallows CMD and the run arguments: they become arguments to sh -c, which ignores them. A shell-form CMD under an exec-form ENTRYPOINT passes the literal words /bin/sh -c … as arguments.

So the useful patterns are:

  • Tool image: ENTRYPOINT ["mytool"] plus CMD ["--help"]. docker run img --version works naturally.
  • Service image: ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"] plus CMD ["server", "--flags"]. You can still run docker run img sh to debug (rung 6).
  • Simple image: CMD ["server", "--flags"] with no ENTRYPOINT. The whole command is replaceable.
ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "ep"]
CMD ["cmd"]

Rule Put what always runs in exec-form ENTRYPOINT and the overridable defaults in exec-form CMD, or use CMD alone.

Why Docker concatenates ENTRYPOINT + (docker run arguments, or else CMD). Only exec form keeps those arguments as separate words.

Trap docker run myimage --debug behaves exactly like docker run myimage. docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}}' myimage shows a string wrapped in ["/bin/sh","-c",…], which is shell form.

Rung 3 Overriding at run time

Everything after the image name replaces CMD. --entrypoint replaces ENTRYPOINT, and it also clears CMD:

$ docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}' pantry-manual:d02-t3
["echo","ep"] ["cmd"]
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint echo pantry-manual:d02-t3 overridden
overridden
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint echo pantry-manual:d02-t3
                                         ← empty: not "cmd"

--entrypoint takes a single executable, not a command line. --entrypoint "python -m pdb" fails. Use --entrypoint python IMG -m pdb app.py. Compose has the same two keys, entrypoint: and command: (D9), and Kubernetes calls them command: and args: (K2). Note that Kubernetes' command replaces ENTRYPOINT, not CMD. The Bridge chapter maps all of them.

docker run --rm --entrypoint sh pantry-manual:d02 -c 'id; ls /app'     # debug shell, bypassing the entrypoint
docker run --rm pantry-manual:d02 --version                             # arguments replace CMD only

Rule Override CMD with arguments after the image name, and use --entrypoint only to get a debugging shell, passing everything you need after the image.

Why --entrypoint resets CMD to empty by design, because the old defaults were written for the old entrypoint.

Trap docker run --entrypoint /usr/local/bin/myserver img starts with no flags at all and fails on "missing --config". The defaults you expected lived in CMD, which --entrypoint threw away.

Rung 4 PID 1 ignores signals it does not handle

Exec form is necessary, and it is not sufficient. Here is Pantry's Flask development server, in exec form:

$ docker exec d02-exec cat /proc/1/cmdline   →  python app.py
$ time docker stop d02-exec                  →  10s

Python is PID 1 now, and it still takes ten seconds. Normally SIGTERM's default action is "terminate". For PID 1 the kernel does not apply default actions: a signal is delivered only if the process installed a handler. Python installs a handler for SIGINT (it raises KeyboardInterrupt) but not for SIGTERM. That gives three fixes, each verified:

  1. Run a program that handles SIGTERM. gunicorn, nginx, the JVM, Node with a process.on('SIGTERM') handler, Go with signal.Notify. The D1 golden image stopped in 0.7 s.
  2. Tell Docker to send a signal it does handle. STOPSIGNAL SIGINT stopped the Flask server in under a second:
  1. Put a real init in front with --init (rung 5). It stopped in 1 s.

The best fix is the first one. A process that handles SIGTERM can finish in-flight requests, and the other two only make it die faster.

Rule Make sure PID 1 handles SIGTERM, preferably by running a server that drains on SIGTERM, otherwise with STOPSIGNAL or an init.

Why The kernel never applies a default signal action to a namespace's PID 1, so a signal without a handler is simply dropped.

Trap The command is in exec form and docker stop still takes the full timeout. Look for the exit code: 137 means it was killed, while 0 or 143 (128 + 15) means it exited on SIGTERM.

Rung 5 An init process, and zombies

PID 1 has a second job. When a process dies, its parent must call wait() to collect its exit status. Until then it is a zombie, an entry in the process table. When the parent dies first, the orphan is re-parented to PID 1, and PID 1 must reap it. A program that never expected to be PID 1 does not do this:

docker run -d --name z alpine:3.20 sh -c 'for i in 1 2 3; do (sleep 0.1 &); done; exec sleep 300'
docker exec z ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm

PID   PPID  STAT COMMAND
    1     0 S    sleep
    8     1 Z    sleep
   10     1 Z    sleep
   12     1 Z    sleep

With --init, Docker starts its bundled tini as PID 1 (/sbin/docker-init). It runs your command as its child, forwards signals to it, and reaps every orphan:

$ docker run -d --init --name z2 alpine:3.20 sh -c '…same…'
