docker run --rm -v d08-named:/named -v "$PWD/bind":/bind --tmpfs /scratch alpine:3.20 sh -c 'cat /named/f /bind/f'

/container  gone
/named      hi
/bind       hi
/scratch    gone
  • Named volume (-v name:/path): storage Docker manages (under /var/lib/docker/volumes on Linux, inside the VM on Desktop). It survives docker rm, needs no host path, and keeps real Linux ownership. Use it for databases and any app data.
  • Bind mount (-v /host/path:/path): a host directory, shared live. Use it for source code during development and for config files you edit on the host. On Docker Desktop it crosses the VM boundary, which is slower for heavy I/O and remaps ownership (D5, rung 6).
  • tmpfs (--tmpfs /path): memory, gone when the container stops. Use it for scratch space and for secrets the app writes at runtime, especially with --read-only (D5).

Rule Put persistent data in named volumes, development source in bind mounts and scratch in tmpfs, and nothing important in the container's writable layer.

Why Each kind has a different lifetime and owner: Docker, the host, or memory. Only named volumes are both persistent and independent of a host path.

Trap After docker compose down and up, or a redeploy, the data is gone. It was written to a path with no mount, inside the container's writable layer. docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' <name> shows which paths are mounted.

Rung 2 Copy-up happens once, and only for empty volumes

When an empty named volume is mounted over a directory that has content in the image, Docker copies that content (and its ownership) into the volume. It happens once. After that, the volume's content wins, whatever newer images contain:

new volume over /srv/assets, v1 image:   VERSION app.css   → v1
same volume, v2 image:                   VERSION app.css   → v1     (v2's files and new.js never appear)
empty bind mount over /srv/assets:       0 entries                  (bind mounts hide, never copy)
--mount …,volume-nocopy:                 0 entries

docker run --rm -v d08-assets:/srv/assets pantry-manual:d08-v1 cat /srv/assets/VERSION    # v1, copied up
docker run --rm -v d08-assets:/srv/assets pantry-manual:d08-v2 cat /srv/assets/VERSION    # still v1

That is the right behaviour for data: a database's files must not be replaced by an image's defaults. It is a disaster for anything that belongs to the image, such as code, static assets or default config. Mount volumes only on paths that hold data the image does not ship. Copy-up is also why the golden Dockerfile creates /data owned by 10001: a new volume there starts with the right owner (D5).

Rule Mount volumes only over data directories, never over paths whose content ships with the image (code, assets, bundled config).

Why Docker copies image content into a volume only while it is empty. Later images cannot update a non-empty volume.

Trap The new release is deployed, the container runs the new image, and users still see the old CSS or old behaviour. docker inspect shows a volume mounted over the app directory, which serves the first version forever.

Rung 3 Prefer --mount, and read-only where you can

-v is short and forgiving. Given a host path that does not exist, it creates an empty directory and mounts that. A typo silently becomes "no config":

-v ./confg:/etc/app          → container sees 0 files; an empty "confg" directory appears on the host
--mount type=bind,src=./confg,dst=/etc/app
                             → invalid mount config for type "bind": bind source path does not exist

--mount takes explicit key=value pairs (type, src, dst, readonly, volume-nocopy, tmpfs-size) and fails on a missing source. Mount anything the container only reads as read-only. A compromised process then cannot tamper with config or with shared data:

docker run --mount type=bind,src="$PWD/config",dst=/etc/pantry,readonly pantry-manual:d05
docker run -v pantry-manual-data:/data:ro alpine:3.20 ls /data                    # short form, read-only

sh: can't create /data/f: Read-only file system

Rule Write mounts with --mount in scripts and docs, and add readonly (:ro) to every mount the container does not need to write.

Why --mount turns a missing source into an error instead of an empty directory, and read-only mounts make writes fail loudly.

Trap A container starts with default settings even though you mounted a config directory. ls on the host shows a new, empty directory next to the real one (confg/ beside config/), created by -v.

Rung 4 Back up and restore through a throwaway container

You never need to know where Docker keeps a volume on disk. To back it up, mount it read-only into a small container next to a host directory, and write a tarball:

The restore mirrors it, and refuses to overwrite a non-empty volume unless told to:

$ docker exec d08-redis redis-cli SAVE
OK
$ ./backup.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups
./backups/pantry-manual-data-20261023T233219Z.tar.gz
$ docker volume rm pantry-manual-data && ./restore.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups/pantry-manual-data-…tar.gz
restored … into pantry-manual-data
visits after restore: 5

--numeric-owner keeps the files' UIDs (Redis's 999 here), so the restored data is readable by the same user. Consistency is the application's business: tar copies files, not transactions. Flush first (redis-cli SAVE, pg_dump instead of copying PostgreSQL's files), or stop the writer for the duration.

Rule Back up volumes with a throwaway container that mounts the volume read-only, after making the application flush or pause, and test restores on a schedule.

Why The container sees the volume as plain files wherever Docker stores them. A backup that has never been restored is a guess.

Trap The backup file is never on the host. The tar wrote into the throwaway container's own filesystem, which --rm deleted, because no host directory was mounted as the destination. Check that the file exists after every run.

Rung 5 Anonymous volumes and how they leak

A volume without a name is anonymous. You get one from -v /path with no name, and from any image that declares VOLUME when you do not mount that path yourself. The official Redis image declares VOLUME /data:

$ docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Volumes}}' redis:7-alpine
{"/data":{}}
$ docker run -d --name d08-anon redis:7-alpine
volume ed73e237d52ca4f2… -> /data
$ docker rm -f d08-anon
ed73e237d52ca4f2… still exists

The data is not lost, but nothing will ever mount that volume again. The next docker run gets a new, empty one. The machine these examples ran on had 121 such orphans. Clean up deliberately:

docker rm -v <container>                   # remove a container and its anonymous volumes
docker run --rm …                          # --rm also removes the anonymous volumes
docker volume ls -f dangling=true          # volumes no container references
docker volume prune                        # removes unused *anonymous* volumes; -a includes named ones

Rule Name every volume you care about, run throwaway containers with --rm, and remove anonymous volumes with rm -v or volume prune.

Why Anonymous volumes outlive their containers but have no name to find them by, so data in them is effectively lost and disk usage only grows.

Trap After recreating a database container, the app starts with an empty database, and the old data is in a hash-named volume. docker volume ls -f dangling=true and docker run --rm -v <hash>:/d alpine ls /d find it. Copy it into a named volume.

Rung 6 tmpfs options, drivers and disk accounting

A tmpfs defaults to half of the machine's memory (3.9 GB in this VM), and it counts against the container's memory limit. Size it and set its mode:

docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m,mode=1777 alpine:3.20 df -h /tmp
docker run --mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=67108864 alpine:3.20 df -h /tmp
docker system df -v                     # space per image, container, volume and build cache

tmpfs                    64.0M         0     64.0M   0% /tmp
dd … stopped at 67108864 bytes (64.0MB)

Volume drivers put a named volume somewhere other than local disk. The built-in local driver can mount NFS or CIFS (syntax: docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=<server>,rw --opt device=:/export pantry-nfs; not run here, it needs an NFS server), and plugins target cloud block storage. Network storage behaves very differently under databases: latency, locking, fsync. Single-host Docker rarely needs it. Kubernetes' PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses are the standard answer at that scale (K7).

Rule Give every tmpfs a size, and check docker system df -v before blaming anything else for a full disk.

Why An unsized tmpfs can take half the host's memory, and volumes and build cache are the usual hidden consumers of disk.

Trap Processes in a memory-limited container die with Killed under load though their own memory looks small. They filled an unsized tmpfs, which counts against the limit: with --memory 64m, writing 200 MB to /tmp got dd killed and docker inspect reported OOMKilled=true. Size the tmpfs below the limit.

Decide

Data Mount Options
Database files, uploads named volume owner set by the image's directory (copy-up)
Source code in development bind mount :ro if the container must not write; --user $(id -u) on Linux
Config edited on the host bind mount, single file or directory readonly
Scratch, caches, PID files tmpfs size=…
Secrets at runtime tmpfs (or a secret mount in Compose, D10) mode=0700
Code, assets, bundled defaults none: they belong in the image
Shared between hosts Kubernetes PV, or NFS via the local driver test fsync and locking

The golden file

Backup and restore for any named volume. Run against Pantry's Redis volume, it round-trips the visit count and keeps owners intact.

docker exec pantry-redis redis-cli SAVE
./backup.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups
FORCE=1 ./restore.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups/pantry-manual-data-<timestamp>.tar.gz

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Pantry with a nightly backup."

This file has 3 problems.

Show answers
  1. Redis has no -v, so its data goes into an anonymous volume created by the image's VOLUME /data. After docker rm -f pantry-redis and the same docker run, Pantry said "You are visitor #1", and the old count was stranded in a hash-named volume. Add -v pantry-data:/data.
  2. -v pantry-code:/app puts a named volume over the code directory. Copy-up filled it once, and after upgrading to an image whose app.py was changed, the container still served the old text. Remove the mount: code belongs in the image.
  3. The backup writes /backup.tar.gz into the throwaway container's own filesystem, and --rm deletes it. No backup file existed anywhere afterwards. Mount a host directory as the destination, flush Redis first (redis-cli SAVE), and read the volume read-only, as backup.sh does.

Docker manual · 9 · 9 min readCompose: The File#

In the story: a dinner menu that cooks several dishes together · The Whole Band

A Compose file describes a project: services (containers built or pulled from one definition), the networks they share, and the volumes they keep. docker compose up turns that description into containers, and running it again changes only what differs. Everything earlier chapters did with docker run flags (ports, mounts, users, capabilities, health checks) has a key here. What Compose adds is relationships: who starts after whom, what counts as ready, and which values come from outside the file.

The golden file for this chapter is Pantry: a built web service, Redis with a health check and a named volume, and a one-shot seed job that must succeed before the web service starts.

The ladder

Rung 1 Services: build, image, and the project

A service either builds an image from a Dockerfile or runs an existing image. With both keys, Compose builds and tags the result with the given name, instead of the generated <project>-<service>:

services:
  web:
    build:
      context: ../../pantry                 # the app's own directory
      dockerfile: ../manual/d05/Dockerfile  # the golden Dockerfile (path relative to the context)
      additional_contexts:
        manual: ../d05                      # what --build-context manual=… did on the command line
    image: pantry-manual:d09
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

The project is the unit Compose manages. Its name comes from the top-level name: key (here pantry-manual-d09), from -p, or from the directory's name. Containers (pantry-manual-d09-web-1), the default network (pantry-manual-d09_default) and volumes (pantry-manual-d09_redis-data) are all prefixed with it, so two copies of the same file in different directories do not collide. Set name: explicitly so the project does not change identity when someone renames a folder.

Rule Give every Compose file a top-level name:, and give built services both build: and an image: name.

Why The project name prefixes every container, network and volume. An explicit name keeps them stable, and a named image can be pushed or reused by other services.

Trap After a colleague clones the repository into a differently named directory, docker compose up starts with an empty database. The project name came from the directory, so the volume name changed (foo_redis-data became bar_redis-data). docker volume ls shows both.

Rung 2 Ports, and the reachability you get for free

Every project gets its own network, and services reach each other by service name on any port. Publish only what the host needs, on loopback, with the port configurable:

    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT:-8000}:8080"  # loopback only; the host port is configurable

redis     running   Up 13 seconds (healthy)   6379/tcp
web       running   Up 6 seconds (healthy)    127.0.0.1:8000->8080/tcp

Redis shows 6379/tcp with no host side: the port exists on the project network and nowhere else. expose: exists, but like the Dockerfile's EXPOSE it only documents (D7, rung 3). Quote port mappings: unquoted 60:60 style values were once parsed by YAML 1.1 as base-60 numbers, and quoting avoids the whole class of problem.

Rule Publish only entry points, always as quoted strings with 127.0.0.1: for local work, and let services reach each other by service name.

Why Compose's project network already connects every service. ports: is only for traffic from outside Docker, and a bare host port binds every interface.

Trap docker compose ps shows 0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp for a database. Anyone who can reach the machine can reach the database (the spot-the-bug file answered PONG from the LAN).

Rung 3 environment, env_file and .env are three different things

These three are confused more than anything else in Compose:

  • environment: sets variables in the container.
  • env_file: loads variables from a file into the container.
  • .env (next to the Compose file) feeds interpolation of the Compose file itself, the ${VAR} expressions, and nothing else.
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis                     # the service name is a DNS name on the project network
      GREETING: ${GREETING:-Hello from Pantry}

Measured:

.env: GREETING=Hello from .env              → "Hello from .env (dev)…"
.env: UNUSED_SECRET=…  (not referenced)     → absent in the container
shell GREETING=… and .env                   → "Hello from the shell (dev)…"   (shell wins)
neither                                     → "Hello from Pantry" (the :- default)
env_file BOTH=from-env_file, environment BOTH=from-environment → BOTH=from-environment

Interpolation order, highest first: the shell's environment, then --env-file/.env, then the default written in the file. Inside the container, environment: wins over env_file:. The operators:

Expression Unset or empty Use
${VAR} empty string (with a warning) rarely
${VAR:-default} default optional settings
${VAR:?message} error, Compose refuses to run required settings and secrets
$$ a literal $ shell commands in command: 
error while interpolating services.web.environment.DB_PASSWORD: required variable DB_PASSWORD is missing a value: set DB_PASSWORD in .env or the shell

Rule Put container settings in environment: with ${VAR:-default} or ${VAR:?message}, keep .env for interpolation values (and out of git when it holds secrets), and remember that .env does not reach the container by itself.

Why Compose resolves ${…} before creating anything, from the shell first and .env second, while the container only ever sees environment: and env_file:.

Trap A variable in .env is "ignored" by the app. It is never passed to the container unless environment: references it (FOO: ${FOO}) or an env_file: lists the file. docker compose config shows the final environment.

Rung 4 Named volumes and networks belong to the project

Top-level volumes: and networks: declare resources that services mount or join by name, created with the project prefix:

  redis:
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data                    # named: survives "down", unlike the image's anonymous VOLUME
volumes:
  redis-data:

pantry-manual-d09_redis-data
$ docker compose down        → containers and network removed, volume kept
$ docker compose down -v     → named volumes declared in the file removed too

Leave out the named volume and Redis's image-declared VOLUME /data still creates an anonymous one. It survives docker compose up re-creations, but down followed by up gets a new, empty one: the spot-the-bug project went from a counter of 1 to 0. To use a volume or network that exists outside the project (shared, or created by an operator), mark it external: true with its real name:, and Compose will neither create nor delete it.

volumes:
  shared-uploads:
    external: true
    name: uploads-prod

Rule Declare every persistent path as a named volume under top-level volumes:, and treat down -v as "delete the data".

Why Named project volumes are created once and reused across up/down cycles. Anonymous volumes are tied to one container's lifetime in practice.

Trap docker compose down && docker compose up -d and the database is empty. docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' <container> shows a 64-character anonymous volume name instead of <project>_<name>.

Rung 5 Health checks and depends_on conditions

depends_on: [redis] only orders container starts. It does not wait for Redis to be ready. With a database that takes a few seconds to start, the one-shot seed job ran too early:

seed-1  | Could not connect to Redis at redis:6379: Connection refused

Give the dependency a healthcheck, and depend on its health:

  redis:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 15
      start_period: 5s
  seed:
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: "no"
  web:
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy          # not just "started": answering PING
      seed:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

The three conditions are service_started (the default), service_healthy (needs a healthcheck) and service_completed_successfully (for jobs: migrations, seeding, cache warm-up). docker compose up -d --wait blocks until every service is running and healthy (or a job has exited 0), and returns non-zero if not. Use it in scripts and CI instead of sleep.

 Container pantry-manual-d09-redis-1  Healthy
 Container pantry-manual-d09-seed-1  Exited
 Container pantry-manual-d09-web-1  Healthy

Startup ordering is not a substitute for retries. Dependencies restart independently later, so the app must still survive a database that goes away for a while.

Rule Give every dependency a healthcheck, depend on service_healthy (or service_completed_successfully for jobs), and start with up --wait.

Why "Started" means the process exists, not that it accepts connections. The healthcheck is the only readiness signal Compose has.

Trap The stack works on a fast laptop and fails on CI with "connection refused" in the first seconds. depends_on was a plain list, so the app raced the database's startup.

Rung 6 Restart policies

restart: tells Docker what to do when the container's main process exits. Measured with a process that exits after one second:

restart: exit 3 (crash) exit 0 (finished) after docker stop/kill
"no" (default) stays exited (0 restarts) stays exited stays stopped
on-failure:2 restarted twice, then gives up stays exited stays stopped
unless-stopped restarted forever (7 in 20 s) restarted forever stays stopped, also after a daemon restart
always restarted forever restarted forever stays stopped until the daemon restarts

Services use unless-stopped. One-shot jobs must use "no" (or on-failure): the spot-the-bug file gave its seed job restart: always, and it ran 8 times in 15 seconds and never stopped. Three details:

  • Docker does not restart a container for being unhealthy. Only Swarm and Kubernetes act on health.
  • /crash killed one gunicorn worker, the master respawned it, and the container never restarted. Supervision inside the container hides crashes from Docker.
  • A manual docker kill or docker stop is never undone by unless-stopped.
    restart: unless-stopped

Rule Use restart: unless-stopped for long-running services and restart: "no" for jobs.

Why Restart policies react only to the main process exiting, and always/unless-stopped treat a successful exit like a crash.

Trap docker compose ps shows a job in Restarting (0) forever. Exit code 0 plus restart: always loops, re-running the job (and its side effects) every few seconds.

Rung 7 Overriding the command, running one-offs, and exec

command: replaces the image's CMD, and entrypoint: replaces its ENTRYPOINT (and, as with --entrypoint, clears CMD, D2). Write both in exec form (lists). In list form, $ must be doubled ($$HOME) when you mean the container's variable rather than Compose interpolation.

  seed:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-cli", "-h", "redis", "SET", "visits", "${SEED_VISITS:-0}", "NX"]

Two commands cover day-to-day use:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python -c "print('one-off in a fresh web container')"   # new container, same config
docker compose exec web id                                                                     # inside the running one

run starts a new container from the service's definition (same image, environment, volumes and networks). --rm removes it afterwards, --no-deps skips starting dependencies, and --service-ports is needed if you want its ports: published. exec enters the existing container.

Rule Override with command:/entrypoint: in list form, run one-off tasks with compose run --rm, and inspect running services with compose exec.

Why run reuses the service's full configuration without touching the running container, and list form avoids shell parsing and signal problems.

Trap docker compose run web leaves a growing list of pantry-manual-d09-web-run-… containers in docker ps -a. Add --rm.

Rung 8 docker compose config is the truth

Compose merges files, applies defaults, resolves ${…}, converts short syntax to long, and warns about obsolete keys before it does anything. docker compose config prints the result. Every "why is it using that value" question starts there:

docker compose config                       # the fully resolved project
docker compose config --quiet               # validate only: exit code and errors
docker compose config --services            # list service names

WARN … the attribute `version` is obsolete, it will be ignored, please remove it to avoid potential confusion

The top-level version: key is from the Compose v1 file formats and Compose v2 ignores it, so delete it. Run docker compose config --quiet in CI. It catches YAML errors, unknown keys, and required variables that are unset.

Rule Validate every Compose file with docker compose config --quiet in CI, and read docker compose config when a value surprises you.

Why It shows exactly what Compose will act on after interpolation and merging, which is often not what the file appears to say.

Trap A setting "has no effect". docker compose config shows it under the wrong service or misspelled, or replaced by an override file (D10).

Decide

You want Compose
Wait for a database healthcheck + depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
Migrations before the app job service, restart: "no", condition: service_completed_successfully
A required secret value ${VAR:?message} (better: secrets:, D10)
An optional setting ${VAR:-default}
Settings for the container environment: (or env_file:)
Values for the file itself .env / shell variables
Data that survives down top-level named volume
A resource managed elsewhere external: true + name:
A one-off task docker compose run --rm <service> <cmd>
Scripted startup docker compose up -d --wait

The golden file

Pantry as one Compose file: the golden Dockerfile built through additional_contexts, loopback-only publishing with a configurable port, interpolated settings with defaults, health-gated startup with a seed job, the D5 runtime hardening as Compose keys, and a named volume.

docker compose config --quiet && docker compose up -d --wait     # redis Healthy → seed Exited → web Healthy
curl -s localhost:8000/                                          # Hello from Pantry (dev). You are visitor #1. …
docker compose down                                              # keeps pantry-manual-d09_redis-data

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Pantry with a seed job." It comes up, and the web page loads.

This file has 6 problems.

Show answers
  1. version: "3.8" is obsolete. Compose warns "the attribute version is obsolete, it will be ignored". Delete it, and add name:.
  2. REDIS_HOST=localhost makes web talk to itself: "Redis at 'localhost' is unreachable". Use redis.
  3. depends_on lists only order starts. The seed job ran before Redis accepted connections ("Could not connect to Redis at redis:6379: Connection refused"). Add a Redis healthcheck and use condition: service_healthy (and service_completed_successfully for web on seed).
  4. restart: always on a one-shot job restarts it after every successful exit: 8 restarts in 15 seconds, state Restarting (0). Use restart: "no".
  5. ports: "6379:6379" publishes Redis on every interface (PONG from the LAN address), and "8000:8080" does the same for web. Remove Redis's ports: and bind web to 127.0.0.1.
  6. Redis has no named volume, so its data lives in the anonymous volume from the image's VOLUME /data. After down and up, the visit count was back to 0 in a new anonymous volume. Add redis-data:/data with a top-level volumes: entry.

Docker manual · 10 · 10 min readCompose: The Project#

In the story: the same dinner menu, cooked for a weeknight and for a wedding · The Whole Band

D9 wrote one file for one environment. Real projects have several environments (a laptop with live reload, CI, a staging host, production), optional tools, secrets that must stay out of git, and parts owned by different teams. Compose handles all of it with a few mechanisms:

  • several files merged in order;
  • profiles;
  • include;
  • extension fields;
  • secrets;
  • develop.watch.

Each mechanism has one rule that surprises people. This chapter measures all of them.

The ladder

Rung 1 One project per environment, by name

A project is identified by its name, and Compose owns every container, network and volume carrying that name, wherever the file that created them lives. D9 said to set name:. The other half of that rule is that two running copies (prod and staging on one host, two feature branches on one laptop) need different names. Otherwise the second up adopts the first copy's resources:

staging checkout (same "name: pantry", port 8100):  docker compose up -d
 Container pantry-redis-1  Running
 Container pantry-web  Recreate
prod :8000 → (gone)      staging :8100 → visitor #4      ← prod's Redis and prod's data

docker compose -p pantry-staging up -d             # or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=pantry-staging in that host's environment
docker compose ls                                  # every project on this Docker host, with its files

The file's name: is the default, and -p or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME overrides it per deployment.

Rule Set name: in the file for the normal case, and give every additional copy on the same Docker host its own -p/COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME.

Why Compose matches existing resources by project-name labels, not by directory or file, so two copies with one name are one project.

Trap Deploying staging takes production down. docker compose ls shows one project whose CONFIG FILES column points at the staging checkout.

Rung 2 Override files and the merge rules

docker compose up with no -f reads compose.yaml and then, if present, compose.override.yaml, merging the second over the first. You can pass any list with -f a.yaml -f b.yaml. Later files win, but "win" means different things for different keys. Measured with docker compose config:

Key kind Example Merge
Scalars image, command, entrypoint, user, read_only replaced
Mappings environment, labels, deploy merged per key, later wins
Lists of strings ports, cap_drop, dns, expose appended
Mounts volumes, secrets merged by target path, later replaces the whole entry
Explicit ports: !override [...] replaced
Explicit build: !reset null, depends_on: !reset [] removed 
ports:   ['127.0.0.1:8000->80', '127.0.0.1:9000->80']      ← both published
volumes: data:/data kept;  /etc/app → conf-dev (and the base's :ro is gone)
with !override: ['127.0.0.1:9000->80'];  with !reset: build and depends_on absent

Appending is the trap. An override that "changes the port" adds a second one, and the spot-the-bug file ended up publishing 0.0.0.0:8080 next to 127.0.0.1:8000. And a volume override on the same target replaces the entry, flags included.

services:
  web:
    ports: !override
      - "127.0.0.1:9000:8080"

Rule Check every override with docker compose config, and use !override to replace lists and !reset to remove keys.

Why Compose appends lists, merges mappings and replaces scalars. Only the !override/!reset tags state the intent explicitly.

Trap After adding a dev override "to change the port", docker compose ps shows two port mappings, one of them on 0.0.0.0. The list was appended.

Rung 3 One base file, one file per environment

Put what every environment shares in compose.yaml. Put development extras in compose.override.yaml, so plain docker compose up on a laptop is the dev setup. Put production in compose.prod.yaml, used only with an explicit -f list, because an explicit list replaces the automatic override:

docker compose up -d --wait                                          # laptop: compose.yaml + compose.override.yaml
REGISTRY=localhost:5001 TAG=1.1.0 \
  docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --wait   # server: no override, a released image

without REGISTRY:  error while interpolating services.web.image: required variable REGISTRY is missing a value: set REGISTRY
with TAG=1.1.0:    web Pulled … Healthy … Hello from Pantry (1.1.0). You are visitor #6.
HostConfig: memory=268435456 nanocpus=1000000000 log=json-file {"max-file":"3","max-size":"10m"}

The production file does what only production needs. build: !reset null means the server never builds: it pulls what CI built and scanned (D6). deploy.resources.limits are enforced by plain docker compose, not just Swarm (256 MiB and one CPU above). logging rotates json-file logs, which otherwise grow without limit. Two more facts were measured. --scale web=2 fails while a fixed host port is published (port is already allocated), so scaling needs a proxy in front. And down interpolates the files too: run it without REGISTRY and TAG and nothing is stopped.

Rule Keep compose.yaml shared, compose.override.yaml for development only, and production in a separate file always named with -f, with images by release tag (or digest), resource limits and log rotation.

Why The override file is loaded automatically wherever docker compose up runs without -f, including on a server where someone typed it from habit.

Trap Production shows the debug banner. The deploy script ran docker compose up -d in a checkout that contains compose.override.yaml, so the dev file was merged in. That is what the spot-the-bug project did: "DEBUG BUILD - do not use".

Rung 4 Profiles: services that start only when asked

A service with profiles: [tools] is ignored by up unless the profile is active. Use it for admin tools, debug containers, load generators and one-off jobs you do not want running all the time:

  redis-cli:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    profiles: [tools]

$ docker compose ps --services           → redis, web            (redis-cli not started)
$ docker compose --profile tools run --rm redis-cli GET visits    → 1
$ docker compose run --rm redis-cli GET visits                    → 6   (run names it, so its profile is enabled)
$ docker compose config --profiles       → tools

COMPOSE_PROFILES=tools,debug activates profiles from the environment. A service without profiles: always starts, so do not make a core service depend on a profiled one.

Rule Put optional services in profiles and run them with docker compose run --rm <service>.

Why Profiles keep the default up to the services the application needs, while the tools stay defined, versioned and on the same networks.

Trap docker compose up fails with service "app" depends on undefined service "debug": invalid compose project. A core service depends_on a profiled one, which does not exist while its profile is off.

Rung 5 include and extends

include: pulls another Compose project fragment (services, volumes, networks, secrets) into this one. Relative paths in the included file resolve against its directory, so a team can own redis/compose.yaml independently:

include:
  - redis/compose.yaml            # services, volumes and secrets from another file, with its own relative paths

extends: copies one service's definition into another, then merges local keys over it, which is useful for a family of similar services (workers on different queues):

services:
  worker:
    extends: {file: common.yaml, service: worker-base}
    command: ["echo", "worker"]
    environment: {QUEUE: emails}

→ cap_drop: [ALL], LOG_LEVEL: info, QUEUE: emails, image: alpine:3.20

The difference: include adds whole resources and refuses to redefine them (services.redis conflicts with imported resource), and extends builds one service from another. Neither is a substitute for override files, which change the same services per environment.

Rule Use include to compose a project from fragments owned elsewhere, extends for services that share most of their definition, and override files for per-environment changes.

Why Each mechanism merges at a different level (project, service, environment), with its own path resolution and conflict rules.

Trap A volume path in an included file "does not exist". It was written relative to the main project, but include resolves it relative to the included file's own directory.

Rung 6 Extension fields and YAML anchors

Top-level keys starting with x- are ignored by Compose, which makes them a place to define reusable blocks. YAML anchors (&name) and merge keys (<<: *name) do the reuse:

x-hardening: &hardening
  read_only: true
  tmpfs: ["/tmp:size=16m"]
  cap_drop: [ALL]
  security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]

services:
  web:
    <<: *hardening
    environment:
      <<: *redis-client
      GREETING: ${GREETING:-Hello from Pantry}

Anchors are plain YAML, resolved when the file is parsed. They work inside one file only (not across -f files or include), and <<: merges mappings, not lists. A list you write next to it replaces the anchored list.

Rule Define repeated blocks (hardening, logging, client settings) once under x- keys and merge them with <<: *anchor.

Why One definition means one place to change, and Compose ignores x- keys, so they cost nothing.

Trap An anchor "does nothing" in the override file. Anchors do not cross files. Repeat the block, or move the setting into the base file.

Rung 7 Secrets (and configs) as files

Compose secrets: mounts a value as a file at /run/secrets/<name>, outside docker inspect's environment listing and outside docker compose config output. The app reads the file. Pantry reads REDIS_PASSWORD_FILE:

secrets:
  redis_password:
    file: ./secrets/redis_password.txt   # git-ignored; bind-mounted read-only

mkdir -p secrets && openssl rand -hex 16 > secrets/redis_password.txt && chmod 600 secrets/redis_password.txt

Compose can also take a secret's value from an environment variable (environment: REDIS_PASSWORD), but it does so by copying the value into the container's filesystem before start. On a hardened service that fails:

secrets: … environment: REDIS_PASSWORD  +  read_only: true
Error response from daemon: container rootfs is marked read-only          (also with a tmpfs at /run/secrets)
secrets: … file: ./secrets/redis_password.txt  → works

Getting the value into a program that wants it as a flag needs one more step, because flags are visible in ps, docker top and docker inspect. The Redis fragment writes the password into a config file on a tmpfs and starts redis-server /tmp/redis.conf, and clients use REDISCLI_AUTH instead of -a. Afterwards the password appeared 0 times in docker top output and 0 times in docker compose config. configs: work the same way for non-secret files (mounted at a path you choose). On Linux the bind-mounted file keeps its host owner and mode, so a 600 file owned by you is unreadable by UID 10001. Docker Desktop hides this. Make it readable by the container's GID.

Rule Pass secrets as secrets: files read by the app (*_FILE variables), keep the files out of git, and never put a secret's value in environment:, command: or the Compose file.

Why Files under /run/secrets do not appear in the environment, inspect output or process lists, and a file-sourced secret is a bind mount, which works with read_only.

Trap A hardened service fails to start with container rootfs is marked read-only after secrets were added. The secret is sourced from environment:. Use file:.

Rung 8 develop.watch: edit, sync, restart, rebuild

develop.watch (with docker compose up --watch or docker compose watch) reacts to file changes without bind mounts:

    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync+restart
          path: ../../pantry/app.py
          target: /app/app.py
        - action: rebuild
          path: ../../pantry/requirements.txt

The actions:

  • sync copies the changed file into the running container, for servers that reload by themselves.
  • sync+restart copies the file, then restarts the container, for servers like gunicorn that need a restart.
  • rebuild rebuilds the image and recreates the container, for dependency changes.

Unlike a bind mount, watch works with the image's own layout and ownership, and does not drag the host's node_modules or __pycache__ into the container.

It needs a writable target, so the dev override sets read_only: false. One more trap, found while testing this chapter on Compose 2.32:

Syncing and restarting service "web" after 1 changes were detected
Error handling changed files for service web: … getent unable to find entry "10001:10001" in passwd database

The copy resolves the container's user string, and uid:gid form is not a passwd entry. With user: "10001" in the override:

Syncing and restarting service "web" after 1 changes were detected
service "web" restarted
Hello from dev (dev). You are visitor #5. Edited live. Edited again. …

Rule Use develop.watch with sync, sync+restart and rebuild in the dev override instead of bind-mounting the source, and give watched services a plain numeric user.

Why Watch keeps the container's image-defined filesystem and copies only what changed, so dev runs the same layout as production.

Trap Saving a file does nothing, and the watch output shows an error copying files. The target is read-only, or the container user is in uid:gid form. Read the line after "Syncing".

Decide

You need Use
Dev-only settings compose.override.yaml (automatic)
Production settings compose.prod.yaml with an explicit -f list
A second copy on the same host -p <name> / COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME
Replace a list in an override !override
Drop a key in an override !reset
Optional tools profiles: + docker compose run --rm
A fragment owned by another team include:
Many similar services extends:
Repeated settings in one file x- + anchors
Passwords and keys secrets: with file: + *_FILE in the app
Live reload without bind mounts develop.watch
Several hosts, self-healing, rolling updates Kubernetes (the rest of this book)

Compose stops being enough at the last row. It runs one project on one Docker host. It does not restart unhealthy containers, does not move work when the host dies, and cannot roll out a new version without a gap. The Bridge chapter maps every key in this chapter to its Kubernetes counterpart.

The golden file

Pantry as a project: a shared base that includes the Redis fragment, uses anchors for hardening and client settings, a tools profile and a file secret; a dev override with watch; and a production file that runs a released image with limits and rotated logs.

mkdir -p secrets && openssl rand -hex 16 > secrets/redis_password.txt && chmod 600 secrets/redis_password.txt
docker compose up -d --wait                       # dev: Hello from dev (dev). …
docker compose --profile tools run --rm redis-cli GET visits
REGISTRY=localhost:5001 TAG=1.1.0 docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --wait

Review checklist

Spot the bug

The project as committed, deployed with git pull && docker compose up -d.

# compose.yaml — deployed on the server with:  git pull && docker compose up -d
name: pantry
services:
  web:
    image: localhost:5001/pantry-manual:1.1.0
    container_name: pantry-web
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      GREETING: Hello from Pantry
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8000:8080"
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes: [redis-data:/data]
volumes:
  redis-data:
---
# compose.override.yaml — "local development tweaks", committed next to it
services:
  web:
    environment:
      GREETING: DEBUG BUILD - do not use
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The deploy command has no -f, so the server merged compose.override.yaml and served "DEBUG BUILD - do not use". Deploy with docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d, and keep dev settings out of whatever the server loads.
  2. The override's ports list was appended, not substituted: 0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp, 127.0.0.1:8000->8080/tcp, and port 8080 answered from the LAN. Use ports: !override [...], and bind to 127.0.0.1.
  3. container_name: pantry-web makes the service impossible to scale ("Docker requires each container to have a unique name") and collides with any second copy. Remove it.
  4. The fixed name: pantry is shared by every checkout. Bringing up a staging copy on port 8100 recreated production's web container and used production's Redis (visitor #4). Give each copy its own -p.

Kubernetes manual · 1 · 8 min readReading Any Manifest#

In the story: forms handed to the front desk at city hall · Meet the City, The Smallest Thing That Runs

Every Kubernetes object, however unfamiliar, has the same skeleton. Four top-level fields describe what you want, and a fifth, written by the cluster, says what it has done about it. Once you can read that skeleton, find the meaning of any field without leaving the terminal, and predict what the API server will accept, no manifest is opaque. This chapter is the reading lesson. Every later chapter is vocabulary.

The ladder

Rung 1 Five fields: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec, status

  • apiVersion is group/version (apps/v1), or just v1 for the core group (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps).
  • kind is the type within that group.
  • metadata holds identity (name, namespace, uid) and description (labels, annotations), plus fields the server manages, such as generation, resourceVersion and creationTimestamp.
  • spec is what you want.
  • status is what the controller observed. You never write status.
$ kubectl -n k01 get deploy pantry -o yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  generation: 1
spec: …
status:
  observedGeneration: 1

generation increases with every change to spec, and the controller copies it to status.observedGeneration once it has acted on it. When the two differ, the controller has not caught up yet. That is the first thing to check when "the change did nothing". -o yaml hides metadata.managedFields (who owns which field, rung 7) unless you add --show-managed-fields.

Rule Read every object as desired state (spec) against observed state (status), and compare metadata.generation with status.observedGeneration before deciding a change was ignored.

Why Kubernetes is declarative. You store intent, and controllers reconcile towards it asynchronously, recording progress in status.

Trap A manifest copied from kubectl get -o yaml and re-applied carries status, uid, resourceVersion and creationTimestamp with it, which causes conflicts or no-ops. Keep the source manifest in git and never round-trip live objects.

Rung 2 kubectl explain is the manual

You never need a browser to find out what a field means, its type or its default. The cluster serves its own schema, so explain is always right for this cluster's version:

kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge
kubectl explain deployment.spec --recursive | less          # every field under spec, indented
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps                      # which kinds exist, and their apiVersion

FIELD: maxSurge <IntOrString>
DESCRIPTION:
    The maximum number of pods that can be scheduled above the desired number of
    pods. Value can be an absolute number (ex: 5) or a percentage of desired
    pods (ex: 10%). … Defaults to 25%.

kubectl api-resources answers "which apiVersion does this kind use here?", including for CRDs the cluster has installed. kubectl create deployment … --dry-run=client -o yaml generates a correct skeleton to start from.

Rule Look fields up with kubectl explain <kind>.<path> and kinds with kubectl api-resources, against the cluster you deploy to.

Why Both read the API server's own OpenAPI schema, so they match its version and its installed CRDs exactly, which no blog post does.

Trap A field from a tutorial is rejected, or silently does nothing, on your cluster. kubectl explain shows that it does not exist at that path or in that version.

Rung 3 Labels identify, selectors find

Labels are key/value pairs that identify an object, and selectors query them. A Deployment finds its Pods, a Service its endpoints and a NetworkPolicy its targets this way, so the most consequential lines in a manifest are often its labels. Use the recommended app.kubernetes.io/* set, which every tool understands:

Label Meaning Example
app.kubernetes.io/name the application pantry
app.kubernetes.io/instance this installation of it pantry-k01
app.kubernetes.io/component its role web, cache
app.kubernetes.io/part-of the larger system pantry
app.kubernetes.io/version the running version "1.1.0"
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by the tool that applied it kubectl, Helm

Three rules are enforced by the API server:

selector ≠ template labels:  `selector` does not match template `labels`
changing a selector:        spec.selector: … field is immutable
label value of 70 chars:    must be no more than 63 characters

kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=pantry,app.kubernetes.io/component=web
kubectl get pods -L app.kubernetes.io/version                # show a label as a column

A Deployment's selector is fixed at creation. Put only stable identity labels in it (name, instance), never version, or every upgrade would need a new selector.

Rule Label everything with the app.kubernetes.io/* set, and select on the smallest stable subset (name + instance).

Why Selectors are how objects find each other. Workload selectors are immutable, and values are capped at 63 characters of [A-Za-z0-9._-].

Trap A Service has no endpoints and every request fails. Its selector matches no Pod's labels, often through a typo or a label used in the Deployment's selector but not in its template. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> shows an empty list.

Rung 4 Annotations describe

Annotations are key/value metadata that nothing selects on. They hold larger, non-identifying data: owners, runbook links, build info, and configuration for tools that read them (ingress controllers, Prometheus scrapers, cert-manager, Argo CD):

  annotations:                              # describe; nothing selects on these
    pantry.example.com/owner: "team-pantry"
    pantry.example.com/runbook: "https://example.com/runbooks/pantry"

Use a domain prefix you own for your own keys. Unprefixed keys and kubernetes.io/ belong to Kubernetes. Annotation values may be long (up to 256 KB in total per object), which is why controllers stash state there. kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration is the client-side apply record.

Rule Put identity in labels and everything else (owners, links, tool configuration) in annotations, under a prefix you own.

Why Labels are indexed for selection and tightly limited. Annotations are free-form and never affect which objects match a selector.

Trap A tool "ignores" its configuration. It was written as a label, or with a misspelled annotation key. The API server accepts any well-formed key, so typos fail silently. Compare with the tool's documented key.

Rung 5 Multi-document files, and order

One file can hold several objects separated by ---. kubectl apply -f file.yaml (or -f dir/) sends them in order, so an object that needs another, such as a namespaced object and its Namespace, or a custom resource and its CRD, must come after it:

ConfigMap first, its Namespace second, in one file:
namespace/k01-late created
Error from server (NotFound): error when creating "order.yaml": namespaces "k01-late" not found

The Namespace was created, so a second apply succeeds. That is why ordering bugs pass on the second CI run and fail on a fresh cluster. Order documents by dependency: Namespaces, CRDs, ServiceAccounts and RBAC, ConfigMaps and Secrets, then workloads and Services. Helm (K10) does this sorting for you. With plain directories, use numbered file names.

kubectl apply -f k01/pantry.yaml           # Namespace document first, then Deployment, then Service

Rule Order objects by dependency (Namespace and CRDs first) in multi-document files and directories, and test applies against an empty cluster.

Why kubectl apply creates objects in the order it reads them, and the API server rejects an object whose namespace or kind does not exist yet.

Trap The first deploy to a new cluster fails with namespaces "…" not found or no matches for kind, and a retry "fixes" it. Order the documents.

Rung 6 Dry runs and diff before apply

Client dry run builds objects locally and validates almost nothing. Server dry run sends them through the API server's full validation and admission (schemas, defaults, admission webhooks, Pod Security) without storing them. kubectl diff shows what would change on the live objects:

into a namespace that does not exist:
--dry-run=client   deployment.apps/pantry created (dry run)
--dry-run=server   Error from server (NotFound): … namespaces "k01-nope" not found

kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f pantry.yaml       # would the cluster accept it?
kubectl diff -f pantry.yaml                         # what would change (exit 1 when there are differences)

-  replicas: 4
+  replicas: 3

Server dry run has one blind spot: it creates nothing, including Namespaces. A file that creates its own namespace fails a server dry run with namespaces "k01" not found. In CI, create namespaces first (or run the dry run against a cluster that has them).

Rule Run kubectl apply --dry-run=server and kubectl diff before every apply in CI, and treat client dry runs as syntax checks only.

Why Only the server knows its schemas, admission policies and current state, and only the server dry run asks it.

Trap CI's --dry-run=client stage is green and the real apply is rejected. The client dry run never contacted the API server.

Rung 7 Server-side apply and field ownership

With server-side apply (kubectl apply --server-side), the API server records which manager owns each field. A second manager changing a field you apply produces a conflict instead of a silent tug-of-war:

$ kubectl -n k01 patch deploy pantry -p '{"spec":{"replicas":4}}' --field-manager=autoscaler-sim
$ kubectl apply --server-side -f deployment.yaml
error: Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "autoscaler-sim" using apps/v1: .spec.replicas
$ kubectl -n k01 get deploy pantry --show-managed-fields -o jsonpath='{range .metadata.managedFields[*]}{.manager} {.operation}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl Apply
autoscaler-sim Update
kube-controller-manager Update

The conflict is the point: someone else (an HPA, an operator, a human with kubectl scale) manages replicas. Either stop setting the field in your manifest, which is right when an HPA owns it (K5), or take it over deliberately with --force-conflicts. Server-side apply also works on objects too large for the client-side last-applied-configuration annotation, as Argo CD's install manifest showed in the story. Pick one mode per object and stay with it: a client-side kubectl apply on an object created server-side prints missing the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation, and the two bookkeeping systems then disagree about who owns what.

kubectl apply --server-side -f pantry.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f pantry.yaml      # only when you mean to take ownership

Rule Apply with --server-side, leave fields owned by controllers (an HPA's replicas) out of your manifests, and use --force-conflicts only to take ownership on purpose.

Why Field ownership turns concurrent changes into explicit conflicts, and every apply re-asserts the fields you own.

Trap Replicas flap: the HPA scales to 6, the next CI apply resets to 2, and the HPA scales up again. The manifest sets spec.replicas on an autoscaled Deployment. Remove the field.

Decide

Question Command
What does this field mean? kubectl explain <kind>.<path>
Which apiVersion for this kind? kubectl api-resources
Is this manifest valid for this cluster? kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f …
What will change? kubectl diff -f …
Who changed this field? kubectl get … --show-managed-fields -o yaml
Has the controller acted on my change? compare metadata.generation and status.observedGeneration
Which objects does this selector match? kubectl get <kind> -l <selector>
A starting skeleton kubectl create <kind> … --dry-run=client -o yaml

The golden file

Pantry's first manifest, written to be read: a Namespace first, explicit namespaces, the recommended labels (reused with a YAML anchor), annotations under an owned prefix, a minimal stable selector, and a named port the Service targets by name.

kubectl create namespace k01 --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -     # so the server dry run can see it
kubectl apply --server-side --dry-run=server -f pantry.yaml && kubectl diff --server-side -f pantry.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side -f pantry.yaml
kubectl -n k01 get pods -L app.kubernetes.io/version

Review checklist

Spot the bug

From an old repository. "It worked in 2018."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 no longer serves Deployments: no matches for kind "Deployment" in version "extensions/v1beta1". Use apps/v1 (Old Maps tells the history).
  2. port: 8080 is not a field. With apps/v1 the server rejects it with strict decoding error: unknown field "spec.template.spec.containers[0].port". It is ports: [{containerPort: 8080, name: http}].
  3. The selector (app: pantry-web) does not match the template's labels (app: pantry): `selector` does not match template `labels`. Select on labels the template has, preferably the app.kubernetes.io/* set.
  4. There is no namespace:. Once the other errors were fixed, it applied into the current context's namespace, which was default here and is something else on your colleague's laptop. State the namespace.

Kubernetes manual · 2 · 9 min readThe Pod Spec#

In the story: an apartment, its tenants, and the helper who arrives before them · The Smallest Thing That Runs

Every workload (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob) wraps the same thing: a Pod template. Learn spec.template.spec once and you can read all of them. This chapter covers how the containers start, what they are told, who runs before and beside them, and which image they get. Security (K3), lifecycle (K4) and resources (K5) are the next three chapters, and they add fields to this same spec.

The ladder

Rung 1 command and args versus ENTRYPOINT and CMD

Kubernetes renamed Docker's two fields. command replaces the image's ENTRYPOINT, and args replaces its CMD. The catch is in the third row:

Pod spec Runs (image: ENTRYPOINT docker-entrypoint.sh, CMD redis-server) Measured
neither docker-entrypoint.sh redis-server redis-server *:6379
args: [redis-server, --port, "6380"] docker-entrypoint.sh redis-server --port 6380 redis-server *:6380
command: [redis-cli] redis-cli (the image's CMD is dropped too) ran alone: "Could not connect…"
command + args exactly what you wrote

So the usual choice is args. It keeps the image's entrypoint script (the D2 exec "$@" pattern) and changes only what it runs. Use command only to bypass the entrypoint, and then write the whole command line. Kubernetes expands $(VAR) in both fields from the container's environment, but there is no shell: command: ["echo", "$HOME"] prints $HOME. Use ["sh", "-c", "…"] when you need one, and write $$ for a literal $.

Rule Override with args to keep the image's entrypoint. Use command only when you mean to replace it, and then also give args.

Why command replaces ENTRYPOINT and discards the image's CMD, while args replaces only CMD.

Trap The container fails with exec: "--workers": executable file not found. Flags intended as arguments were written under command, so the first flag became the program.

Rung 2 env and envFrom

env sets variables one by one: a literal value, or valueFrom a ConfigMap key, a Secret key, the Pod's own fields, or its resource limits. envFrom imports every key of a ConfigMap or Secret. When both define a name, env wins:

      envFrom:
        - configMapRef: {name: pantry-settings}          # every key becomes a variable
      env:
        - {name: LOG_LEVEL, value: debug}                # env wins over envFrom

GREETING=Hello from a ConfigMap   ← envFrom
LOG_LEVEL=debug                   ← env beat the ConfigMap's "info"

Environment variables are read once, at start. Changing the ConfigMap does not change a running container's environment, which is K6's subject. envFrom also imports keys you did not expect: anyone who adds a key to the ConfigMap adds a variable to your process. Prefer explicit env entries for anything that matters, and envFrom for whole, purpose-made groups.

Rule Use env with explicit valueFrom references for settings the code depends on, and envFrom only for ConfigMaps or Secrets made for that one workload.

Why env documents every name the process receives and takes precedence, while envFrom imports whatever keys exist at start time.

Trap A Pod fails to start with CreateContainerConfigError, configmap "…" not found or couldn't find key …. A referenced ConfigMap or key does not exist. Add optional: true only when the program really copes without it.

Rung 3 $(VAR) expansion and its order

A variable's value may reference earlier variables with $(NAME). "Earlier" is literal, meaning above it in the list:

        - {name: EARLY, value: "$(LATE)/x"}              # LATE is defined below: not expanded
        - {name: LATE, value: "late"}
        - {name: URL, value: "http://$(POD_IP):8080/"}   # POD_IP is defined above: expanded

EARLY=$(LATE)/x
URL=http://10.244.2.12:8080/

A reference to an unknown or later variable is left as literal text, with no error. Variables from envFrom count as defined before every env entry (REF: "got $(GREETING)" with GREETING from a ConfigMap gave got Hello from Pantry). $$(NAME) escapes to a literal $(NAME).

Rule Order env entries so every $(VAR) refers to a variable defined above it, and check the result with kubectl exec … -- env.

Why Kubernetes expands references in one pass, top to bottom, and leaves anything it cannot resolve untouched.

Trap The app logs a connection string containing the literal text $(REDIS_HOST). The reference sits above the variable it names.

Rung 4 The downward API: facts about this Pod

The downward API exposes the Pod's own metadata and resources to its containers, through env (fieldRef, resourceFieldRef) or as files in a downwardAPI volume (which, unlike env, update when labels and annotations change):

        - name: POD_NAME
          valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
        - name: NODE_NAME
          valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}
        - name: MEM_LIMIT_MB
          valueFrom: {resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory, divisor: 1Mi}}

POD_NAME=env-demo
NODE_NAME=manual-worker
POD_IP=10.244.2.12
MEM_LIMIT_MB=64

Typical uses: log lines that name the Pod and node, metrics labels, sizing a runtime's heap from its limit (JVMs, Node's --max-old-space-size), and peer discovery. The golden Pantry reports k02 on $(NODE_NAME) as its version, so every response says which node served it.

Rule Get the Pod's name, namespace, IP, node and limits from the downward API, never by calling the Kubernetes API or guessing from the hostname.

Why The kubelet fills these values when it creates the container, without the Pod needing any API access or RBAC (K9).

Trap A process sized from the node's memory (/proc/meminfo) gets OOM-killed. It sees the node's RAM, not its own limit. Pass limits.memory through resourceFieldRef and size from that.

Rung 5 Init containers run first, one at a time, to completion

initContainers run in order before any main container starts, and each must exit 0. Use them for preconditions: wait for a dependency, run a migration, render config into a shared emptyDir, fix volume permissions.

      initContainers:
        # Runs to completion before the app starts; the Pod stays in Init:0/1 until Redis answers.
        - name: wait-for-redis
          image: redis:7-alpine
          command: ["sh", "-c", "until redis-cli -h redis ping; do echo waiting for redis; sleep 2; done"]

init-waits   0/1   Init:0/1     0             20s     "…redis:6379: Name does not resolve"
(after the redis Service was created)
init-waits   1/1   Running
init-fails   0/1   Init:Error   2 (28s ago)   30s     "migration failed"

A failing init container is retried with back-off (Init:Error, then Init:CrashLoopBackOff), and the app never starts. Init containers run on every Pod start, including after a node move, so make them idempotent. A wait loop at startup is still not a substitute for the app handling a dependency that disappears later (K4).

Rule Use init containers for preconditions that must hold before the app starts, make them idempotent and bounded, and keep long-running helpers out of them (rung 6).

Why Init containers are sequential and blocking by design, so the main containers start only after every one of them has exited 0.

Trap A Pod sits in Init:0/1 forever. An init container never exits: it waits on something that will never appear, or it is a long-running helper put in the wrong list. kubectl logs <pod> -c <init container> shows what it is waiting for.

Rung 6 Native sidecars

A helper that must run alongside the app (a proxy, a log shipper, a config reloader) used to be a second entry in containers. That has two problems: no guarantee it starts first, and it keeps a Job's Pod alive after the work is done. A native sidecar is an init container with restartPolicy: Always. It starts in init order, does not block the next init container once started, runs for the Pod's lifetime, and is stopped after the main containers exit (stable since Kubernetes 1.33):

classic-sidecar   Running    0/1           25s        ← never completes: the helper never exits
native-sidecar    Complete   1/1           7s
helper log:       helper stopping                      ← SIGTERM after main exited

The golden file's seed Job uses one: a socat proxy on 127.0.0.1:6379 that forwards to the Redis Service, which is the same shape as a cloud database proxy next to a migration job.

Rule Declare helpers that run beside the app as native sidecars (initContainers with restartPolicy: Always), never as extra containers, especially in Jobs.

Why Native sidecars start before the main containers, restart independently, and are terminated after them, so Jobs complete and the helper outlives the app's shutdown.

Trap A Job never completes: kubectl get job shows 0/1, and the Pod shows one container finished and one running. The helper is in containers. Move it to initContainers with restartPolicy: Always.

Rung 7 Image references and the pull policy

imagePullPolicy decides whether the kubelet pulls before every start. If you omit it, it is defaulted when the object is created: Always for :latest or no tag, IfNotPresent otherwise.

pantry-manual:latest   pullPolicy defaulted to: Always         ImagePullBackOff   (the image exists only on the nodes)
pantry-manual:d05      pullPolicy defaulted to: IfNotPresent   Running

The default is stored. A Deployment created with :latest and later changed to a pinned tag kept imagePullPolicy: Always, and failed to pull an image that every node had:

image=pantry-manual:d05 pullPolicy=Always          ← after changing the tag in an existing Deployment
fresh: image=pantry-manual:d05 pullPolicy=IfNotPresent

In production, reference images by immutable tag or, better, by digest (image: registry/app@sha256:…, the output of D6's release script). A digest makes "which bytes are running" unambiguous, and IfNotPresent is then always correct. Private registries need imagePullSecrets (K9).

          image: localhost:5001/pantry-manual@sha256:6cb0485b09bed372b17a62389b0ba943c742f5d524df7ab9914aa446729faad2
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

Rule Reference images by digest or an immutable release tag, never :latest, and set imagePullPolicy explicitly.

Why A tag can move under a running Deployment, and the pull policy is defaulted from the tag once, at creation, then stored.

Trap Pods on different nodes run different code after a rollout, or an image present on every node goes into ErrImagePull. Check kubectl get deploy -o jsonpath='{..imagePullPolicy}' and the tag. :latest gives Always, and the stored value survives tag changes.

Rung 8 Pod-level fields to recognise

A few Pod-level fields change behaviour for every container. Recognise them in review:

spec:
  restartPolicy: Always          # Always (Deployments), OnFailure/Never (Jobs)
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30   # K4
  hostNetwork: false             # true = the node's network namespace: port clashes, no NetworkPolicy isolation
  shareProcessNamespace: false   # true = containers see (and can signal) each other's processes
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst        # Default = the node's resolv.conf, so Service names stop resolving
  enableServiceLinks: false      # stops Docker-link-style *_SERVICE_HOST variables for every Service in the namespace
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # K9

enableServiceLinks deserves a word. By default, every container gets environment variables for every Service in its namespace (REDIS_SERVICE_HOST, REDIS_PORT=tcp://…). In a busy namespace that is hundreds of variables, and they override the image's own ENV: an image built with ENV REDIS_PORT=6379, run in a namespace with a Service named redis, saw REDIS_PORT=tcp://10.96.3.96:6379. Explicit env entries in the Pod spec still win, and KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST is always set.

Rule Leave hostNetwork, hostPID and shareProcessNamespace false unless there is a reviewed reason, and set enableServiceLinks: false on new workloads.

Why Each of these widens what one container can see or affect, and service links inject variables you did not choose.

Trap An app's REDIS_PORT default is suddenly tcp://10.96.3.96:6379 and the client fails to parse it. A Service named redis exists in the namespace, and service links overrode the image's ENV. Set enableServiceLinks: false, or set the variable explicitly in env.

Decide

You need Use
Different flags, same image entrypoint args
A different program entirely command + args
One setting from a ConfigMap/Secret env[].valueFrom
A purpose-made group of settings envFrom
The Pod's name, node, IP, limits downward API
Something done once before start init container
A helper running for the Pod's lifetime native sidecar (initContainers + restartPolicy: Always)
Immutable image reference image@sha256:… + IfNotPresent

The golden file

Pantry's Pod spec: Redis started through args, the web Deployment with an init container, explicit and imported environment, downward API values and named ports, and a seed Job whose proxy runs as a native sidecar.

kubectl apply --server-side -f pantry.yaml
kubectl -n k02 wait --for=condition=complete job/seed && kubectl -n k02 rollout status deploy/pantry
kubectl -n k02 port-forward deploy/pantry 8020:8080 & curl -s localhost:8020/   # … (k02 on manual-worker2). You are visitor #101.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Adds a log shipper and four workers."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The log shipper is a plain init container that never exits, so the Pod sat in Init:0/1 and the app never started. Make it a native sidecar with restartPolicy: Always.
  2. pantry-manual:latest defaulted the pull policy to Always, which gave ErrImagePull on a cluster whose nodes had the image. Pin a tag or digest, and set imagePullPolicy explicitly (and, on an existing Deployment, set it: the stored Always survives a tag change).
  3. command: ["--workers", "4"] replaces the image's command with a flag: exec: "--workers": executable file not found. Write the server command under args (args: [gunicorn, --bind, 0.0.0.0:8080, --workers, "4", app:app]).
  4. GREETING references $(REDIS_HOST), which is defined below it, so the app said "Hello from $(REDIS_HOST)". Move REDIS_HOST above it.

Kubernetes manual · 3 · 8 min readSecurity Context#

In the story: the building's house rules: who may live here, and what they may do inside · Districts, Key Cards and Rush Hour

D5 hardened Pantry with docker run flags. In Kubernetes the same protections are fields in securityContext, set at the Pod level (for every container and for volumes) and at the container level. A namespace label then decides which Pods the API server will even admit. This chapter moves each D5 flag into its field, measures what the restricted Pod Security Standard demands, and ends with a Pod it admits.

docker run (D5) Pod spec
USER 10001:10001 in the image runAsUser: 10001, runAsGroup: 10001, runAsNonRoot: true
--read-only readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
--tmpfs /tmp an emptyDir (medium: Memory) mounted at /tmp
--cap-drop ALL capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
--security-opt no-new-privileges allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
default seccomp profile seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
volume ownership through the image's directory fsGroup: 10001
userns-remap on the daemon hostUsers: false per Pod

The ladder

Rung 1 Pod Security Admission: labels on the namespace

Kubernetes ships three Pod Security Standards. privileged allows everything. baseline blocks known escalations: host namespaces, privileged containers, dangerous capabilities. restricted requires the hardened settings of this chapter. A built-in admission controller applies them per namespace, through labels:

$ kubectl -n k03 run bare --image=pantry-manual:d05
Error from server (Forbidden): pods "bare" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.37":
  allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "bare" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false),
  unrestricted capabilities (container "bare" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]),
  runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "bare" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true),
  seccompProfile (pod or container "bare" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")

The error is the checklist: four fields. enforce rejects, warn prints a warning to whoever applies, and audit records the violation in the audit log. Pin *-version: without it the rules are latest, and they can tighten when the cluster is upgraded (the unpinned warn above evaluated restricted:latest). Pod Security Admission replaced PodSecurityPolicy, which was removed in Kubernetes 1.25 (2022).

The admission check applies to Pods. A Deployment that violates the standard is still created, and its Pods are refused:

deployment.apps/bare created
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
bare   0/1     0            0
event FailedCreate: Error creating: pods "bare-…" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.37": …

Rule Label every application namespace enforce: restricted, with warn and audit too, and pin enforce-version to the cluster's minor version.

Why The labels make the API server reject non-compliant Pods before they run, and a pinned version stops an upgrade from silently changing the rules.

Trap kubectl apply succeeds and nothing runs: the Deployment shows 0/1 with no Pods. Admission rejected the ReplicaSet's Pods. kubectl get events --field-selector reason=FailedCreate shows violates PodSecurity.

Rung 2 runAsNonRoot needs a number the kubelet can check

runAsNonRoot: true makes the kubelet refuse to start a container whose user would be UID 0. It checks runAsUser if set, and otherwise the image's USER, which must be numeric (D5, rung 2). An image that runs as root fails at container creation:

redis:7-alpine with runAsNonRoot and no runAsUser:  CreateContainerConfigError
container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root (pod: "redis-root_k03(…)", container: web)

Set runAsUser and runAsGroup explicitly to the image's numbers. That documents the UID in the manifest and still works if a future image forgets its USER. Third-party images that start as root and drop privileges themselves (the official Redis and PostgreSQL images do) need a numeric runAsUser that the image supports, or a non-root variant of the image.

  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    runAsGroup: 10001

Rule Set runAsNonRoot: true with explicit numeric runAsUser and runAsGroup matching the image's USER.

Why The kubelet can verify only numbers, and explicit values make the identity independent of what the image declares.

Trap A Pod is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError with image will run as root (or non-numeric user). The image has no numeric USER. Set runAsUser, or fix the image (D5).

Rung 3 fsGroup: who owns the volumes

fsGroup makes every volume that supports ownership management group-owned by that GID, with the setgid bit, and adds the GID to every container's supplementary groups. A non-root process can then write its volumes without a chown init container:

$ kubectl -n k03 exec pantry -- ls -ld /tmp
drwxrwsrwt 2 root pantry 60 Oct 24 00:29 /tmp       ← group pantry (10001), setgid "s"

On large persistent volumes, the recursive ownership change at every mount is slow. Set fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch to skip it when the volume's root already has the right owner (K7). Volumes that cannot change ownership (some NFS, hostPath, Secret and ConfigMap projections with their own defaultMode) ignore fsGroup.

  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 10001
    fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch

Rule Set fsGroup to the app's GID on every Pod that writes to volumes, with fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch for large persistent volumes.

Why Kubernetes applies group ownership to the volume at mount time, which replaces D5's "create the directory in the image with the right owner".

Trap A Pod with a big PVC takes minutes to start, and nothing is in the logs. The kubelet is recursively changing the group of every file on each mount. Add fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch.

Rung 4 readOnlyRootFilesystem, with emptyDir where the app writes

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is D5's --read-only, with the same failure when the app needs scratch space:

without the /tmp emptyDir:   Error, RESTARTS 2
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No usable temporary directory found in ['/tmp', '/var/tmp', '/usr/tmp', '/app']
with it:                     touch: cannot touch '/app/x': Read-only file system ; /tmp writable

Give every path the app writes an emptyDir (or a PVC for data). medium: Memory makes it a tmpfs. It counts against the container's memory limit, so give it a sizeLimit. A disk-backed emptyDir counts against ephemeral storage, and exceeding its sizeLimit evicts the Pod (K7).

      volumeMounts:
        - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 16Mi}

Rule Run every container with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, and mount a sized emptyDir on each path it writes.

Why A read-only root makes every unexpected write fail, and emptyDir volumes make the expected ones explicit.

Trap The Pod crash-loops right after readOnlyRootFilesystem was enabled, with "Read-only file system" or "No usable temporary directory". Run the image with docker run --read-only (D5) to list the paths it writes, and mount emptyDirs there.

Rung 5 No privilege escalation, no capabilities

allowPrivilegeEscalation: false sets the no_new_privs bit, so setuid binaries cannot raise privileges (D5, rung 5). capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] removes root's powers. restricted allows adding back exactly one capability, NET_BIND_SERVICE:

add NET_ADMIN:         violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.37": unrestricted capabilities (container "web" must not include "NET_ADMIN" in securityContext.capabilities.add)
add NET_BIND_SERVICE:  pod/pantry-bind created
golden Pod:            CapEff: 0000000000000000   NoNewPrivs: 1

      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]

privileged: true gives a container every capability and every host device, so it is effectively root on the node. It is banned by baseline, and should exist only in reviewed system agents (CNI plugins, storage drivers), each in its own privileged namespace.

Rule Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] on every container, add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE when needed, and never privileged: true in application namespaces.

Why These close the two remaining routes from a non-root process to root's powers: setuid escalation and inherited capabilities.

Trap An image that worked under Docker now fails with Operation not permitted (for example ping, or a chown in an entrypoint script). It relied on a capability from Docker's default set. Find which one, then remove the need from the image rather than adding the capability back.

Rung 6 seccomp and AppArmor

seccomp filters system calls. RuntimeDefault is the container runtime's profile, which blocks a few dozen dangerous syscalls (such as mount, kexec_load, unshare into new namespaces) and allows everything ordinary programs use. restricted requires RuntimeDefault or a Localhost profile:

Seccomp: 2          ← /proc/1/status in the golden Pod: filter mode active

  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
