The default container is Unconfined unless the kubelet is configured otherwise, so set it at Pod level. AppArmor (on Ubuntu/Debian nodes) is configured with securityContext.appArmorProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} and works the same way. It was not tested on this kind node. A Localhost seccomp profile lets you go further, with only the syscalls your app uses, generated by tracing it in a test environment.

Rule Set seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} at Pod level on every workload.

Why It costs nothing for normal programs and blocks the syscalls most container escapes use, and restricted refuses Pods without it.

Trap A Pod that passes baseline is rejected after a namespace is moved to restricted, only for seccompProfile. Earlier hardening forgot it because Docker applies its default profile without being asked.

Rung 7 User namespaces: UID 0 inside is nobody outside

hostUsers: false gives the Pod its own user namespace. UIDs inside map to an unprivileged range on the node, so even a process that is root in the container is an ordinary user on the host. Measured on this cluster (kernel 6.12, containerd 2.3, runc 1.4):

inside:   uid=10001 gid=10001     /proc/self/uid_map:  0 1089929216 65536
on node:  1089939217 sleep 3600                         ← 1089929216 + 10001
without:  10001 /venv/bin/python /venv/bin/gunicorn …   ← the same number on the node

spec:
  hostUsers: false

User namespaces for Pods became generally available in Kubernetes 1.36 (2026), after being enabled by default since 1.33. They need Linux 6.3+ and a recent containerd/CRI-O and runc. They combine with everything above: defence in depth, not a replacement for runAsNonRoot.

Rule Add hostUsers: false where the nodes support it, on top of the rest of this chapter.

Why A container escape then lands as an unprivileged UID on the node, which turns most breakouts from "root on the node" into "nobody on the node".

Trap Pods with hostUsers: false fail to start on some nodes, with an error about idmap mounts or user namespaces. Those nodes run an older kernel or runtime. Check uname -r and the runtime versions before rolling it out cluster-wide.

Rung 8 Turning restricted on for an existing namespace

Labelling a namespace does not evict running Pods. It refuses new ones, so the next rollout or node drain is what breaks. Preview the effect first with a server-side dry run of the label:

kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns k03-legacy pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

Warning: existing pods in namespace "k03-legacy" violate the new PodSecurity enforce level "restricted:latest"
Warning: old: allowPrivilegeEscalation != false, unrestricted capabilities, runAsNonRoot != true, seccompProfile

The rollout is three steps:

  1. Add warn and audit at restricted, and keep enforce at baseline.
  2. Fix workloads until the warnings stop.
  3. Then switch enforce.

A cluster-wide default for unlabelled namespaces can be set in the API server's PodSecurity admission configuration.

Rule Introduce restricted with warn/audit first, check existing Pods with a dry-run label, and only then set enforce.

Why Enforcement applies at Pod creation, so violations in running Pods surface later, during a rollout, a node drain or an autoscale.

Trap Weeks after a namespace was labelled, a node drain leaves an app with no Pods. Its replacements were rejected (FailedCreate), while the old Pods had kept running until evicted.

Decide

Workload Namespace label Notes
Your applications restricted, pinned version the golden Pod
Third-party apps that need a little more baseline + warn: restricted track what blocks restricted
CNI, CSI, node agents privileged, in their own namespace reviewed, minimal RBAC
Anything needing hostPath, hostNetwork not in an app namespace redesign first

The golden file

Pantry as a single Pod that restricted:v1.37 admits: Pod-level identity, group ownership and seccomp, and container-level escalation, capabilities and a read-only root with a memory-backed /tmp. K5 turns this Pod spec into the golden Deployment.

kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml -f pod.yaml
kubectl -n k03 exec pantry -- sh -c 'id; grep -E "^(CapEff|NoNewPrivs|Seccomp):" /proc/1/status'

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It is applied to the restricted namespace. "The security team said to add a securityContext, so we did."

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. allowPrivilegeEscalation: true is rejected: allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "web" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false).
  2. No capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]: must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"].
  3. add: ["NET_RAW"] is not allowed: must not include "NET_RAW" in securityContext.capabilities.add. Only NET_BIND_SERVICE may be added under restricted.
  4. No seccompProfile: must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost". Add it at Pod level.
  5. With those fixed, the Pod is admitted and then crash-loops: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true without a writable /tmp gave No usable temporary directory found. Mount a sized emptyDir at /tmp.

Kubernetes manual · 4 · 9 min readLifecycle and Rollouts#

In the story: the doorbell test, and moving tenants without anyone noticing · Are You Alive?, Someone Who Never Sleeps

A Deployment promises a number of running Pods. Running is not the same as able to serve, though, and replacing a Pod is not the same as replacing it without dropping requests. This chapter is about the gap between those. Three probes tell Kubernetes what "able to serve" means. A preStop hook and a grace period make shutdown clean. A rollout strategy and a PodDisruptionBudget bound how much capacity may be missing at any moment.

Every claim below was measured with a load generator sending a request through the Service every 50 ms during rollouts, drains and outages.

The race in the middle is why preStop exists. Removal from endpoints and SIGTERM begin at the same moment, but it takes time for every node's kube-proxy (and every ingress or gateway) to stop sending traffic to the Pod. If the app stops accepting connections first, those requests fail.

The ladder

Rung 1 Three probes, three questions

Probe Question On failure
startupProbe Has it finished starting? keeps checking until failureThreshold, then restarts. Liveness and readiness wait for it
readinessProbe Can it serve traffic now? removed from Service endpoints, not restarted
livenessProbe Is the process stuck beyond repair? container restarted 
          readinessProbe:                   # in the Service's endpoints only while this passes
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}   # /healthz checks Redis: no traffic if the Pod cannot serve it
            periodSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:                    # restart only if the process itself is stuck
            httpGet: {path: /livez, port: http}     # never a dependency: Redis being down must not restart Pantry
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3

Pantry has two endpoints for this reason. /livez answers if the process is alive, and /healthz answers if it can reach Redis. Readiness uses the one that includes dependencies, and liveness the one that does not. Probes can be httpGet, tcpSocket, grpc or exec. Prefer HTTP or gRPC: exec forks a process every period.

Rule Give every serving container a readiness probe that includes what it needs to serve, and a liveness probe that checks only the process itself.

Why Readiness failures only take a Pod out of rotation, which is safe and reversible. Liveness failures restart it, which is right for a deadlock and wrong for a dependency outage.

Trap Without a readiness probe, a Pod is added to endpoints the moment its container starts, before the app listens, and every new Pod costs a burst of failed requests. kubectl get endpointslices lists it as ready while its log is still printing startup lines.

Rung 2 Never point liveness at a dependency

Redis was scaled to zero for 75 seconds, with two variants running side by side:

liveness on /healthz (checks Redis):   READY false   RESTARTS 2   (all 3 Pods)
golden (liveness on /livez):           READY false   RESTARTS 0   (all 3 Pods)

Both correctly stopped serving, since readiness failed. The first variant also restarted every Pod, twice. In a real outage that turns "the database is slow" into "every app Pod is restarting, re-warming caches and reconnecting at the same moment the database recovers". That kind of self-inflicted thundering herd prolongs outages. Liveness should detect only what a restart fixes: a deadlock, a wedged event loop, exhausted internal state.

          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /livez, port: http}

Rule Make liveness checks local (process responsive, no dependencies), and leave dependency health to readiness.

Why Restarting a container cannot fix a remote dependency, but it adds load and startup time at the worst moment.

Trap During a database incident, application RESTARTS counts climb on every Pod at once, and kubectl describe pod shows Liveness probe failed: …/healthz. Move the dependency check to readiness.

Rung 3 startupProbe for slow starters

A liveness probe that runs before the app has started kills it while it is still starting. With START_DELAY=25 (Pantry sleeps before binding) and liveness every 5 s × 3:

no startupProbe:     RESTARTS 3, never Ready after 90 s
with startupProbe:   RESTARTS 0, Ready

          startupProbe:                     # until this passes, liveness and readiness are not run
            httpGet: {path: /livez, port: http}
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 30            # up to 60 s to start

The startup probe gives a generous budget (periodSeconds × failureThreshold) for the first start only. Once it passes, liveness takes over with its tighter settings. This replaces the old habit of a long initialDelaySeconds, which delays the first check on every restart, even a fast one.

Rule Add a startupProbe (same endpoint as liveness) with a budget covering the slowest realistic start, and keep initialDelaySeconds off liveness and readiness.

Why The startup probe holds the other probes back until the app is up, so liveness can be strict without killing slow starts.

Trap A Pod is stuck in a restart loop after a change that made startup slower (a bigger cache warm-up, a slower node, a JVM with less CPU), with Liveness probe failed: connection refused in its events. It never got the time to start. Add or widen the startup probe.

Rung 4 Graceful shutdown: preStop, SIGTERM and the grace period

When a Pod is deleted, it is removed from endpoints, and the kubelet runs preStop and then sends SIGTERM. Both start at once, so the app must keep serving for a few seconds while every proxy catches up. Measured with kubectl rollout restart under load:

naive (no probes, no preStop):           12 failed requests
probes, no preStop:                      0 and 1 failed requests (two runs)
golden (probes + preStop sleep 5):       0 and 0

      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30     # preStop + the app's own drain must fit inside this
          lifecycle:
            preStop:                        # runs before SIGTERM; meanwhile the Pod leaves the endpoints
              sleep: {seconds: 5}

kind updates endpoints almost instantly. On larger clusters, and behind ingress controllers or cloud load balancers, the window is longer, and a missing preStop costs more. The sleep action needs no sleep binary in the image, so it works with distroless. The grace period covers preStop and the app's own drain, after which SIGKILL ends everything (exit 137, D2). The API rejects a preStop sleep that does not fit (must be non-negative and less than terminationGracePeriodSeconds), but an exec of sleep 10 with a 5 s grace period is accepted, and fails with FailedPreStopHook events.

Rule Add a preStop sleep of a few seconds to every serving container, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds above preStop plus the app's drain timeout (gunicorn --graceful-timeout 8 here).

Why The sleep keeps the old Pod serving while the endpoint removal propagates. Only then does SIGTERM start the app's own graceful shutdown.

Trap Every deploy produces a short burst of 502s or "connection refused" at the edge, though readiness is perfect. Traffic reached Pods that had already stopped accepting connections. Add the preStop sleep.

Rung 5 Rollout strategy and the progress deadline

RollingUpdate replaces Pods in steps bounded by maxSurge (extra Pods allowed) and maxUnavailable (missing Pods allowed). maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 never drops below full capacity. minReadySeconds requires a new Pod to stay Ready for a while before it counts, which catches crash-after-start. progressDeadlineSeconds marks a stuck rollout as failed:

$ kubectl -n k04 set image deploy/pantry web=pantry-manual:does-not-exist
error: deployment "pantry" exceeded its progress deadline
Progressing=False ProgressDeadlineExceeded
1 × 0/1 ErrImagePull, 3 × 1/1 Running        failed requests while stuck: 0 (of 600)
$ kubectl -n k04 rollout undo deploy/pantry
deployment "pantry" successfully rolled out

With maxUnavailable: 0, a broken image never took capacity away. The rollout stalled with the old Pods serving. The opposite setting replaces everything at once. With Pantry's two-second start, kube-proxy hid the gap by sending traffic to terminating Pods that were still serving. With a 15-second start, maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 3 lost 9 requests over 17 seconds, and the golden strategy lost none. Recreate stops all old Pods before starting new ones. It is for apps that cannot run two versions at once (a single-writer volume, an incompatible schema), and it always means downtime.

kubectl -n k04 rollout status deploy/pantry       # waits, fails on ProgressDeadlineExceeded
kubectl -n k04 rollout history deploy/pantry      # revisions kept (revisionHistoryLimit)
kubectl -n k04 rollout undo deploy/pantry         # back to the previous ReplicaSet

Rule Use RollingUpdate with maxSurge: 1 (or 25%) and maxUnavailable: 0, set minReadySeconds and progressDeadlineSeconds, and gate deploy pipelines on kubectl rollout status.

Why These bound capacity during a rollout, and turn "the new version never became ready" into a visible failed rollout instead of a slow outage.

Trap A pipeline reports success while the new version crash-loops. It ran kubectl apply without rollout status, which is the step that waits and fails.

Rung 6 What triggers a rollout, and what does not

Only a change to spec.template creates a new ReplicaSet and rolls Pods: image, env, probes, annotations on the template. Changing replicas scales in place. A changed ConfigMap or Secret that the Pod consumes as environment variables does not restart anything (K6). kubectl rollout restart works by stamping a kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation on the template, which is why it rolls.

kubectl -n k04 rollout restart deploy/pantry
kubectl -n k04 get deploy pantry -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations}'
kubectl -n k04 rollout pause deploy/pantry       # batch several template changes into one rollout
kubectl -n k04 rollout resume deploy/pantry

rollout pause lets you apply several template changes, then roll once on resume. The golden pipeline changes the image and annotations together in one apply instead.

Rule Change workloads only through the Pod template (declaratively, in one apply), and use rollout restart when a dependency changed outside the template.

Why The Deployment controller compares templates. Anything outside the template is invisible to it.

Trap A ConfigMap was updated, "deployed", and nothing changed. The template did not change, so no rollout happened. Use a config-hash annotation (K6) or rollout restart.

Rung 7 PodDisruptionBudgets protect against voluntary disruptions

Node drains (upgrades, autoscaler scale-downs, maintenance) evict Pods through the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. A rolling update is not an eviction and is governed by the strategy instead. The worst case, measured with all three Pods packed on the drained node, a 15-second start and no preStop:

no PDB:                drain 4 s;  31 failed requests (00:58:27 → 00:58:45)
PDB minAvailable: 2:   drain 42 s; "Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget" (retried); 2 failed

Without the PDB, the drain evicted all three at once and the app was gone for 18 seconds. With it, the drain waited for replacements to become Ready elsewhere before evicting more. When the Pods were already spread over two nodes (K5), even the no-PDB drain failed nothing, because one Pod elsewhere kept serving. Spreading and PDBs work together.

apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: {name: pantry, namespace: k04}
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app.kubernetes.io/name: pantry}}

A PDB that allows no disruption blocks drains forever: minAvailable: 3 with 3 replicas gave ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0, sixteen eviction retries and a timed-out drain. Cluster upgrades then stall, or someone --forces through.

Rule Give every replicated workload a PDB that allows at least one disruption (minAvailable: replicas - 1, or maxUnavailable: 1), and spread its Pods across nodes.

Why The Eviction API refuses evictions that would breach the budget, so drains proceed only as fast as replacements become Ready.

Trap kubectl drain hangs, printing Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget forever. kubectl get pdb shows ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0: the budget equals the replica count, or the Pods are not Ready.

Decide

Situation Setting
Normal web service readiness (with deps) + liveness (local) + startup, preStop sleep 5, maxSurge 1 / maxUnavailable 0, PDB maxUnavailable: 1
Slow or variable startup startupProbe with a large failureThreshold
Long requests or WebSockets longer preStop and app drain, terminationGracePeriodSeconds to match
Can't run two versions at once strategy: Recreate (plan the downtime)
Single replica PDB is pointless, so run 2 if it must survive drains
Batch / queue workers no readiness needed, liveness on progress, a grace period long enough to finish one item

The golden file

Pantry, rolled out and shut down without dropping a request: three probes with distinct jobs, a preStop sleep inside a sufficient grace period, a strategy that never removes capacity, deadlines that make failures visible, and a PodDisruptionBudget. K5 adds resources and placement to this same Deployment.

kubectl apply -f base.yaml -f deployment.yaml && kubectl -n k04 rollout status deploy/pantry
kubectl -n k04 rollout restart deploy/pantry && kubectl -n k04 rollout status deploy/pantry
kubectl -n k04 logs loader | grep -c FAIL          # 0

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Probes, preStop and a PDB, as the checklist says."

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. There is no readiness probe (and no startup probe), so new Pods receive traffic as soon as their container starts, before the app listens, and Pods that lose Redis keep receiving traffic. Add readiness on /healthz and a startup probe.
  2. The liveness probe checks /healthz, which includes Redis. During a Redis outage, every Pod restarted twice in 75 seconds. Point liveness at /livez.
  3. maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 3 replaces all three Pods at once. With a 15-second start it failed 9 requests in one rollout (the golden strategy failed none). Use maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0.
  4. The preStop runs sleep 10 inside a 5-second grace period, so the kubelet kills the container mid-hook (FailedPreStopHook) and the app never drains. Make the grace period longer than preStop plus the drain (the sleep action form is validated and rejects this outright).
  5. minAvailable: 3 with 3 replicas allows zero disruptions. kubectl drain retried evictions until it timed out, which blocks node maintenance. Use maxUnavailable: 1.

Kubernetes manual · 5 · 9 min readResources and Placement#

In the story: the lease (what you are promised and the ceiling you cannot exceed), and which building you may live in · Are You Alive?, The Landlord's Week

Two questions decide where a Pod runs and how it behaves under pressure: how much it asks for, and where it may go. Requests are a reservation the scheduler honours. Limits are a ceiling the kernel enforces, with very different consequences for memory and for CPU. Affinity, taints, spread constraints and priorities shape placement. Get them right and a node failure, a drain or a noisy neighbour is a non-event. Get them wrong and Pods are OOM-killed, throttled, stacked on one node, or Pending forever.

The ladder

Rung 1 Requests are what the scheduler reserves

The scheduler places a Pod only on a node whose unreserved capacity covers its requests. It does not look at actual usage:

requests cpu: "5"  →  Pending
0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu.

          resources:
            requests:                       # what the scheduler reserves, and what the HPA's % is based on
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi

Requests are also what the Pod is guaranteed under contention, and what an HPA's percentage is relative to (the golden file autoscales on it). Set them from measurement: kubectl top pod under realistic load, plus headroom. Too low and nodes are overpacked and contended. Too high and the cluster looks full while it idles. On kind every node reports the whole Docker VM (4 CPUs, about 8 GB here) though all three share it, so scheduling looks roomier than reality.

kubectl top pod -n k05 --containers
kubectl describe node manual-worker | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"

Rule Give every container CPU and memory requests based on measured usage, not on guesses or defaults.

Why The scheduler packs nodes by requests alone, so requests decide both whether a Pod fits and how crowded its node is.

Trap A Pod is Pending with Insufficient cpu on a cluster whose nodes are mostly idle. Requests, not usage, filled the nodes. kubectl describe node shows "Allocated resources" near 100% while kubectl top node is low.

Rung 2 A memory limit is a hard wall

When a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills it. There is no slowdown first:

PANTRY_HOG_MB=200, limits.memory 128Mi  →  restarts=2  last=OOMKilled  exit=137

            limits:
              memory: 256Mi                 # a memory limit: past it the kernel kills the container (OOMKilled)

Always set a memory limit. Without one, a leak takes memory from every other Pod on the node until the node itself starts evicting. Set the limit above the real peak (startup, cache warm-up, the largest request), and size runtimes from it: JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, Node --max-old-space-size, or the downward API (K2). Memory-backed emptyDirs and tmpfs count against it (D8). A container with only a limit gets a request equal to the limit ({"limits":{"memory":"32Mi"},"requests":{"memory":"32Mi"}}), which is fine for memory.

Rule Set a memory limit on every container, comfortably above its measured peak, and make the runtime aware of it.

Why Memory cannot be throttled, only reclaimed by killing. The limit decides whether it is this container or a random neighbour that dies.

Trap kubectl get pods shows climbing RESTARTS, with OOMKilled / exit 137 in kubectl describe pod under Last State. The limit is below the real peak, or the runtime is sized from the node's memory rather than the limit.

Rung 3 A CPU limit throttles, even when the node is idle

A CPU limit is enforced by the CFS quota: in every 100 ms period, the container may use its quota and then waits. A busy loop limited to 200m:

cpu.max          20000 100000
nr_periods       401
nr_throttled     396           ← throttled in 99% of periods
throttled_usec   17321250      ← 17 s spent waiting in ~40 s
kubectl top:     200m

The node had idle cores the whole time. For latency-sensitive services, that throttling shows up as tail latency, because a request that needs 30 ms of CPU in a period that has 20 ms left waits for the next period. Two common positions exist:

  • No CPU limit, honest requests. The container borrows idle CPU and is only slowed by real contention, in proportion to its request. The golden file does this.
  • CPU limit = request (Guaranteed QoS). Predictable and isolated, and required on some multi-tenant platforms. Size it generously and watch nr_throttled.
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
              # no CPU limit: CPU above the request is borrowed, never throttled (rung 3)

Rule Set CPU requests on everything, and set CPU limits only where isolation matters more than latency, then monitor throttling.

Why A CPU limit caps usage per scheduling period regardless of free capacity, while requests already guarantee each container its share under contention.

Trap p99 latency is bad, CPU usage graphs sit exactly at the limit, and the node is mostly idle. Check /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat in the container: a high nr_throttled against nr_periods is the throttling.

Rung 4 QoS classes decide who is evicted first

Every Pod gets a QoS class from its resources:

QoS class Condition Measured on
Guaranteed every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits requests = limits
Burstable at least one request or limit, not Guaranteed requests only, the golden Pantry
BestEffort no requests or limits at all nothing set 
kubectl get pods -n k05 -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass

When a node runs short of memory, the kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable Pods using the most above their requests, and Guaranteed last. The kernel's OOM killer uses the same ranking. A Pod with no requests at all is the first thing to go, and it was also scheduled as if it needed nothing.

Rule Never run production workloads as BestEffort, and make the critical ones Guaranteed for memory (memory request = limit) when the node's memory is tight.

Why QoS class is the eviction order under node pressure, and it follows mechanically from requests and limits.

Trap Under memory pressure, the same Pods are evicted again and again (The node was low on resource: memory in kubectl describe pod). They are BestEffort or far above their requests.

Rung 5 LimitRange and ResourceQuota: the namespace's guard-rails

A LimitRange fills in defaults for containers that state nothing, and bounds what any one may ask for. A ResourceQuota caps the namespace's total:

defaulted:     {"limits":{"memory":"256Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"50m","memory":"64Mi"}}
limit 2Gi:     pods "huge" is forbidden: maximum memory usage per Container is 1Gi, but limit is 2Gi
quota, no LimitRange, no resources:
               pods "noreq" is forbidden: failed quota: ceiling: must specify limits.memory for: c; requests.cpu for: c; requests.memory for: c

A quota on requests.cpu makes every Pod in the namespace state a CPU request. Without a LimitRange to supply defaults, Pods that do not are rejected. Rejections happen when the Pod is created, so for Deployments they show up as FailedCreate events on the ReplicaSet, not as errors from kubectl apply (K3, rung 1).

Rule Give each team namespace a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange with sensible defaults, and still set explicit resources in every manifest.

Why Quotas cap a namespace's share of the cluster. Defaults keep unannotated Pods from being rejected or running as BestEffort.

Trap A Deployment scales to 0 ready Pods after a quota was added, and kubectl get events shows exceeded quota or must specify requests.cpu. The Pods do not fit the quota or do not state requests.

Rung 6 Choosing nodes: affinity, taints and tolerations

nodeSelector and nodeAffinity pull Pods towards nodes with given labels. Taints push Pods away from nodes, unless they tolerate the taint. A toleration only permits, it never attracts. With manual-worker2 tainted dedicated=batch:NoSchedule:

no toleration (4 Pods):                   4 manual-worker
toleration only (6 Pods):                 3 manual-worker; 3 manual-worker2     ← still lands on both
toleration + nodeAffinity zone-b (3):     3 manual-worker2

      tolerations:
        - {key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule}
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
              - matchExpressions: [{key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, operator: In, values: [zone-b]}]

Dedicating nodes takes both halves: a taint so nothing else lands there, and affinity plus a toleration so the intended Pods do. preferredDuringScheduling… variants are soft and only weigh the score. NoExecute taints also evict running Pods that do not tolerate them, and Kubernetes itself uses them for unreachable or not-ready nodes.

Rule To dedicate nodes, taint them and give the intended Pods both a toleration and node affinity, and use soft (preferred) rules unless the requirement is absolute.

Why Taints keep others off and affinity pulls the right Pods on. Either one alone leaks in one direction.

Trap "Dedicated" GPU or batch nodes fill with ordinary web Pods, or the batch Pods run everywhere. Only half of the pattern was applied: a toleration without affinity, or affinity without a taint.

Rung 7 Spreading replicas: anti-affinity and topology spread

Replicas on one node or in one zone fail together. Two tools spread them. Required pod anti-affinity is absolute:

3 replicas, required anti-affinity on hostname, 2 schedulable nodes:
1 Pending; 1 manual-worker; 1 manual-worker2
0/3 nodes are available: … 2 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.

Topology spread constraints say "at most maxSkew apart" per topology domain, and can be soft:

      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1                        # zones: never more than one Pod apart
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: {app.kubernetes.io/name: pantry, app.kubernetes.io/component: web}
          matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]   # count only this revision's Pods during a rollout
        - maxSkew: 1                        # nodes: prefer one apart, but do not block scheduling
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway

zone spread, 4 replicas:   2 manual-worker (zone-a); 2 manual-worker2 (zone-b)
golden (HPA min 3):        manual-worker2, manual-worker, manual-worker

matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash] makes each rollout's Pods spread among themselves, instead of being skewed by the old revision's Pods that are about to go away. Combined with a PDB (K4), spreading is what made drains failure-free.

Rule Spread replicas with topologySpreadConstraints: hard across zones, soft across nodes, with matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]. Keep required anti-affinity for the rare "never two on one node" case.

Why Spread constraints bound imbalance without blocking scheduling, while required anti-affinity caps replicas at the number of nodes and leaves the rest Pending.

Trap After a scale-up, some replicas stay Pending with didn't match pod anti-affinity rules. Required anti-affinity allows only one Pod per node. Replace it with a soft spread constraint.

Rung 8 Priority and preemption

When the cluster is full, a PriorityClass decides who waits and who is evicted. A higher-priority Pod that does not fit causes the scheduler to preempt (evict) lower-priority Pods:

batch (4 × 1500m, batch-low) filled both workers:   4 Running
critical (pantry-critical) created:                 event: Preempted by pod … on node manual-worker2
after the victim's grace period:                    batch 1 Pending, 3 Running | critical Running

The evicted batch Pod's replacement stayed Pending, because preemptionPolicy: Never stops low-priority work from evicting anyone itself. Preemption respects graceful termination, so the critical Pod waited for the victim's grace period, and it tries to respect PDBs but will break them if it must. Kubernetes' own components use system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical. Keep application priorities below those.

Rule Give customer-facing workloads a higher PriorityClass than batch and best-effort work, and give the batch classes preemptionPolicy: Never.

Why Under pressure, the scheduler evicts lower-priority Pods to place higher ones, which decides who loses capacity when the cluster is full.

Trap A low-value job, given a high priority "so it starts quickly", evicts production Pods during a busy period. Look for Preempted by pod … events, which name the preemptor.

Decide

Workload Requests Limits Placement
Latency-sensitive web measured CPU + memory memory only zone spread (hard), node spread (soft), PDB, high priority
Strict multi-tenant CPU + memory equal to requests (Guaranteed) as above
Batch / queue workers measured memory; CPU optional tolerate batch nodes + affinity, low priority, preemptionPolicy: Never
Databases (StatefulSet) generous memory = request one per node (anti-affinity) per zone, PDB maxUnavailable: 1
Node agents (DaemonSet) small memory tolerate everything they must run on

The golden file

The golden Pantry Deployment: K3's security context, K4's probes and rollout, measured requests, a memory limit and no CPU limit, zone and node spreading, a priority class, an HPA that owns the replica count, and a PDB. K9 puts this Deployment into the full namespace bundle.

kubectl apply --server-side -f deployment.yaml && kubectl -n k05 rollout status deploy/pantry
kubectl -n k05 get pods -o wide -l app.kubernetes.io/name=pantry      # spread over both zones
kubectl -n k05 get hpa pantry                                         # cpu: 1%/70%, 3 replicas

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Autoscaled, spread, and memory-capped."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The Deployment sets replicas: 1 while an HPA manages it. Every re-apply scaled it from 3 back to 1 (Scaled down replica set … from 3 to 1) until the HPA restored it. Remove replicas.
  2. There is no CPU request, so the HPA cannot compute utilisation: missing request for cpu in container web. Autoscaling never happens. Add measured CPU and memory requests.
  3. limits.memory: 32Mi is below Pantry's footprint, and the Pods were OOMKilled (3 restarts each within a minute). Measure, then set the limit above the peak.
  4. Required anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname with minReplicas: 3 and two schedulable nodes left one replica Pending ("didn't match pod anti-affinity rules"). Use a topology spread constraint instead.

Kubernetes manual · 6 · 9 min readConfig and Secrets#

In the story: sticky notes on the fridge, and the locked drawer · Sticky Notes and the Locked Drawer

ConfigMaps and Secrets get configuration out of images and into the cluster, and both reach a Pod the same three ways: environment variables, mounted files, or single files via subPath. Those three behave very differently when the value changes. "Secret" means much less than the name suggests, too. This chapter measures what updates and when, what a Secret actually protects, and how to make a configuration change roll out the way a code change does.

The ladder

Rung 1 Environment variables are read once

A container's environment is fixed when the container starts. Changing the ConfigMap behind valueFrom or envFrom changes nothing in a running Pod. One ConfigMap was consumed three ways, then changed from v1 to v2:

changed at 01:22:19
01:23:33 env=v1 dir=v1 subPath=v1
01:23:38 env=v1 dir=v2 subPath=v1        ← the directory mount updated ~79 s later
01:23:48 env=v1 dir=v2 subPath=v1        ← env and subPath never change

The directory mount updated. The kubelet refreshes projected files on its sync loop, typically within a minute or two, by swapping a ..data symlink so that readers see either the old set or the new set, never half of each. The environment variable never changes. Only a new container picks up a new value, which in practice means a rollout (rung 7).

Rule Treat environment variables from ConfigMaps and Secrets as fixed at Pod start, and ship changes to them as a rollout.

Why The kubelet resolves valueFrom and envFrom once, when it creates the container, and the kernel offers no way to change another process's environment.

Trap A ConfigMap was changed and the app still uses the old value. Some Pods use the new value and some the old after a node replacement, depending on when each Pod started. kubectl exec … -- env shows the value each one has.

Rung 2 subPath mounts never update

subPath mounts one key as one file at an exact path, which is handy for dropping nginx.conf into a directory that has other files. It is a bind mount of the file as it was at start, so it never sees updates:

        - {name: cfg, mountPath: /etc/one/GREETING, subPath: GREETING}  # one key as a single file

subPath file 100 s after the ConfigMap edit:  still "Hello from Pantry"

To get a single file that does update, mount the whole ConfigMap as a directory somewhere neutral (/etc/pantry/) and point the app at the file inside it, or symlink to it from the image. To place one file among others, use a directory mount with items: selecting which keys appear.

Rule Use subPath only for configuration that changes with a rollout, and mount directories for anything that must update live.

Why A subPath mount binds the file's inode at container start, while directory mounts follow the kubelet's atomic symlink swap.

Trap A "live reloadable" config never reloads, though the app watches its file correctly. The file is mounted with subPath. kubectl get pod -o yaml shows subPath: on that mount.

Rung 3 Files: projected volumes, modes and ownership

Files are the better way to deliver secrets: not visible in env, /proc/<pid>/environ or crash dumps, and with permissions. A projected volume merges several sources (Secrets, ConfigMaps, the downward API, service-account tokens) into one directory:

      volumes:
        - name: secrets
          projected:                                      # several sources in one directory
            defaultMode: 0440
            sources:
              - secret:
                  name: redis-auth                        # rewritten to the hashed name too
                  items: [{key: password, path: redis-password}]
              - downwardAPI:
                  items: [{path: pod-name, fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}]

The files are owned by root. Whether a non-root process can read them depends on the mode and on fsGroup:

defaultMode 0400, no fsGroup:     PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/etc/pantry/redis-password'
defaultMode 0400, fsGroup 10001:  -r--r----- 1 root pantry … redis-password    (group read added)

Rule Mount secrets as files (a projected volume when there are several sources), read-only, with defaultMode: 0440 and the Pod's fsGroup set to the app's GID.

Why Files keep secrets out of environment dumps. fsGroup gives the files the app's group, which is the only way a non-root process reads root-owned 04x0 files.

Trap A hardened Pod crash-loops with Permission denied on its secret file right after runAsUser was added. The file is 0400 root:root and the Pod has no fsGroup.

Rung 4 Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets

immutable: true freezes the data. The API server rejects changes, and the kubelet stops watching the object, which takes load off the API server in clusters with thousands of Pods:

The ConfigMap "frozen" is invalid: data: Forbidden: field is immutable when `immutable` is set

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: pantry-settings-2gfkk74k97}
immutable: true
data: {GREETING: "Hello again from Pantry"}

Immutability fits naturally with hashed names (rung 7): each version is a new object, never edited, and the old ones remain for rollback until they are cleaned up.

Rule Make versioned ConfigMaps and Secrets immutable: true, and change configuration by creating a new object, never by editing one in place.

Why An object that cannot change cannot drift between Pods, and the kubelet does not need to watch it.

Trap Someone "just edits" a ConfigMap to fix production, and half the Pods pick it up (directory mounts) while half do not (env), with no record in git. Immutable objects make that edit fail.

Rung 5 What a Secret does and does not protect

A Secret is base64-encoded, not encrypted. On this cluster it was also stored in plain text in etcd:

.data.password: czNjcmV0LW5vdC1yZWFsLTQy → base64 -d → s3cret-not-real-42
etcdctl get /registry/secrets/k06/redis-auth → … s3cret-not-real-42 …         (no encryption at rest)
envFrom a Secret, then exec: /proc/1/environ → TOKEN=tok-visible-in-environ
client-side apply of stringData: last-applied-configuration annotation → "stringData":{"password":"hunter2"}

What makes a Secret different from a ConfigMap is access control and handling, not cryptography:

  • RBAC can grant ConfigMaps but not Secrets.
  • The kubelet keeps Secret volumes in memory (tmpfs) on the node.
  • Tooling redacts them in describe output.

So access is what to protect. Anyone with get secrets in a namespace can read them all, and anyone who can create Pods there can mount any of them (K9). Encrypt etcd at rest (the API server's EncryptionConfiguration, ideally with a KMS provider), and keep secret values out of git entirely.

Rule Treat Secrets as access-controlled, not encrypted: restrict get/list on them and Pod creation via RBAC, enable encryption at rest, deliver them as files, and keep their values out of git.

Why base64 is an encoding, etcd stores what it is given, and env vars and client-side apply annotations copy values into more places.

Trap A "secret" manifest with stringData: is committed to the repository, so the password is now in git history forever. Rotate the credential, purge the history, and switch to a generator from an ignored file, Sealed Secrets/SOPS, or an external store (rung 8).

Rung 6 Typed Secrets are validated

The type field tells the API server which keys must exist, and tells consumers how to use the Secret:

Type Required keys Used by
Opaque none your apps
kubernetes.io/tls tls.crt, tls.key Ingress / Gateway TLS, cert-manager
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson .dockerconfigjson imagePullSecrets (K9)
kubernetes.io/basic-auth username and/or password some controllers
kubernetes.io/service-account-token filled in by Kubernetes legacy long-lived tokens (avoid, K9) 
type: kubernetes.io/tls with only cert.pem:
The Secret "bad-tls" is invalid: * data[tls.crt]: Required value * data[tls.key]: Required value

kubectl -n k06 create secret tls pantry-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl -n k06 create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=… --docker-username=… --docker-password=…

Rule Use the matching typed Secret (tls, dockerconfigjson) and the kubectl create secret <type> helpers, rather than Opaque with hand-named keys.

Why Typed Secrets are validated on admission, and controllers find the keys where they expect them.

Trap A Gateway's HTTPS listener reports InvalidCertificateRef or serves a default certificate. The Secret is Opaque or has cert.pem instead of tls.crt.

Rung 7 Make configuration changes roll

Since environment values only change with a new container (rung 1), the safe way to change configuration is to change the Pod template when the configuration changes. Kustomize's generators do this by appending a hash of the content to the name and rewriting every reference:

kubectl apply -k pantry           → configmap/pantry-settings-9m5c7d52k9 created, secret/redis-auth-8h7bb9cg7d created
(edit config.env)
kubectl apply -k pantry           → configmap/pantry-settings-2gfkk74k97 created; deployment.apps/pantry configured
rollout history:                    1, 2           both ConfigMaps kept; GREETING in new Pods: Hello again from Pantry

Configuration now behaves like code. It rolls with the Deployment's strategy and probes (K4), a bad value fails the rollout instead of breaking every Pod at once, and kubectl rollout undo brings back the previous ConfigMap because the old template still names it. Helm does the same with a checksum annotation on the template (K10). Old generated objects accumulate, so prune them periodically, or let Argo CD's pruning handle it.

Rule Generate ConfigMaps and Secrets with content-hashed names (kustomize generators, or a checksum annotation in Helm), so every configuration change is a rollout.

Why A changed name changes the Pod template, and template changes are the only thing a Deployment rolls out and can roll back.

Trap A configuration change "takes effect" in one Pod (it restarted) and not in the others, or a bad value breaks every Pod at once on their next restart with no rollout to stop it. The ConfigMap is edited in place under a fixed name.

Rung 8 Encryption at rest and external secret stores

The cluster-side and git-side fixes, briefly:

  • Encryption at rest. The API server's EncryptionConfiguration encrypts chosen resources in etcd. KMS providers keep the key outside the cluster, in a cloud KMS or Vault. Managed clusters usually offer this as a checkbox. kind does not enable it: encryption-provider-config was absent from this API server's flags.
  • External Secrets Operator, or the Secrets Store CSI Driver, reads values from a cloud secret manager or Vault and creates or mounts them, so git holds only a reference.
  • Sealed Secrets or SOPS encrypt values so the ciphertext can live in git, and decryption happens in-cluster or in CI.
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep encryption-provider-config   # empty on kind

Rule In production, enable encryption at rest with a KMS provider, and source secrets from an external store or an encrypted-in-git format, never from plain manifests.

Why These are the only controls that protect secret values from someone who obtains etcd data, a backup, or the repository.

Trap etcd backups are copied to a shared bucket "because they are just cluster state", and every Secret in the cluster is in them in plain text.

Decide

You need Use
A setting read at start env.valueFrom a ConfigMap (rolled with hashed names)
A config file the app reloads ConfigMap volume (directory), no subPath
A file placed among others in a directory subPath, accepting it updates only on rollout
A password or key Secret as a file in a projected volume, 0440 + fsGroup
TLS certificate kubernetes.io/tls Secret (cert-manager in production)
Registry credentials kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson + imagePullSecrets
Config changes as rollouts kustomize generators or Helm checksum annotations
Secrets out of git External Secrets / CSI driver, or Sealed Secrets / SOPS

The golden file

Pantry's configuration as a kustomize directory: settings from a plain config.env, the Redis password from a git-ignored file, both generated with content-hashed names, the password delivered as a file through a projected volume with group-readable mode, and Redis reading the same secret into a tmpfs config file.

openssl rand -hex 16 | tr -d '\n' > pantry/redis-password.txt      # git-ignored
kubectl apply -k pantry && kubectl -n k06 rollout status deploy/pantry
# edit pantry/config.env, apply again: a new pantry-settings-<hash>, and the Deployment rolls

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Password in a Secret, greeting in a ConfigMap, both mounted as files."

This file has 3 problems.

Show answers
  1. The password is in the manifest as stringData: {password: hunter2}: in git, readable by anyone with the repository. After a client-side kubectl apply, it was also copied verbatim into the last-applied-configuration annotation. Generate the Secret from an ignored file or an external store.
  2. The secret file is mounted 0400 with no fsGroup, so as UID 10001 the app crashed with PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/etc/pantry/redis-password'. Add fsGroup: 10001 (the file became -r--r----- root pantry), or use defaultMode: 0440.
  3. Both files are mounted with subPath, so they never update. 100 seconds after the ConfigMap was edited, the file still said "Hello from Pantry". Mount the ConfigMap as a directory, and roll config changes with hashed names.

Kubernetes manual · 7 · 8 min readStorage#

In the story: storage units: the unit itself, the rental request, and the storage company · Memory That Survives, Again

A Pod's filesystem lasts as long as the Pod. Anything else needs a volume, and in Kubernetes persistent volumes come with three layers of indirection:

  • a PersistentVolumeClaim, what the Pod asks for: "1 GiB, one writer";
  • a StorageClass, who provides it and how;
  • a PersistentVolume, the actual disk.

Most storage incidents come from misreading one of those layers: a claim that waits forever, an access mode that does not mean what it says, a reclaim policy that deletes data with the app, a Deployment where a StatefulSet belonged. This chapter measures each on kind's built-in local-path provisioner and says plainly what kind cannot show.

The ladder

Rung 1 emptyDir: scratch space with a limit

emptyDir lives as long as the Pod (it survives container restarts, not Pod deletion). It is backed by the node's disk, or by memory with medium: Memory. Disk-backed emptyDirs count against the Pod's ephemeral storage, and exceeding a sizeLimit evicts the Pod:

emptyDir sizeLimit 20Mi, 60 MB written:
phase=Failed reason=Evicted message=Usage of EmptyDir volume "s" exceeds the limit "20Mi".

  volumes:
    - name: cache
      emptyDir: {sizeLimit: 512Mi}            # disk; evicts the Pod if exceeded
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 16Mi}   # tmpfs; counts against the memory limit (D8, K3)

Use emptyDir for caches, scratch files, sockets and files shared between containers in one Pod (an init container rendering config for the main one). An unbounded emptyDir lets one Pod fill the node's disk and trigger evictions of other Pods.

Rule Give every emptyDir a sizeLimit, and never keep data in one that must survive the Pod.

Why emptyDir is deleted with the Pod, and an unbounded one consumes the node's ephemeral storage, which the kubelet defends by evicting Pods.

Trap Pods on one node are evicted with The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage. Some Pod's unbounded emptyDir or container log filled the disk. kubectl describe node shows DiskPressure.

Rung 2 Claims, classes, and waiting for the first consumer

A PVC asks for storage, and its StorageClass's provisioner creates a PV to satisfy it. With volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, provisioning waits until a Pod using the claim is scheduled, so the volume is created where the Pod will run (the right zone, or with local-path the right node):

data-rwo   Pending   …   waiting for first consumer to be created before binding
(after a Pod used it)
data-rwo   Bound     pvc-55ba6d07-…   1Gi   RWO   standard

kubectl get storageclass                                   # which classes exist, which is (default)
kubectl get pvc,pv -n k07

A Pending claim with that message is normal. A Pending claim with a consumer is a real problem: read its events. Name the StorageClass explicitly in manifests. "The default" differs between clusters and can change.

Rule Set storageClassName explicitly, prefer classes with WaitForFirstConsumer, and read a Pending claim's events before assuming it is broken.

Why Late binding places volumes where their Pods land, and an explicit class makes the manifest mean the same thing on every cluster.

Trap A Pod is Pending with volume node affinity conflict or didn't find available persistent volumes. Its volume was bound in another zone before the Pod was scheduled (an Immediate binding mode), or the class cannot provision there.

Rung 3 Access modes: RWO means one node, not one Pod

The access mode describes how many nodes (or Pods) may mount a volume:

Mode Meaning Measured on local-path
ReadWriteOnce (RWO) read-write by one node, any number of Pods on it 2 Pods, both on manual-worker, both writing
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) read-write by one Pod second Pod Pending: … ReadWriteOncePod access mode already in-use
ReadWriteMany (RWX) read-write by many nodes NodePath only supports ReadWriteOnce and ReadWriteOncePod (never bound)
ReadOnlyMany (ROX) read-only by many nodes needs suitable storage

The RWO surprise is the dangerous one. Two Pods of a Deployment shared one RWO claim, the scheduler placed both on the PV's node, and both wrote to it. For a database, that is two processes on one data directory (the spot-the-bug shows the result). RWX needs storage built for it: NFS, CephFS, a cloud file service. Block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk, local disks) cannot provide it.

        accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]    # exactly one Pod may use it

Rule Use ReadWriteOncePod for single-writer data, request ReadWriteMany only from a class that supports it, and never share a writable claim between replicas of a database.

Why Access modes are enforced per node for RWO and per Pod only for RWOP, and RWX is a capability of the storage, not a setting.

Trap Two replicas of a stateful app "share" a volume and the data is corrupted or inconsistent. The claim was RWO and both Pods landed on one node. Use RWOP and a StatefulSet.

Rung 4 Reclaim policy: what happens to the disk when the claim goes

When a PVC is deleted, its PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy decides the data's fate. Dynamically provisioned volumes inherit Delete from their class:

Delete (default):   PV pvc-55ba6d07-… after deleting its claim: NotFound      ← the data is gone
Retain (patched):   pvc-90e5ed89-…  Retain  Released                          ← the disk and "precious" remain

kubectl patch pv <pv-name> -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'

A Released PV is not reused automatically. It keeps its old claimRef until an admin clears it or copies the data out, which is the point. Deleting a namespace deletes its PVCs, and with Delete, their disks. So does kubectl delete -f on a file that contains the PVC next to the app.

Rule Use a Retain StorageClass (or patch the PV) for data you cannot regenerate, keep PVCs out of app manifests that get deleted and re-applied, and back up anyway (snapshots or app-level dumps).

Why With Delete, removing the claim, by hand, by namespace deletion or by a manifest delete, destroys the underlying disk immediately.

Trap "Recreating the namespace to start fresh" wiped the production database. The PVCs went with the namespace and the class's policy was Delete. kubectl get pv showed nothing left to recover.

Rung 5 StatefulSets: stable names, stable storage

A StatefulSet gives each replica a stable identity: an ordinal name (redis-0), a DNS name through a headless Service (redis-0.redis.k07.svc), and its own claim from volumeClaimTemplates (data-redis-0). Pods are created in order, and a replaced Pod gets back the same name and the same claim:

SET visits 42; delete Pod redis-0          → redis-0 back, visits=42
nslookup redis-0.redis.k07.svc.cluster.local → 10.244.2.128 (the Pod's own IP)
delete the StatefulSet                     → data-redis-0 still Bound
re-create it                               → visits=42

spec:
  serviceName: redis                       # gives each Pod the stable name <pod>.redis.<ns>.svc
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain                    # deleting the StatefulSet keeps the data (the default, written down)
    whenScaled: Retain                     # scaling down keeps redis-1's claim for when it comes back

The headless Service (clusterIP: None) is what makes per-Pod DNS names exist, and clustered databases use those names to find each other. StatefulSets do not replicate data. They give each replica a stable place to keep its own copy. Replication is the database's job.

Rule Run anything with per-replica persistent state as a StatefulSet with a headless Service and volumeClaimTemplates, never as a Deployment with a shared claim.

Why StatefulSets bind each ordinal to its own claim and DNS name for life, which is exactly what databases and quorum systems assume.

Trap After scaling a StatefulSet down and up, a replica comes back with old data. Its claim was retained by design (whenScaled: Retain) and re-attached. Delete the claim explicitly if the data should not return.

Rung 6 Volume ownership: fsGroup, and where it does not apply

fsGroup makes volumes group-writable for a non-root Pod (K3), and fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch avoids re-chowning large volumes at every mount. Not every volume type honours it:

emptyDir with fsGroup 10001 (K3):          drwxrwsrwt root pantry      ← applied
local-path PV with fsGroup 1000 (here):    drwxrwxrwx root root        ← ignored; writable only because it is 0777

      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 1000                      # volume group-owned by redis
        fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch   # skip the recursive chown once ownership is right (K3)

Block-based CSI volumes (cloud disks) support fsGroup. hostPath-based provisioners like local-path, and many NFS setups, do not. Check with ls -ld in the container rather than assuming.

Rule Set fsGroup and fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch on stateful Pods, and verify the mounted directory's owner and mode on each storage class you use.

Why Ownership changes are applied by the kubelet only for volume types that support them. Others keep whatever owner and mode the provisioner chose.

Trap A database that runs as non-root fails with Permission denied on one cluster's storage and works on another. One class honours fsGroup and the other does not. ls -ld /data in the container shows it.

Rung 7 Expansion, snapshots, and what kind cannot show

Two features depend entirely on the CSI driver behind the class:

  • Expansion. With allowVolumeExpansion: true, edit the PVC's resources.requests.storage upwards and the driver grows the disk, often online. Volumes never shrink.
  • Snapshots. VolumeSnapshot objects, backed by a VolumeSnapshotClass, take point-in-time copies that can seed new claims.

On kind, neither exists:

allowVolumeExpansion=[]
error: the server doesn't have a resource type "volumesnapshotclasses"

kubectl get storageclass -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,EXPAND:.allowVolumeExpansion,RECLAIM:.reclaimPolicy
kubectl api-resources | grep snapshot.storage.k8s.io

local-path volumes are directories on one node, so a node failure takes the data with it. That is fine for learning and wrong for production. On a real cluster, check that each class you depend on supports expansion and snapshots before you need them, and that snapshots are actually restorable.

Rule Before relying on a StorageClass, confirm its access modes, reclaim policy, binding mode, expansion and snapshot support, and test a restore.

Why All of these are properties of the CSI driver, and they differ completely between local, network and cloud storage.

Trap A disk fills, someone edits the PVC to grow it, and the API refuses: persistentvolumeclaims "data-redis-0" is forbidden: only dynamically provisioned pvc can be resized and the storageclass that provisions the pvc must support resize (measured here). The class does not allow expansion. Find out before the disk is full.

Decide

Data Use Access mode Reclaim
Scratch, cache, render output emptyDir with sizeLimit n/a gone with the Pod
Single database / queue StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates RWOP Retain
Clustered database (3 replicas) StatefulSet, anti-affinity per zone RWOP each Retain
Files shared by many Pods RWX class (NFS, CephFS, cloud files) RWX per data value
Static content bake it into the image, or object storage n/a n/a
Config ConfigMap (K6), not a volume you edit ROX via projection n/a

The golden file

Redis with storage that outlives its Pods: a headless Service for stable DNS, a StatefulSet with an explicit retention policy, a single-Pod claim per replica from an explicit class, non-root identity with fsGroup and OnRootMismatch, a readiness probe, and resources.

kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml -f redis.yaml && kubectl -n k07 rollout status sts/redis
kubectl -n k07 exec redis-0 -- redis-cli SET visits 42
kubectl -n k07 delete pod redis-0 && kubectl -n k07 wait --for=condition=Ready pod/redis-0
kubectl -n k07 exec redis-0 -- redis-cli GET visits        # 42

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Redis with a persistent volume, two replicas for safety."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. ReadWriteMany from a class that cannot provide it: the claim and both Pods stayed Pending (NodePath only supports ReadWriteOnce and ReadWriteOncePod). Request what the class supports, and RWOP for a single writer.
  2. A Deployment with two replicas on one claim. With RWO, both Pods ran on the same node over one data directory, and each Redis answered GET who with its own value. Two processes, one set of files. Use a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates (one claim each), and Redis replication if you need two copies.
  3. The PVC sits in the same file as the app and the class's policy is Delete, so kubectl delete -f on this file deleted the PV and the data (NotFound). Keep data claims out of app manifests (or use volumeClaimTemplates with whenDeleted: Retain), and use a Retain class.
  4. There is no storageClassName, so the claim gets whatever the cluster's default is (here local-path, on a different cluster something else, with different modes and reclaim policy). Name the class.

Kubernetes manual · 8 · 10 min readNetworking#

In the story: the phone number that never changes, the city's front gate, and which corridors connect which districts · A Number That Never Changes, Districts, Key Cards and Rush Hour

Kubernetes networking is three layers:

  • Services give a set of Pods one stable name and virtual IP, and keep their EndpointSlices up to date.
  • Gateways (or the older Ingress) bring traffic in from outside by hostname and path.
  • NetworkPolicies decide which Pods may talk to which.

Each layer has a status you can read. Most "the network is broken" incidents are one of those statuses saying exactly what is wrong while nobody looks.

The ladder

Rung 1 Service types, and targeting ports by name

Type Reachable from Notes
ClusterIP (default) inside the cluster name.namespace.svc DNS + a virtual IP
NodePort every node's IP on a high port (30000–32767) building block for LBs and kind
LoadBalancer an external IP from a cloud or bare-metal controller <pending> forever where there is none, as on kind
ExternalName DNS CNAME to an outside name no proxying, no ports
headless (clusterIP: None) DNS returns Pod IPs directly StatefulSets (K7)

Target container ports by name, so the port number can change in one place:

  ports: [{name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http}]    # targets the container port *named* http

A name that matches no container port fails silently. The Service exists, has endpoints, and has no ports:

targetPort: web   →   EndpointSlice ports: null   endpoints: ["10.244.2.141"]
through the gateway: 503

Rule Use ClusterIP Services for everything internal, expose externally through a Gateway, name every container port, and target it by name.

Why Named ports decouple the Service from the container's port number, and a single entry point (the Gateway) replaces one LoadBalancer per Service.

Trap A Service has endpoints and every request fails or returns 503. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> -o yaml shows ports: null: the targetPort name matches no container port.

Rung 2 EndpointSlices: who is actually behind the Service

A Service is only as good as its EndpointSlices. They list the Pods whose labels match the selector, with ready, serving and terminating conditions. Readiness probes (K4) control ready, and kube-proxy sends traffic only to ready endpoints. When none are ready it falls back to terminating ones that are still serving, which is why the K4 drains lost nothing.

kubectl -n k08 get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pantry -o wide
kubectl -n k08 get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pantry -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].endpoints[*]}{.addresses} ready={.conditions.ready}{"\n"}{end}'

A Service with no endpoints refuses connections outright: right after creation, a client got Connection refused until the first endpoint appeared. That is not a NetworkPolicy, which times out instead (rung 7). The difference between "refused" and "timed out" is the first diagnostic.

Rule When traffic to a Service fails, read its EndpointSlices first: empty means the selector or readiness, ports: null means the target port, and only then look further.

Why Every Service problem below the Gateway appears in the slices: no matching Pods, unready Pods, or no matching port.

Trap Connection refused from a Service whose Pods look Running. They are not Ready (a failing readiness probe), so the slice has no ready endpoints. kubectl describe pod shows Readiness probe failed.

Rung 3 externalTrafficPolicy and the client's address

For NodePort and LoadBalancer Services, externalTrafficPolicy decides what happens to traffic arriving at a node. With Cluster, any node accepts and forwards, but the source address is rewritten. With Local, only nodes with a ready Pod accept, and the client's address survives:

echo Pod on manual-worker; requests from 172.20.0.5
Cluster via manual-worker:    client seen as 10.244.2.1     (SNAT)
Cluster via manual-worker2:   client seen as 172.20.0.7     (SNAT to that node)
Local   via manual-worker:    client seen as 172.20.0.5     (real address)
Local   via manual-worker2:   no answer (timeout)

This bit the golden setup itself. Envoy Gateway creates its proxy Service with Local, kind maps host port 30090 to manual-worker, and the proxy ran on manual-worker2, so requests from the laptop got an empty reply until the EnvoyProxy set Cluster. Cloud load balancers handle Local correctly by health-checking nodes. A static port mapping, as on kind, does not.

      envoyService:
        type: NodePort
        externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster     # Envoy Gateway defaults to Local: only the node running the proxy would answer

Rule Use externalTrafficPolicy: Local only behind a load balancer that health-checks nodes and when you need client IPs, and otherwise use Cluster (or get client IPs from the proxy's X-Forwarded-For).

Why Local avoids the extra hop and SNAT but drops traffic at nodes without a ready Pod. Cluster always forwards and hides the client.

Trap An externally exposed Service works only some of the time, or only from some load balancer nodes. The policy is Local, and traffic reaches nodes without a Pod. kubectl get svc -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalTrafficPolicy}' shows it.

Rung 4 Gateway API: three objects, three owners

Gateway API splits ingress into objects owned by different people. The GatewayClass (the infrastructure team) names the implementation. The Gateway (the platform team) is an entry point with listeners, and says which namespaces may attach routes. The HTTPRoute (the app team) maps hostnames and paths to Services:

gateway/public    CLASS eg   ADDRESS 172.20.0.7   PROGRAMMED True
route from k08 (namespace labelled gateway-access):   Accepted=True
route from an unlabelled namespace:                   Accepted=False NotAllowedByListeners: No listeners included by this parent ref allowed this attachment.

That last line is the point of the split. An app team cannot claim pantry.example.test on the shared Gateway from a namespace the platform team has not approved. Gateway API reached v1.0 (GA) in October 2023, and it is what the Kubernetes project now points Ingress users towards.

Rule Expose services through Gateway API: one GatewayClass per implementation, Gateways owned by the platform with allowedRoutes restricted by namespace selector, and HTTPRoutes in the app namespaces.

Why The role split puts each decision (implementation, entry point and TLS, routing) with the team that owns it, enforced by the API rather than by convention.

Trap A route is applied and traffic never arrives (404). Its status says NotAllowedByListeners, or it has no status at all because its parentRefs points to a Gateway in the wrong namespace. Read kubectl get httproute -o yaml → status.parents.

Rung 5 HTTPRoutes: status tells you everything

An HTTPRoute matches on hostname, path, headers, method or query parameters, and can split traffic by weight between backends (canaries), rewrite paths, redirect, and set headers:

HTTPRoute k08/pantry:  Accepted=True Accepted   ResolvedRefs=True ResolvedRefs
Host pantry.example.test → 200      Host other.example.test → 404

  rules:
    - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]
      backendRefs:
        - {name: pantry, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: pantry-canary, port: 80, weight: 10}

The status conditions separate the failures. Accepted=False means the Gateway refused the route (namespace, listener or hostname mismatch). ResolvedRefs=False means a backend is missing (BackendNotFound), or is in another namespace without a ReferenceGrant. A 404 from the gateway means no route matched the host or path. A 503 means it matched but no backend endpoint answered. In this chapter's spot-the-bug, fixing each layer in turn moved the response from 404 to 503 to a timeout to 200.

Rule After applying a route, check status.parents[].conditions for Accepted and ResolvedRefs, and read 404 as "no route matched" and 503 as "no backend answered".

Why The gateway controller reports exactly why a route is not in effect, and the HTTP status code says which layer stopped the request.

Trap A cross-namespace backendRef shows ResolvedRefs=False RefNotPermitted. The target namespace needs a ReferenceGrant allowing routes from the route's namespace.

Rung 6 Ingress: the legacy form

Ingress is the older API: one object with host and path rules, interpreted by whichever controller owns its ingressClassName. It still works where a controller is installed, and much existing YAML uses it. With no controller, it is accepted and does nothing, without an error:

$ kubectl get ingressclass
No resources found
$ kubectl -n k08 get ingress pantry
NAME     CLASS   HOSTS                 ADDRESS   PORTS
pantry   nginx   pantry.example.test             80          ← no address, ever

The most widely deployed controller, ingress-nginx, was retired by the Kubernetes project: announced in November 2025, with best-effort maintenance ending in March 2026 and no further releases or security fixes after that. Existing installations keep working, but they are now unmaintained software at the edge of the cluster. Advanced behaviour in Ingress lived in controller-specific annotations, which is the main thing a migration has to translate (the Ingress2Gateway tool helps).

Rule Write new routing as Gateway API, plan migrations off retired Ingress controllers, and when you must read an Ingress, check its class and controller first.

Why Ingress semantics beyond host and path rules are controller-specific annotations, and the most common controller no longer receives security fixes.

Trap An Ingress copied from another cluster has no ADDRESS and traffic never arrives. No controller serves its ingressClassName here. kubectl get ingressclass shows what exists.

Rung 7 NetworkPolicy: default deny, and the DNS trap

Without any NetworkPolicy, every Pod can reach every other Pod in the cluster. A policy selecting a Pod makes it default-deny for the directions it lists, plus whatever its rules allow. Policies are additive. Start with deny-all for the namespace, then allow flows one by one. The first flow to allow is DNS, or nothing resolves:

default-deny (Ingress + Egress) only:
  socket.gaierror: [Errno -3] Temporary failure in name resolution
  new Pod after restart: 0/1 (readiness needs Redis, which needs DNS)
  through the gateway: 000 (timeout)

with the golden policies:   rollout completes; through the gateway: Hello from Pantry …
other Pod in k08 → redis:   blocked (timed out)

Policies select peers by labels: podSelector for Pods in the same namespace, namespaceSelector (with kubernetes.io/metadata.name, which every namespace has) for other namespaces, or both together to mean "these Pods in that namespace". Denied traffic is dropped, so it shows up as a timeout, not a refusal.

Rule Put a default-deny policy (Ingress and Egress) in every application namespace, allow DNS egress to kube-dns explicitly, then allow each required flow by label.

Why NetworkPolicies are allow-lists once a Pod is selected, so DNS, like every other flow, must be listed or it is blocked.

Trap Right after adding NetworkPolicies, new Pods fail with Temporary failure in name resolution or time out to every name. Egress was denied without the DNS rule.

Rung 8 NetworkPolicy details that cause outages

Three measured details:

  • Ports are the Pod's ports, not the Service's. A rule allowing port: 80 (the Service port) blocked the gateway, because the Pods listen on 8080. The response went from 200 to a timeout. Use the named port (port: http) and the mismatch cannot happen.
  • kubectl port-forward ignores NetworkPolicy. With deny-all in place, port-forward to a Pod still answered alive, because the kubelet connects inside the Pod's network namespace. "It works with port-forward" proves nothing about the policy.
  • Established connections can outlive a new policy. Pods with an open Redis connection stayed Ready after deny-all was applied, while new Pods could not connect. A policy change can look harmless until the next restart.
      ports: [{port: http}]                 # the container port's name, never the Service port

Rule Reference Pod ports by name in policies, test policies with real traffic through the real path (not port-forward), and restart a workload after changing its policies to see the steady state.

Why Policies match packets at the Pod, by the Pod's port, after Service translation. port-forward does not traverse that path, and existing flows may be tracked from before the change.

Trap A policy change "passes testing" with kubectl port-forward and breaks production traffic through the gateway. The port in the rule is the Service port, or the gateway's namespace and Pod labels do not match the from selector.

Decide

Need Use
Internal service-to-service ClusterIP + DNS name svc.namespace
Per-Pod DNS (databases) headless Service + StatefulSet
External HTTP(S) Gateway + HTTPRoute (one shared Gateway per environment)
External TCP/UDP Gateway TCPRoute/UDPRoute, or a LoadBalancer Service
Client IP at the app X-Forwarded-For from the gateway, or externalTrafficPolicy: Local behind a health-checking LB
Canary / weighted traffic HTTPRoute backendRefs with weight
Isolation default-deny + DNS + explicit allows, per namespace
Existing Ingress YAML keep running where maintained, and migrate to Gateway API (Ingress2Gateway)

The golden file

Pantry's network, owned by three teams: the GatewayClass and proxy exposure (infrastructure), the shared Gateway with namespace-restricted routes (platform), and the app's Services, HTTPRoute and NetworkPolicies (app team: default-deny, DNS, and exactly the flows Pantry needs).

kubectl apply -f gatewayclass.yaml -f gateway.yaml && kubectl -n gateway wait --for=condition=Programmed gateway/public
kubectl apply -f pantry.yaml -f networkpolicy.yaml && kubectl -n k08 rollout status deploy/pantry
curl -s -H "Host: pantry.example.test" http://127.0.0.1:30090/          # Hello from Pantry …

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Exposes Pantry on bug.example.test and locks the namespace down." Applied next to the golden Pantry Deployment.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. parentRefs: [{name: public}] has no namespace, so it means a Gateway public in k08, which does not exist. The route got no status, and bug.example.test returned 404. Add namespace: gateway.
  2. targetPort: web matches no container port. The EndpointSlice had ports: null, and the gateway returned 503. Use targetPort: http.
  3. The ingress rule allows port: 80, the Service's port, but policies match the Pod's port (8080). The gateway timed out until the rule said port: 8080 (better: port: http).
  4. Egress is denied except to Redis, with no DNS rule. Existing Pods kept working, but after a restart new Pods failed with Temporary failure in name resolution and stayed 0/1. Allow UDP and TCP 53 to kube-dns.
  5. type: LoadBalancer gives a second, direct way in that bypasses the Gateway. On kind it stayed EXTERNAL-IP <pending>, and on a cloud it would create a public load balancer. Use ClusterIP and route through the Gateway.

Kubernetes manual · 9 · 9 min readIdentity and Access#

In the story: the key cards that say who may open which door · Districts, Key Cards and Rush Hour

Two kinds of client talk to the Kubernetes API: ServiceAccounts (workloads in the cluster) and users (humans and CI, authenticated outside the cluster). Both are authorised the same way, by RBAC: Roles list what may be done, and bindings say who may do it. The default is deny, but the defaults around it are generous, and the common mistakes, a token nobody needs, a ClusterRoleBinding where a Role belonged, a wildcard "to save time", all grant far more than intended. This chapter builds least privilege and ends with Pantry's whole namespace in one file.

The ladder

Rung 1 ServiceAccount tokens, and turning them off

Every Pod runs as a ServiceAccount (the namespace's default if none is named). By default the kubelet mounts a short-lived, audience-scoped token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, which the Pod can use to call the API. Most Pods never call the API, so the token is pure attack surface. Turn it off:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: pantry-web, namespace: k09}
automountServiceAccountToken: false

with automount off: ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount → exit code 1 (directory absent)
default token claims: aud [https://kubernetes.default.svc...], exp−iat = 1 year (bound to the Pod), warnafter = iat + ~1h
token after the Pod is deleted: 401                  (bound tokens die with the Pod)

Modern projected tokens are bound to the Pod and rotated hourly by the kubelet, so a stolen one is far less useful than the old, never-expiring Secret tokens (Old Maps). Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the ServiceAccount (covering every Pod that uses it) or on the Pod spec.

Rule Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on every ServiceAccount, and turn it back on per Pod only where the workload calls the API.

Why A mounted token is a credential inside the container. A Pod that never uses it loses nothing by not having it, and an attacker who lands in the container loses a starting point.

Trap A compromised web Pod can list Secrets cluster-wide. It had an automounted token and the default ServiceAccount had been granted broad rights. kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.automountServiceAccountToken}' and the SA's bindings show it.

Rung 2 A ServiceAccount per workload

The default ServiceAccount is shared by every Pod in the namespace that names none, so anything granted to default is granted to all of them. Give each workload its own:

    spec:
      serviceAccountName: pantry-web
      automountServiceAccountToken: false

Then each workload's rights are exactly its own, bindings read clearly, and an audit of "what can the web tier do" is a question about one ServiceAccount. Granting rights to default is the opposite: invisible, and inherited by every Pod that forgot to set serviceAccountName.
