Rule Create a named ServiceAccount per workload and set serviceAccountName on the Pod spec. Never grant rights to the default ServiceAccount.

Why Permissions attach to a ServiceAccount, and a shared account spreads whatever it is granted to every Pod that uses it.

Trap A new Pod unexpectedly has API access it never asked for. It uses default, which someone bound a role to long ago. kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide | grep ':default' finds them.

Rung 3 Roles, bindings, and resourceNames

A Role is a list of rules: API groups, resources, verbs, and optionally resourceNames. A RoleBinding grants a Role to subjects (ServiceAccounts, users, groups) in one namespace. Least privilege down to a single object:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: read-pantry-settings, namespace: k09}
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [configmaps]
    resourceNames: [pantry-settings]        # this one object, nothing else
    verbs: [get, watch]

get configmap/pantry-settings  yes
get configmap/other            no
list configmaps                no          ← list/watch cannot be limited by resourceNames
get secrets                    no

resourceNames restricts get, update, patch and delete to named objects, but not list or watch, because those return collections. So a role that can list configmaps can read every configmap, resourceNames or not. Grant list/watch deliberately. RBAC is additive and has no deny rules: a subject may do the union of everything bound to it.

Rule Write Roles that name the exact apiGroups, resources and verbs needed, use resourceNames for single-object access, and never grant list/watch on Secrets casually.

Why RBAC only adds permissions, and list/watch ignore resourceNames, so a "read one ConfigMap" role that uses list reads them all.

Trap A role meant to read one object reads every object of that kind. It granted list or watch, which resourceNames does not constrain.

Rung 4 Role versus ClusterRole, RoleBinding versus ClusterRoleBinding

The scope comes from the binding, and this is the most consequential RBAC mistake:

Role type Binding Grants
Role RoleBinding the Role's rules, in that one namespace
ClusterRole RoleBinding the ClusterRole's rules, in that one namespace
ClusterRole ClusterRoleBinding the ClusterRole's rules, in every namespace and cluster-wide

A ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding is the useful, safe pattern: define view/edit-style rules once, grant them per namespace. A ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding grants them everywhere. The spot-the-bug file binds the built-in edit ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount with a ClusterRoleBinding:

SA pantry (ClusterRoleBinding → edit):  get secrets -n kube-system: yes ;  get secrets -n k09: yes

The web app can now read every Secret in the cluster. The fix is a RoleBinding in its own namespace. Use ClusterRoleBinding only for genuinely cluster-wide subjects (controllers, node agents), and keep its roles minimal.

Rule Grant namespaced access with a RoleBinding (to a Role or a ClusterRole), and reserve ClusterRoleBinding for truly cluster-wide needs.

Why A ClusterRoleBinding ignores namespaces, so it grants its role in all of them at once, including kube-system.

Trap A workload or user can act in namespaces it should never touch. kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide shows a binding to a namespaced subject. Replace it with a RoleBinding per namespace.

Rung 5 Built-in roles and least privilege

Kubernetes ships aggregated ClusterRoles: view (read, no Secrets), edit (write, no RBAC), admin (edit plus RBAC within a namespace), cluster-admin (everything). They are convenient and usually too broad:

view → get secrets:  no
edit → get secrets:  yes          ← edit can read Secrets
edit → create pods:  yes

edit reading Secrets surprises people. For an on-call human who should restart a rollout and read logs but never read Secrets, a purpose-built Role is safer than edit. The golden bundle's pantry-oncall Role allows read on the workload resources, logs, and patch on the one Deployment named pantry:

on-call (group pantry-oncall) in k09:
  get pods yes ; get pods/log yes ; get secrets no ; patch deployment/pantry yes ; patch deployment/other no ; delete pods no ; create pods no

Rule Start from a purpose-built Role, use the built-in view/edit/admin only when their breadth is acceptable, and never bind cluster-admin to a workload.

Why The built-in roles are deliberately broad, and edit includes reading Secrets, which is rarely what "let them edit" is meant to allow.

Trap "We gave the team edit so they could deploy" also gave them every Secret in the namespace. Check with kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=….

Rung 6 Permissions that grant more than they say

Some verbs are escalation paths, because they let a subject change the permission system itself:

  • create/patch on roles/rolebindings lets a subject grant itself anything (RBAC prevents granting more than you hold, but escalate/bind verbs override that check).
  • create pods in a namespace means mounting any ServiceAccount there and using its token, and setting nodeName to skip the scheduler.
  • get/list secrets includes ServiceAccount tokens and TLS keys.
  • create pods/exec, pods/attach, pods/portforward is a shell in any Pod.
  • impersonate (users, groups, serviceaccounts) is acting as anyone.
  • escalate/bind on roles, approve on certificatesigningrequests, write on validatingwebhookconfigurations are cluster-takeover primitives.

The spot-the-bug file's wildcard Role (apiGroups ["*"], resources ["*"], verbs ["*"]) on the default ServiceAccount grants all of these in its namespace:

SA default (wildcard Role) → delete rolebindings: yes ;  create roles: yes

Treat these verbs as privileged wherever they appear, and never use resource or verb wildcards in application roles.

Rule Audit for create pods, Secret read, exec/attach, impersonate, write on roles/bindings/webhooks and * wildcards, and grant them only to trusted operators.

Why These permissions let a subject reach other identities, run code in other Pods, or edit RBAC itself, so they are effectively administrative however narrowly the manifest reads.

Trap A seemingly modest role "to let the CI deploy" includes create pods and create secrets, which together let it mint and mount privileged identities. Review the verbs, not the role's name.

Rung 7 imagePullSecrets and workload identity

Two more things attach to a ServiceAccount. imagePullSecrets on the SA are added to every Pod that uses it, so private-registry credentials live in one place:

ServiceAccount with imagePullSecrets [regcred] → Pod spec.imagePullSecrets: [{"name":"regcred"}]  (injected)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: pantry-web, namespace: k09}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]        # added to every Pod using this SA

And for workloads that do call cloud APIs, the ServiceAccount is the identity to federate: a projected token with a cloud audience, exchanged for cloud credentials (IRSA on EKS, Workload Identity on GKE, Azure Workload Identity). That keeps long-lived cloud keys out of the cluster entirely. It is cloud-specific, so it is out of scope here, but the principle is the same: the Pod's identity is its ServiceAccount.

Rule Put imagePullSecrets on the ServiceAccount, and federate the ServiceAccount to the cloud's identity system rather than storing cloud keys in Secrets.

Why Both are properties of the workload's identity, so attaching them to the ServiceAccount keeps credentials in one audited place and out of Pod specs.

Trap The same registry secret is pasted into every Deployment, and rotating it means editing them all. Move it to the ServiceAccount's imagePullSecrets.

Rung 8 Humans: groups, impersonation and can-i

Kubernetes does not store users. It trusts an external authenticator (client certs, OIDC, a cloud IAM) to assert a username and groups, and RBAC binds to those. Bind Roles to groups, not individuals, so joining the team is adding a person to a group, not editing RBAC:

subjects: [{kind: Group, name: pantry-oncall, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}]

Two commands make RBAC debuggable without handing out credentials:

kubectl auth whoami                                               # who the API thinks you are
kubectl auth can-i patch deploy/pantry -n k09 --as=alice --as-group=pantry-oncall
kubectl auth can-i --list -n k09 --as=system:serviceaccount:k09:pantry-web

kubectl auth whoami → Username kubernetes-admin, Groups [kubeadm:cluster-admins system:authenticated]

--as/--as-group impersonate a subject to test what they can do (it needs the impersonate permission, which is itself privileged, rung 6). can-i --list dumps everything a subject may do. Use them in CI to assert that a role grants no more than intended.

Rule Authenticate humans through your identity provider, bind Roles to groups, and verify every role with kubectl auth can-i --as/--as-group (ideally in CI).

Why Binding to groups keeps membership out of RBAC, and impersonation checks turn "does this role over-grant?" into a test you can run.

Trap Access was granted by binding to individual usernames, and an offboarded employee's access lingers, or a role grants more than anyone realised. Bind to groups, and audit with can-i --list.

Decide

Subject Identity Authorisation
App that never calls the API (Pantry) own SA, automountServiceAccountToken: false no RBAC
Controller / operator own SA, token on the minimal ClusterRole it needs
App calling cloud APIs own SA federated to cloud IAM cloud-side
On-call humans identity provider group purpose-built Role via RoleBinding
Namespace admins group admin ClusterRole via RoleBinding
CI deploying one namespace SA or user Role via RoleBinding, no create pods + create secrets together
Cluster operators group cluster-admin, few people, audited

The golden file

Pantry's entire namespace, assembled from K1–K9: PSA labels and quotas (K3, K5), a ServiceAccount per workload with tokens off (K9), an on-call Role bound to a group, Redis as a StatefulSet (K7), the web Deployment with probes, resources, spread and a priority class (K2–K5), the Service, HPA and PDBs (K4, K5, K8), the HTTPRoute and NetworkPolicies (K8).

kubectl apply --server-side -f bundle.yaml          # needs the k08 GatewayClass + Gateway and metrics-server
kubectl -n k09 rollout status sts/redis && kubectl -n k09 rollout status deploy/pantry
curl -s -H "Host: pantry-k09.example.test" http://127.0.0.1:30090/
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n k09 --as=alice --as-group=pantry-oncall      # no

On this cluster the bundle came up with Pods spread across both zones, served traffic through the Gateway, survived a drain of a worker with zero failed requests (PDB + spread), autoscaled from 3 to 6 under load, blocked an unlisted Pod from Redis, and let the on-call group restart the Deployment but not read Secrets.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Gives the Pantry app and the team the access they need."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The pantry ServiceAccount is bound to the built-in edit ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding, so it can read Secrets in every namespace (get secrets -n kube-system: yes). Use a RoleBinding in k09-bug, and a far narrower role.
  2. A Role grants apiGroups ["*"], resources ["*"], verbs ["*"] to the default ServiceAccount: every Pod with no serviceAccountName (including this Deployment's) can create roles and delete rolebindings in the namespace (rung 6). Remove it; grant specific rights to named SAs.
  3. The Deployment sets no serviceAccountName, so its Pods run as default and inherit that wildcard Role, and it does not set automountServiceAccountToken: false, so the token is mounted. Name a dedicated SA with the token off.
  4. Even corrected, the app needs no API access at all. Pantry never calls the API, so the right answer is its own ServiceAccount with no RBAC and no mounted token.

Kubernetes manual · 10 · 8 min readPackaging: Helm and Kustomize#

In the story: flat-pack furniture, and the same blueprint with a different overlay per district · Flat-Pack Furniture, Nobody Touches the City by Hand

The K9 bundle is one file for one environment. Real deployments need the same manifests across dev, staging and several production clusters, with a few differences each. The two standard tools take opposite approaches. Helm is templates plus values: one parameterised chart, installed with different values per environment, and a release you can roll back. Kustomize is a base plus overlays: plain manifests, patched per environment, with no templating language. This chapter builds the golden bundle both ways and says when to pick which.

The ladder

Rung 1 Chart layout

A chart is a directory with a fixed shape. Chart.yaml is metadata, values.yaml holds the defaults, templates/ holds the manifests, and templates/tests/ holds test hooks:

chart/
  Chart.yaml            name, version (the chart's), appVersion (the app's)
  values.yaml           defaults
  values.schema.json    validates values (rung 4)
  templates/
    _helpers.tpl        named template snippets
    deployment.yaml     …and one file per object
    tests/connection.yaml   a test hook (must be under templates/)

helm lint ./chart        → 1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
helm template r ./chart  → the rendered manifests, for review and diff

The two versions matter. version is the chart's own, bumped when the chart changes. appVersion is the application's, and it is the default image tag here. helm template renders without touching the cluster, which is what to read in code review and diff in CI. Files whose names start with _ (like _helpers.tpl) render nothing themselves; they define reusable snippets.

Rule Keep the standard layout, bump version on chart changes and appVersion on app releases, and review charts by reading helm template output.

Why Helm relies on the directory shape (templates/, templates/tests/, _ for partials), and helm template is the deterministic preview of what will be applied.

Trap helm test reports TEST SUITE: None though a test file exists. It is in a top-level tests/ directory; Helm only renders files under templates/. Move it to templates/tests/.

Rung 2 Helpers and the DRY labels

_helpers.tpl defines named templates for things repeated across files: the release-qualified name, the recommended labels (K1), the selector subset, the image reference:

metadata:
  name: {{ include "pantry.fullname" . }}
  labels: {{- include "pantry.labels" . | nindent 4 }}

include "name" . renders a named template with the current context. nindent 4 adds a newline and indents each line by four spaces, which is how a multi-line block is placed under a key. The fullname helper uses the common idiom: when the release name already contains the chart name, use it alone, otherwise join them, so a release called pantry produces objects named pantry, not pantry-pantry. Keep the selector labels (name + instance) in their own helper, because a Deployment's selector is immutable (K1) and must never include volatile labels like version.

Rule Define the fullname, full label set, selector subset and image reference as helpers, and build every object's metadata and selectors from them.

Why One definition of the labels keeps every object consistent and keeps the immutable selector stable across upgrades.

Trap An upgrade fails with field is immutable on the Deployment selector. A helper used for both the selector and the labels included a changing value (the chart version or app version). Keep the selector helper minimal.

Rung 3 Template the right things, and only those

Values should cover what differs between environments: replica count, image tag, resources, whether optional pieces (an HTTPRoute, autoscaling) are on. Everything that is the same everywhere (the security context, probes, the preStop hook) stays literal in the template. Over-parameterising a chart makes it as hard to read as the manifests it replaced.

Two patterns here. {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}replicas:{{- end }} omits replicas entirely when the HPA owns it (K1), instead of fighting over it. {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} renders a whole values sub-tree as YAML, which is how a map value reaches the manifest. Writing {{ .Values.resources }} instead prints Go's map[...] representation and breaks the render (the spot-the-bug does exactly that).

Rule Parameterise only what changes between environments, keep invariant hardening literal, and render map and list values with toYaml | nindent.

Why A small values surface is readable and safe, and toYaml is the only correct way to emit a structured value.

Trap helm template fails with error converting YAML to JSON or a manifest shows map[cpu:100m ...]. A structured value was emitted with {{ .Values.x }} instead of {{ toYaml .Values.x | nindent N }}.

Rung 4 values.schema.json catches bad values before the cluster does

A chart can ship a JSON Schema that Helm validates values against, at template, install and upgrade:

--set replicaCount=two       → Error: at '/replicaCount': got string, want integer
--set imagePullPolicy=Always → Error: values don't meet the schema   (additionalProperties: false rejects the typo)
helm install bad … --set replicaCount=two → INSTALLATION FAILED: values don't meet the schema

The schema turns "the chart does something odd with a wrong value" into "install fails with a clear message". additionalProperties: false is the most useful line: it rejects a mistyped value key (imagePullPolicy at the top level instead of image.pullPolicy), which is otherwise silently ignored. A schema cannot catch a typo in the template (a reference to .Values.appName that no one defined renders empty), so helpers and review still matter.

Rule Ship a values.schema.json with types, required, enums and additionalProperties: false, and rely on it to reject bad and misspelled values.

Why The schema validates every values source (defaults, files, --set) before anything is applied, turning wrong values into a failed command.

Trap A value set with --set foo.bar=x has no effect and no warning. The key is not where the chart reads it. additionalProperties: false in the schema would have rejected it.

Rung 5 Install, test, upgrade, roll back

A Helm release is a named, versioned installation. Each install/upgrade is a revision, and rollback goes back to one:

helm install pantry ./chart -n k10 --wait   → STATUS deployed, REVISION 1, 3 web pods + redis-0 Running
helm test pantry -n k10                      → TEST SUITE pantry-test, Phase Succeeded
helm upgrade pantry ./chart --set image.tag=d05 → REVISION 3, image pantry-manual:d05
helm rollback pantry 2 -n k10                → "Rollback was a success"; image back to pantry-manual:1.1.0

helm install pantry ./chart -n k10 --wait --timeout 3m
helm test pantry -n k10                       # runs the test hooks
helm history pantry -n k10                    # revisions
helm rollback pantry <revision> -n k10
helm uninstall pantry -n k10

--wait makes install and upgrade block until the workloads are ready (Helm 4 uses kstatus to decide), and fail otherwise, which is what a deploy pipeline wants. A test hook (helm.sh/hook: test) is a Pod Helm runs on helm test, for a smoke check against the live release. Helm stores each revision's manifests, so rollback re-applies an earlier one exactly.

Rule Install and upgrade with --wait, provide a helm test smoke check, and treat helm rollback as the recovery path, with chart revisions bumped so history is meaningful.

Why Releases and revisions give Kubernetes deployments the one thing raw kubectl apply lacks: a recorded, reversible history.

Trap helm upgrade --wait reports failure but the old Pods still serve, and a plain helm upgrade would have reported success while the new version crash-looped. Always --wait, and helm rollback on failure.

Rung 6 Kustomize: base plus overlays, no templating

Kustomize takes plain manifests (a base) and transforms them per environment (overlays) with patches, name prefixes, namespaces, image tags and replica counts. No templating language:

kubectl kustomize overlays/dev  → namespace pantry-dev,  replicas 1, image pantry-manual:d05
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod → namespace pantry-prod, replicas 5, image pantry-manual:1.1.0, + startup/liveness probes
kubectl apply -k overlays/dev   → deployment "pantry" successfully rolled out

Overlays set structured fields natively: images rewrites tags and digests, replicas sets counts, namespace moves everything, and patches apply strategic-merge or JSON 6902 patches. A strategic-merge patch (above) names only the fields it changes, and merges container lists by name, so adding two probes to the web container needs only those probes. kubectl apply -k and kubectl kustomize are built into kubectl; the standalone kustomize binary has the newest features. Prefer labels: over the deprecated commonLabels, with includeSelectors: false so the immutable selector is left alone.

Rule Keep a clean base and small overlays, use the typed transformers (images, replicas, namespace) for structured changes and strategic-merge patches for the rest, and leave selectors out of label transformers.

Why Kustomize layers plain YAML without a templating language, so the base stays valid and reviewable and each overlay shows exactly its environment's diff.

Trap kubectl apply -k fails with field is immutable on the selector. A labels/commonLabels transformer added labels to the selector too. Set includeSelectors: false.

Rung 7 Choosing between them, and hooks

You want Helm Kustomize
Distribute to others strong (chart repos, versioning) weaker (share a git ref)
Per-environment values values-<env>.yaml overlays
Validation of inputs values.schema.json none (plain YAML)
Release history and rollback built in none (git + kubectl apply)
Conditionals and loops templating none (that is the point)
Readable output helm template kubectl kustomize
Learning curve a templating language just YAML + patches 
helm template pantry ./chart > rendered.yaml        # then a kustomization with resources: [rendered.yaml]
kustomize build .                                   # applies overlays on top

Many teams use both: Kustomize overlays on the manifests Helm renders (a kustomization whose resources is Helm's output), or a GitOps tool doing exactly that (the next chapter is debugging; Argo CD is Act III of the story). Helm hooks (helm.sh/hook: pre-install, post-upgrade, test) run Jobs at points in a release's life, for migrations and smoke tests. Use them sparingly: a hook that fails can wedge a release, and much of what hooks were used for (ordering, waiting) is better done with init containers, --wait and native sidecars (K2).

Rule Choose Helm when you distribute charts or need release history and input validation, Kustomize when you want plain, un-templated YAML, and combine them rather than reinventing either.

Why They solve different problems: Helm packages and versions a configurable application, Kustomize layers edits onto static manifests.

Trap A chart is so full of {{ if }} and nested values that no one can read helm template output. The configuration surface grew without limit. Split it, or switch the parts that only differ by field values to overlays.

Decide

Situation Tool
Internal app, a few environments Kustomize (simplest)
App shipped to other teams/customers Helm (versioned chart)
Needs input validation Helm + values.schema.json
Needs rollback by command Helm releases
Third-party app to tweak Kustomize overlay on their manifests, or a Helm chart's values
GitOps either, applied by Argo CD (the GitOps chapter)

The golden file

Pantry as a Helm chart: schema-validated values, helpers for the recommended labels and names, the full golden workload from K1–K9 as templates, an HPA that owns the replica count, a test hook, and the Kustomize equivalent alongside for comparison. The complete chart and overlays are under examples/manual/k10/.

helm lint ./chart
helm install pantry ./chart -n k10 --create-namespace --wait          # image default is appVersion 1.1.0
helm test pantry -n k10
helm upgrade pantry ./chart -n k10 --set image.tag=d05 --wait
helm rollback pantry 1 -n k10                                          # back to 1.1.0
kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/prod                              # the Kustomize equivalent

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A Deployment template from a chart pull request. The chart ships the values.schema.json above.

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. app: {{ .Values.appName }} references a value that does not exist (the key is not in the schema or values.yaml), so it renders app: empty. A schema cannot catch a template typo, only a values one. Use the pantry.labels helper.
  2. resources: {{ .Values.resources }} emits the resources map as Go's map[cpu:100m ...], which fails the render (error converting YAML to JSON). Use {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}.
  3. image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }} with the default empty tag renders pantry-manual: (no tag). Fall back to appVersion with a helper (default .Chart.AppVersion).
  4. The labels and selector are hand-written app: pantry instead of the recommended app.kubernetes.io/* helpers, and replicas is hardcoded even though the chart's HPA manages it. Use the helpers, and omit replicas when autoscaling is enabled.

Kubernetes manual · 11 · 8 min readDebugging#

In the story: reading the status words when the city stops cooperating · The Night It Fell Over, Again

When a workload will not run, Kubernetes almost always says why, in an event, a status field, or a log line. Debugging is knowing where it says it and in what order to look, so you reach the cause in four commands instead of forty. This chapter is a fixed triage order, the handful of commands that answer each step, and kubectl debug for the Pods that have no shell. Every output below comes from a namespace with five deliberately broken workloads.

The ladder

Rung 1 Events first, always

Most failures announce themselves as events. Read the namespace's warnings newest-last before anything else:

kubectl -n k11 get events --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl -n k11 describe pod <name>        # the Events: section at the bottom is per-object

FailedScheduling   toobig     0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu
Failed             badimage   Failed to pull image "pantry-manual:v9.9.9-does-not-exist": … pull access denied
BackOff            crasher    Back-off restarting failed container c
Unhealthy          pantry     Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

Four different failures, each named in one line. kubectl get events is the namespace-wide view; the Events section of kubectl describe pod is the per-object view and usually the richer one. Events expire (an hour by default), so a problem that is hours old may need describe on the object instead. kubectl events --for deploy/pantry filters to one object's events.

Rule Start every investigation with the warning events, namespace-wide then on the specific object, before reading any logs or YAML.

Why The kubelet, scheduler and controllers report why they could not do something as events, so the cause is usually there in plain words.

Trap Time is lost reading logs for a Pod that never started. There are no application logs because there is no running container. kubectl describe pod shows a scheduling or image-pull event instead.

Rung 2 Read the Pod's status and phase

kubectl get pods plus the right columns tells you which stage failed. A STATUS word maps to a stage (Old Maps and chapter 15 list the full set):

kubectl -n k11 get pods -o wide
kubectl -n k11 get pod <name> -o custom-columns=\
PHASE:.status.phase,READY:.status.containerStatuses[0].ready,\
WAITING:.status.containerStatuses[0].state.waiting.reason,\
LASTEXIT:.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.exitCode

badimage   Pending   false   ImagePullBackOff   -
crasher    Running   false   <none>             1       (restarts: 5)
toobig     Pending   <none>  <none>             -
pantry     Running   false   <none>             -       (readiness 503)
  • Pending with ImagePullBackOff/ErrImagePull: the image. Check the tag, registry and imagePullSecrets (K9).
  • Pending with no container status: scheduling. describe shows FailedScheduling (requests, taints, affinity, K5).
  • CrashLoopBackOff / Running with climbing restarts and lastExit: the container exits. Go to its logs (rung 3).
  • Running but not Ready: the readiness probe (rung 5), often a dependency.
  • CreateContainerConfigError / CreateContainerError: the spec, a missing ConfigMap/Secret key (K6), or a Pod Security violation (K3).

Rule Read phase, ready, the waiting reason and the last exit code to place the failure at a stage, then use the command for that stage.

Why Each stage (schedule, pull, start, become ready) fails with a distinct status, so the status tells you which command answers next.

Trap A Pod is "stuck" and the fix depends on which Pending it is. Image pull and unschedulable both show Pending; the container status (or its absence) and describe separate them.

Rung 3 Logs, and the previous container's logs

For a container that ran and exited, its current logs may be empty (it is restarting); the previous container's logs hold the crash:

kubectl -n k11 logs <pod>                      # the current container
kubectl -n k11 logs <pod> --previous           # the one that just crashed  ← the useful one for CrashLoop
kubectl -n k11 logs <pod> -c <container>        # a specific container (init, sidecar, K2)
kubectl -n k11 logs deploy/pantry --all-pods --tail=20   # across a Deployment's Pods

$ kubectl -n k11 logs crasher-… --previous
starting
config missing

The crasher exits 1 after printing config missing, which is the whole story. For init containers and sidecars, name the container with -c (a Pod stuck in Init: logs its init container, K2). --timestamps and --since=5m narrow a noisy log, and --all-pods/-l <selector> reads across a Deployment.

Rule For a crashing container, read logs --previous, and name the container with -c for init containers and sidecars.

Why A restarting container's current logs are from the new, not-yet-crashed instance; the previous instance's logs hold the failure.

Trap kubectl logs is empty or says container … is waiting to start, and the crash is invisible. Add --previous, or the container never started (go back to rung 2).

Rung 4 kubectl debug: a shell when the Pod has none

Hardened images (D4, D5) have no shell, so kubectl exec … sh fails. kubectl debug attaches an ephemeral container with its own tools to the running Pod, sharing its network and (optionally) process namespace. In a restricted namespace the debug container must itself be compliant, which --profile=restricted arranges:

kubectl -n k11 debug <pod> -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13 --target=web --profile=restricted

# inside the ephemeral container, in the Pod's network namespace:
nslookup redis   →  ** server can't find redis: NXDOMAIN
curl localhost:8080/livez  →  200

# without a profile, in a restricted namespace:
Error from server (Forbidden): … violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.37": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false …

--target=web shares the target container's process namespace (so ps shows its processes). The ephemeral container cannot be removed, so it adds a little clutter until the Pod is replaced. For a Pod that crashes before you can look, --copy-to makes an editable copy with a changed command that stays up:

kubectl -n k11 debug crasher-… --copy-to crasher-debug --container c --image=busybox:1.37-musl \
  --profile=restricted -- sh -c 'sleep 600'

crasher-debug   1/1   Running        ← a copy with the command overridden, safe to exec into; the original keeps crashing

Rule Debug shell-less Pods with kubectl debug … --profile=restricted (ephemeral container), and crash-looping Pods with --copy-to and an overridden command, instead of adding tools to production images.

Why Ephemeral containers bring debugging tools into the Pod's namespaces without changing the image, and a profile keeps them compliant with Pod Security.

Trap kubectl debug fails with a Pod Security violation, or the debug container cannot do what you need. Add --profile=restricted (or --profile=sysadmin for node debugging), matching the namespace's enforcement.

Rung 5 Service, DNS and NetworkPolicy (the K8 layer)

When Pods are Ready but traffic does not flow, the problem is in the networking layer (K8), diagnosed from an ephemeral or throwaway Pod in the right namespace. The order is endpoints, then DNS, then connect:

kubectl -n k11 get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pantry -o yaml   # any ready endpoints?
# from a debug/throwaway pod:
nslookup pantry.k11.svc.cluster.local            # does the name resolve?
nc -zv pantry 80                                 # does the port connect?

Service selector {app: pantry-web} vs Pod labels {app: pantry}  →  EndpointSlice endpoints: null
pantry Pod readiness /healthz  →  503 (Redis absent), so even a correct selector would have no *ready* endpoint

Two independent faults here: a selector typo (no endpoints at all) and a failing readiness probe (no ready endpoints). An empty EndpointSlice means the selector matches nothing or nothing is Ready; a Connection refused means no endpoints; a timeout means a NetworkPolicy is dropping the packet (K8, rung 7). DNS NXDOMAIN from inside the cluster means the wrong name, the wrong namespace, or a missing DNS egress rule.

Rule For "Pods are Ready but requests fail", check EndpointSlices, then DNS, then connectivity, and read refused as no-endpoint and timeout as blocked-by-policy.

Why The networking failure is always one of selector/readiness (no endpoints), DNS (wrong name or blocked), or policy (dropped), and each has a distinct signature.

Trap A Service "is down" and every Pod is healthy. Its selector does not match the Pods' labels, so kubectl get endpointslices is empty. Compare the Service selector with the Pod labels.

Rung 6 Node and cluster-level tools

A few commands for when the problem is below the Pod:

kubectl debug node/manual-worker -it --image=busybox:1.37-musl --profile=sysadmin \
  -- nsenter --target 1 --mount df -h /          # a privileged pod in the node's namespaces
kubectl get --raw '/healthz?verbose'             # is the API server itself healthy?
kubectl get pods -v=6                            # the HTTP requests kubectl makes (bump to -v=8 for bodies)
kubectl top nodes ; kubectl top pods -n k11      # live CPU/memory (needs metrics-server)
kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail

node debug → node hostname manual-worker; overlay 1007G 67G 889G 7% /    (the node's real root filesystem)
get --raw /healthz?verbose → healthz check passed
get pods -v=6 → GET https://…/api/v1/namespaces/k11/pods?limit=500

kubectl debug node/<name> runs a Pod in the node's namespaces to inspect its disk, processes and network. -v=6/-v=8 show exactly what kubectl sends, which is how you turn "kubectl does something odd" into a concrete request. kubectl top needs metrics-server (K5). Cluster-wide warning events catch problems that are not in the namespace you were looking at.

Rule Drop to node debugging (kubectl debug node/), get --raw and -v=6 only after the Pod-level triage has placed the problem below the application.

Why These inspect the node, the API server and kubectl itself, which matters only once the ordinary Pod-level signals have ruled out the application.

Trap An investigation jumps straight to node internals for a problem that kubectl describe pod already explained. Exhaust the events and status first.

Rung 7 The reusable triage order

The whole order, as a script you can keep: warning events, the not-Ready Pods, then each one's newest warning and last log line.

== pods that are not Ready ==
badimage   Pending   false   ImagePullBackOff   -   0
crasher    Running   false   -                  1   5
pantry     Running   false   -                  -   0
toobig     Pending   -       -                  -   -

Running it against the broken namespace surfaces all five failures in one pass, each at the right stage. In practice the first screen of its output names the cause most of the time, and the rungs above are how you follow the one line that matters.

Rule Keep a read-only triage script that prints warning events and the not-Ready Pods with their reasons, and run it first on any misbehaving namespace.

Why A fixed first pass over events and Pod status finds the stage of every failure at once, so you spend your attention on the cause, not on remembering which command to run.

Trap Each incident starts from scratch with half-remembered commands. A saved triage script makes the first five minutes identical and fast every time.

Decide

Symptom Look at
Pending, ImagePullBackOff tag, registry, imagePullSecrets (K9)
Pending, no container status describe → FailedScheduling: requests, taints, affinity (K5)
CrashLoopBackOff logs --previous, then exit code and command
CreateContainerConfigError missing ConfigMap/Secret key (K6), or PSA violation (K3)
Running, not Ready readiness probe and its dependency (K4)
Ready, but requests fail EndpointSlices → DNS → NetworkPolicy (K8)
No shell to exec into kubectl debug … --profile=restricted
Crashes before you can look kubectl debug --copy-to … -- sleep
Node-level suspicion kubectl debug node/…, kubectl top
"kubectl does something odd" -v=6/-v=8, get --raw

The golden file

A read-only triage script: warning events, the Pods that are not Ready, and for each its newest warning and last (or previous) log line. Run it first on any namespace that is misbehaving.

kubectl apply -f broken.yaml        # five planted failures in namespace k11
./triage.sh k11                     # one pass names all five

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A Deployment and its Service. Symptom: the Pod never becomes Ready, and curl to the Service hangs. Name why, by reading (you can apply it and run ./triage.sh k11-bug).

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. image: pantry-manual:latest is not in the cluster (and :latest is unpinned, K2): the Pod sits in ImagePullBackOff. Pin a tag that exists.
  2. The readiness probe targets port: 80, but the container listens on 8080. Even with the image fixed, readiness would fail with connection refused. Use port: 8080 (or a named port).
  3. The Service selector is {app: web} while the Pod's label is {app: pantry}, so the EndpointSlice is empty and curl to the Service hangs with no backend. Match the labels.
  4. /healthz checks Redis (via REDIS_HOST=redis), but no Redis Deployment or Service exists, so once the image and probe port are fixed the probe still returns 503 and nslookup redis is NXDOMAIN. Deploy Redis (or point readiness at /livez, K4).

Part IV · 6 min readThe Bridge#

You have written a hardened Dockerfile and a Compose project (the Docker manual), and a namespace of manifests (the Kubernetes manual). This chapter connects them. Almost everything the Docker manual taught has a direct counterpart in Kubernetes: the same intent, a different field, and usually one thing that changes in meaning on the way across. Read a row as "what I wrote in Docker → where it lives in Kubernetes → the catch".

The links point to the manual chapter on each side.

The image: build once, run anywhere

The image is the one thing that crosses unchanged. A well-built image (small, non-root, signal-correct, pinned) is exactly what makes the Kubernetes side easy: runAsNonRoot just works, probes are simple, and restricted admits the Pod on the first try.

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
FROM, multi-stage, distroless (D4) the image reference, spec.containers[].image (K2) identical image; a smaller, non-root image makes the restricted standard (K3) trivial to meet
image@sha256: digest pin (D6) image: repo@sha256: (K2) same digest; Kubernetes adds imagePullPolicy and imagePullSecrets (K9)
docker buildx multi-platform (D6) nodes of each architecture; the index is pulled per node (K2) the registry serves the right variant to each node automatically

Running the process

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
ENTRYPOINT (D2) command (K2) same idea; command replaces the image's entrypoint
CMD (D2) args (K2) same; command without args drops the image's CMD too
ENV / --env (D1) env, envFrom (K2), from ConfigMaps (K6) read once at start, both places; a config change is a rollout (K4)
--user / USER 10001 (D5) securityContext.runAsUser / runAsNonRoot (K3) numeric UID is required, not just preferred: runAsNonRoot rejects a named user
--read-only + --tmpfs /tmp (D5) readOnlyRootFilesystem: true + an emptyDir (K3) a memory emptyDir is the tmpfs, and it counts against the memory limit (K5)
--cap-drop ALL / --security-opt no-new-privileges (D5) capabilities.drop: [ALL], allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (K3) same, plus seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault is required by restricted
--init / tini as PID 1 (D2) usually unnecessary; shareProcessNamespace or a native sidecar for helpers (K2) one container per concern, so PID 1 reaping rarely bites
STOPSIGNAL + stop timeout (D2) terminationGracePeriodSeconds + preStop (K4) the grace period covers preStop and the app's drain, then SIGKILL (exit 137 either way)

Health, lifecycle and scaling

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
HEALTHCHECK (D1) readinessProbe and livenessProbe (K4) Kubernetes ignores the image's HEALTHCHECK; and one healthcheck becomes two probes with different jobs
Compose depends_on: service_healthy (D9) initContainers that wait + readiness; the app still retries (K2, K4) ordering is best-effort; the app must survive a dependency that leaves later
depends_on: service_completed_successfully (D9) an init container, or a Job the app waits on (K2) one-shot setup becomes an init container or a Job
restart: unless-stopped (D9) a Deployment (restartPolicy: Always) (K4) the controller also reschedules onto another node when one dies
deploy.replicas / --scale (D10) spec.replicas, or an HPA that owns it (K5) real horizontal scaling across nodes, autoscaled on CPU
deploy.resources.limits (D10) resources.requests and resources.limits (K5) requests (what Compose had no concept of) drive scheduling and QoS
rolling restart by hand RollingUpdate strategy, rollout (K4) zero-downtime rollouts and rollout undo are built in

Networking

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
user-defined network + service name DNS (D7) a Service and its name.namespace DNS (K8) the Service IP is stable while Pods come and go
-p 8000:8080 publish (D7) a Gateway + HTTPRoute (or a LoadBalancer) (K8) routing by hostname/path, TLS, and a role split across teams
EXPOSE / Compose expose (D1) containerPort (documentation) + a named Service port (K8) both are documentation; membership, not expose, controls reachability
--internal network (D7) a default-deny NetworkPolicy + explicit allows (K8) isolation is an allow-list, and DNS egress must be allowed explicitly
127.0.0.1: bind to avoid exposure (D7) ClusterIP (never published) (K8) internal services are simply never put behind a Gateway

Data and configuration

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
named volume (D8) a PersistentVolumeClaim (K7) a StorageClass provisions it; access modes and reclaim policy are explicit
tmpfs mount (D8) emptyDir with medium: Memory (K7) same, and it counts against the memory limit (K5)
bind mount for data a PVC, or emptyDir for scratch (K7) Pods move between nodes, so a host path is not portable
Redis with a named volume a StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates + headless Service (K7) stable per-replica identity, storage and DNS
Compose configs (D10) a ConfigMap mounted as files or env (K6) env never updates; a file directory does; roll it with hashed names
Compose secrets file (D10) a Secret in a projected volume (K6) access-controlled, not encrypted; set fsGroup for a non-root reader
--secret build mount (D6) build-time, so it stays in CI, not the cluster (D6) build secrets never become Kubernetes objects

Project structure and operations

Docker / Compose Kubernetes What changes
compose.yaml + compose.override.yaml (D10) a base + Kustomize overlays, or a Helm chart's values (K10) per-environment differences become overlays or values, versioned
Compose profiles (D10) separate manifests, a Helm value, or a Kustomize component (K10) optional pieces are toggled by values or overlay membership
x- anchors / extends (D10) Helm helpers (_helpers.tpl) or Kustomize bases (K10) reuse moves from YAML anchors to templates or bases
docker compose up --wait (D9) kubectl rollout status / helm install --wait (K4, K10) the deploy gate that fails on a bad rollout
docker compose logs / exec / ps kubectl logs / exec / kubectl debug (K11) a shell-less image needs kubectl debug, not exec
docker compose config (D9) kubectl apply --dry-run=server + kubectl diff (K01) the server validates against admission and current state, not just syntax
--cpus / docker stats requests/limits + kubectl top (K5) requests are new: a reservation, not just a ceiling

What has no clean equivalent

A few things do not map one to one:

  • Compose has no requests. It only has limits (deploy.resources). Kubernetes requests (the reservation the scheduler honours, and the basis of QoS and autoscaling, K5) have no Compose counterpart, and they are the single biggest new idea when crossing over.
  • Kubernetes ignores the image's HEALTHCHECK and STOPSIGNAL entirely. Both have to be re-expressed as probes (K4) and terminationGracePeriodSeconds + preStop. An image that relies on them behaves differently under Kubernetes.
  • Pod Security, RBAC and ServiceAccounts (K3, K9) have no Compose analogue at all. A single-host Compose project trusts whoever can reach the Docker socket; a cluster is multi-tenant, so identity and admission are first-class.
  • The node and the scheduler (K5) have no equivalent either. Compose runs everything on one host; affinity, taints, spread and priority exist because Kubernetes places Pods across many.
  • Going the other way, Compose's developer conveniences (develop.watch, D10) have no built-in Kubernetes equivalent; tools like Tilt or Skaffold fill that gap, and a local Compose remains the fastest inner loop even for teams that deploy to Kubernetes.

The rule across the whole bridge: the image and the intent carry over; Kubernetes adds a scheduler, multi-tenancy and a controller that keeps reconciling, and it drops two image-level features (HEALTHCHECK, STOPSIGNAL) that you must restate as Pod fields.
